questions.question: How does the Sarek workflow architecture address the dual needs of computational reproducibility and scientific best practices in variant calling?
questions.expected_answer:
Reproducibility: Sarek is implemented in Nextflow and adheres to the nf-core portability and documentation guidelines. To ensure reproducibility, all required tools are installed in Conda and pushed to DockerHub, so Sarek and its dependencies can be used from a Conda environment or as Docker or Singularity containers. Nextflow downloads the specified pipeline version (2.5.2) from GitHub with the corresponding container, and fetches the reference files from AWS-iGenomes. A small test dataset and a suite of tests verify the installation, and they are also used for Continuous Integration testing with GitHub Actions. The complete run was executed by a single command with no manual intervention. The paper concludes that, thanks to its design, Sarek installs easily and reproducibly on all POSIX compatible systems. The abstract adds that support for Docker and Singularity containers as well as Conda environments makes Sarek ideal for easy deployment on any POSIX-compatible computers and cloud compute environments.

Best practice: Sarek follows the GATK best-practice recommendations for read alignment and pre-processing (BWA-MEM alignment, then GATK deduplication and recalibration). Beyond pre-processing, it includes a wide range of software for the identification and annotation of both germline and somatic variants. Its tools are selected for being high quality, well-maintained and robust. It generates a wide range of quality control metrics, aggregated across samples with MultiQC. Using the intersection of GATK4 Mutect2 and Strelka2, Sarek gave F1 score = 0.80 for SSMs and 0.58 for SIMs. That is in the top range of the 18 somatic variant calling procedures in the original benchmarking study, which indicates that the workflow operates as intended. The paper sets two limits. Sarek leaves it to the user to combine and filter results from different callers. Careful parameter tuning, downstream variant filtering and qualitative assessment by the user remain important.

questions.expected_answer: The intersection of GATK4 Mutect2 and Strelka2 gave an F1 score of 0.80 for SSMs. Table 3 gives the same F1-score, 0.80, with recall 0.74 and precision 0.88 against the SSM Gold Set (n=1263).

questions.question: How does Snakemake's implementation of a blockchain-style hashing scheme facilitate cross-workflow result caching?
questions.expected_answer: Snakemake uses workflow-inherent information to calculate a hash value for each job, prior to actually generating the file. The hash captures exactly how the output file is generated. For a job eligible for caching, the hash is a SHA-256 hash value calculated from the job's code, parameters, raw input files and software environment, plus the hashes of its dependencies. The scheme is blockchain-style because the hash function is applied recursively: for each dependency, a hash value is included in the hash of the job, which is the hashing principle behind blockchains. As a result, the hash describes everything that affects the content of the job's output files, including the input generated by jobs it depends on. The output files are stored under this hash in a central cache, such as a folder on the same machine or in a remote storage. If a rule is marked as eligible for caching, Snakemake can obtain its output from the cache when the file has been created before in a different workflow or by a different user on the same system. Subsequent runs of the same job (with the same dependencies) in other workflows can then skip the execution and take the output files directly from the cache. This saves computation time, as well as disk space: on local machines the file can be linked instead of copied. The hash is only descriptive if the workflow developer ensures that the cached result is generated in a deterministic way. For example, downloading from a URL that yields data which may change over time should be avoided.
expected_concepts: prior to actually generating the file
created before in a different workflow

questions.question: Explain the technical approach Snakemake uses to optimize job scheduling and how it handles job submission overhead in cluster or cloud environments.
questions.expected_answer:
Scheduling: Snakemake solves the scheduling problem at the start of execution and again whenever a job finishes and new jobs become pending. The first releases used a greedy scheduler. The current implementation solves a mixed integer linear program (MILP) whenever there are free resources. The MILP optimizes four criteria in lexicographical order: (1) prefer jobs with high priority, (2) maximize the number of used cores (the extent of parallelization), (3) delete existing temporary files as soon as possible, and (4) reduce the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass. The order is enforced by multiplying each criterion sum by a value at least as high as the maximum the terms to its right can reach. Constraint (2) ensures the selection does not exceed the available amount of each resource.

Cluster and cloud: with middleware such as SLURM, PBS, LSF or Kubernetes, Snakemake does not need to govern all resources at a global level. Some resources are handled by the middleware, and constraint (2) can be dropped for them. Snakemake can pass the resource requirements to the middleware, which can use them to choose the best fitting machine. By default runtime, threads, memory and disk usage are local resources passed to the middleware; all other resources are global and are still governed by Snakemake via constraint (2). The number of jobs queued or running at a time is limited by the same kind of constraint.

Submission overhead: by default every job is submitted separately to the queuing system. For short-running jobs this can cause considerable overhead, as jobs wait in a queue, and may add delays or cost when accessing files from remote storage or network file systems. To minimize it, Snakemake can partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs by assigning rules to groups. Connected subgraphs with the same group are submitted together as a single cluster or cloud job (a group job) instead of each job separately. For each group, the number of connected subgraphs spanned per submission can be defined (one by default), so the partition size can be adjusted to the computational platform. A group job's resource usage is computed by sorting its jobs topologically, summing resource usage per level and taking the maximum over all levels. For runtime it is the other way round: the maximum per level, summed over all levels.
expected_concepts: maximize the number of used cores
partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs

questions.question: How does the nf-core/sarek 3.1.1 pipeline leverage architectural and methodological changes to optimize cost and performance for large-scale data analysis?
questions.expected_answer:
nf-core/sarek 3.1.1 is a full rewrite as a modular re-implementation in the Nextflow DSL2 framework, focused on reducing required compute resources. The abstract names two main changes: the CRAM format for storage and increased intra-sample parallelization for runtime.

Parallelization: FastQ files are split into shards with fastP (optional adapter trimming) and mapped in parallel, so alignment runs on smaller machines. Median mapping runtime falls to 37%, with a plateau at 12 shards. Genomic regions are processed in parallel after duplicate marking, small regions are grouped to reduce the number of jobs, and scatter-gathering covers all applicable variant callers. Runtime was lowest at 21 interval groups. Going from 21 to the 124-group default raised BQSR storage by a factor of five, so the default is being set to 21.

Storage: merging, duplicate marking and CRAM conversion run in one process. CRAM cuts pre-processing work-directory storage by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB), at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage. Less scattering reduces storage by a further factor of 5, which lets the pipeline run on smaller systems.

Other changes: Qualimap is replaced by mosdepth, and a new parameter skips germline-only calling for paired samples. Combining trimming, QC and sharding plus tailored interval splitting reduces CPU hours by 66%.

Cloud: on AWS Batch with spot instances (Tower Forge, fusion mounts), one normal sample cost $20.82 with 3.1.1 against $68.04 with 2.7.2. Runtime fell from 46h8m to 12h4m and CPU hours from 1118.4 to 342.5, a reduction of about 70% in CPU hours and 84% in runtime. The paper states the cost saving four ways: a 70% cost reduction (abstract), a 69% reduction versus 2.7.2 (introduction, about $20 per sample), costs reduced to approximately 30% (Results) and costs reduced to 50% (Discussion). It says this keeps costs and CO2 emissions low but gives no CO2 figure.

questions.expected_answer: Sharding the input FastQ files reduced the median runtime of the mapping processes (fastP, BWA-MEM and GATK4 Markduplicates) to 37%. The overall runtime fell as the number of shards increased, until it reached a plateau at 12 shards.

questions.question: What design choices and implementation strategies allow fastp to achieve higher performance and lower I/O overhead than traditional FASTQ tools?
questions.expected_answer:
fastp is much faster than its peers because of a set of design choices. The paper argues its I/O advantage but never measures I/O.
The problem it addresses: traditional preprocessing chains separate tools (FASTQC, Cutadapt, Trimmomatic), so the data are read and loaded multiple times, which makes preprocessing slow and I/O inefficient; most of those tools are written in Python or Java with limited multi-threading support. The paper states the I/O inefficiency of separate tools in the abstract, the introduction and the UMI preprocessing section (separate UMI tools need individual execution that consumes additional I/O and computational resources), but shows no I/O measurement.
The design choices:
1. All-in-one, single scan: quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering, per-read quality pruning, polyG/polyX tail trimming, UMI preprocessing and other operations run in a single scan of the FASTQ data.
2. Written in C/C++ with a solid multi-threading implementation, which the authors say makes it much faster than its peers.
3. Overall design for multi-threading parallel processing: reads are packed with a size of N = 1000, each pack is consumed by one thread in the pool, each thread keeps an individual context of statistics (per-cycle quality profiles, per-cycle base contents, adapter trimming results, k-mer counts), and these are merged after all reads are processed.
4. UMI preprocessing integrated with little overhead: fastp runs approximately 3 times faster than UMI-tools or umis even when performing other tasks simultaneously (Section 3.3: 2.7 times faster than umis, 6.1 times faster than UMI-tools).
5. Duplication evaluation: duplication keys are stored in a duplication array D and a counting array C instead of FASTQC's hash table, for much faster access, with key2 as a 64-bit long integer for fast comparison.
6. Overrepresented sequence analysis: an efficient two-step method.
Result: fastp is 2–5 times faster than Trimmomatic or Cutadapt despite performing far more operations, measured with all tools on a single thread; in multi-thread mode it may show even higher performance, but no multi-threading comparison is provided. No experiment credits the speed-up to any single design choice.
expected_concepts: single scan of the FASTQ data
read and load data multiple times
packed with a size of N
duplication array D and a counting array C

questions.question: How does fastp's methodology for adapter detection differ between single-end and paired-end sequencing data?
questions.expected_answer: fastp uses different algorithms for the two data types. For single-end data, adapter sequences are detected by assembling the high-frequency read tails: it computes k-mers (k = 10) of the first 1 M reads, takes sequences with occurrence frequency >0.0001 as adapter seeds (low-complexity sequences removed), and extends them with a tree-based algorithm (forward extension to check validity, then backward extension to obtain the complete adapter), assuming only one adapter exists in the data and adapters exist only in read tails. For paired-end data, fastp finds the overlap of each pair (an algorithm derived from AfterQC) and considers the bases that fall out of the overlapped region as adapter content; this overlap analysis can trim adapters with even only one base in the tail. A user-given adapter sequence also behaves differently: for SE data it disables automatic detection; for PE data it is used for sequence-matching-based trimming only when fastp fails to detect a good overlap in the pair.
expected_concepts: finding the overlap of each pair
fall out of the overlapped regions
automatic adapter-sequence detection will be disabled
fails to detect a good overlap

questions.question: How does MultiQC's approach to data presentation assist researchers in identifying quality issues across large-scale projects?
questions.expected_answer: MultiQC scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and builds a single summary report that visualizes output from multiple tools across all samples, so global trends and biases can be identified quickly. Collecting the data in one report gives a fast way to scan key statistics, and a general statistics table gathers metrics from different tools for each sample. Shared plots allow accurate comparison between samples and detection of subtle differences not noticeable when switching between different files. Data visualization aids batch effect detection and minimizes the risk of confounding factors. Plots are resizeable and interactive, and a report toolbox lets samples be renamed, hidden and highlighted; highlighting helps identify groups of samples behaving in an irregular manner. For large projects MultiQC parses data for thousands of samples within minutes and adapts the report output. For reports with hundreds of samples it renders plots as images with MatPlotLib instead of HighCharts. The reports reveal overall analysis success, make abnormal samples easy to identify and give the overview required to spot failing samples. Routine use aids quality control early in data processing, reducing the risk of batch effects and other downstream analysis problems.

questions.question: Which specific software libraries and architectural mechanisms does MultiQC use to handle data visualization and support custom extensions?

Reports with hundreds of samples become too large for HighCharts, so MultiQC switches to rendering plots as images at run-time with the Python plotting library MatPlotLib, and the images are embedded within the HTML to keep a stand-alone file. The final report is rendered from a template parsed with the Jinja2 package. Extensions: MultiQC is built so custom code can be tied into its functionality. Code hooks allow external plugins to access and modify the internal workings of the program, and Python setuptools entry points allow modules, templates and plugins to be kept within a separate code base while still executing as part of the main MultiQC program (example: the MultiQC_NGI plugin).
expected_concepts: Images are embedded within the HTML

It surpasses all other existing RNA-seq aligners by a factor of 50 (the Discussion's figure; the Abstract and Results text layer prints "450", a mis-encoded ">50"), outperforming the second fastest mapper, TopHat2, which reaches 10.1 million read pairs/hour at 12 threads (RUM 7.6, MapSplice 3.1, GSNAP 2.8).

questions.question: How does the Maximum Mappable Prefix (MMP) search mechanism facilitate the identification of diverse sequence features beyond simple genomic mapping?
questions.expected_answer:
STAR runs the MMP search sequentially. It applies the search only to the part of the read that is still unmapped, which finds several kinds of feature:
- Splice junctions: a read with a splice junction cannot be mapped contiguously, so the first seed maps to a donor splice site. The repeated search on the unmapped portion then maps to an acceptor splice site. This gives precise locations of splice junctions in a single alignment pass, with no a priori knowledge of where the junctions are.
- Mismatches and indels: the MMP search enables finding multiple mismatches and indels. When mismatches stop the search before the end of the read, the MMPs serve as anchors in the genome that can be extended.
- Tails: when extension does not yield a good genomic alignment, poly-A tails, library adapter sequences or poor sequencing quality tails are identified.
- Multimapping reads: for each MMP, the suffix-array (SA) search can find all distinct exact genomic matches.
The search runs in both forward and reverse directions and can start from user-defined points in the read. This helps find anchors for reads with errors near the ends. The MMP search itself finds only seeds that match the genome exactly. The stitching procedure that follows aligns reads with many mismatches, indels and splice junctions.

questions.question: How does Salmon's method of bias correction specifically improve the outcomes of differential expression (DE) analysis?
questions.expected_answer:
The paper says that correcting fragment GC content bias improves the reliability of downstream DE analysis. Left uncorrected, such biases can cause high false positive rates in DE studies. With Salmon's estimates, the paper reports:
(1) Higher sensitivity at the same FDR. The main text gives 53% to 250% higher. The Figure 1c legend gives 53%–450% greater than kallisto and 210%–250% greater than eXpress, on Polyester simulated data whose two 8-sample groups differ in fragment GC bias.
(2) Fewer false-positive DE calls. On 30 GEUVADIS samples where the groups differ only by sequencing center (a technical confound), Salmon makes fewer than half as many DE calls as the other methods at an expected FDR of 1%.
(3) At the gene level, the number of genes called DE falls by a factor of about 2.6.
(4) Dominant isoform switching seen with kallisto or eXpress is eliminated under Salmon's GC bias aware estimates, and Salmon reduces the isoform switching rate across thresholds and gene categories.
Caveat: bias correction was enabled for all methods, and the results text credits the gains to the dual-phase inference algorithm and the sample-specific bias models together.

questions.question: Describe the algorithmic components and optimization techniques Salmon uses to achieve speed comparable to ultra-fast alignment-free tools while maintaining accuracy.
questions.expected_answer:
The paper claims that Salmon achieves greater accuracy than tools such as kallisto and eXpress, employs sample-specific bias models (sequence-specific, fragment-GC and positional biases), and achieves the same order-of-magnitude speed benefits as kallisto and Sailfish. Salmon has three components: a lightweight-mapping model, an online phase that estimates initial expression levels and model parameters, and an offline phase that refines the expression estimates.

Speed: mapping uses a built-in, ultra-fast procedure called quasi-mapping. It quantifies raw FASTA/Q reads directly, without intermediate alignment files. This saves considerable time and space, because quasi-mapping is faster than traditional alignment. The online phase is a streaming variant of stochastic, collapsed variational Bayesian inference. It updates read-count estimates after each mini-batch (1,000 alignment groups by default), and mini-batches are processed asynchronously and in parallel. The only synchronization is an atomic compare-and-swap loop that updates the global transcript weights. The paper says that, because the updates are stochastic and additive, this has little-to-no detrimental effect. The updates are also sparse, so they can be performed efficiently. During the online phase Salmon also builds a highly-reduced representation: rich fragment-level equivalence classes, held in a concurrent cuckoo hash map that many threads can query and write with very little contention. The offline phase runs a standard EM algorithm or a variational Bayesian EM algorithm over the equivalence classes until a data-dependent convergence criterion is met. Equivalence classes have been shown to greatly reduce the time needed for this iterative optimization. The auxiliary models are learned from the first 5,000,000 observations by default and then applied to all later ones. Salmon is designed to take advantage of multiple CPU cores.

Accuracy: unlike pseudoalignment, the mapping tracks, by default, the position and orientation of all mapped fragments. The two-phase inference supports a model that includes terms not considered by Sailfish and kallisto. That model covers positional coverage biases, 5′ and 3′ sequence-specific biases, fragment-level GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution. The equivalence-class weights carry the full model's conditional probabilities without revisiting every fragment. The extra cost of bias correction is typically small (full bias modeling added 119 seconds with 16 threads on sample ERR188021), and its learning and application are parallelized. Its cost scales with the number of expressed transcripts rather than reads, and stored cumulative GC counts per transcript make GC computation efficient.

Result: Salmon quantified about 600 million 75 bp paired-end reads in about 23 minutes (1384 seconds) using 30 threads. On the same machine with the same number of threads, kallisto took about 20 minutes (1198 seconds).
expected_concepts: quasi-mapping is faster than traditional alignment

questions.question: In the reproducibility analysis where a dataset was split into two independent halves, what specific improvement in the overlap of the top 100 genes was observed when using shrunken MAP estimates compared to standard MLE estimates?
questions.expected_answer: The Bottomly et al. samples were split into two groups, I and II. Ranking genes by unshrunken LFC estimates found only 21 of group I's top 100 up- or down-regulated genes among group II's top 100. Ranking by shrunken LFC estimates raised the overlap to 81 of 100 genes. The paper calls the shrunken MAP LFCs a more reproducible quantification than standard MLE LFCs.

questions.question: How does the DESeq2 framework utilize Empirical Bayes shrinkage to handle the high uncertainty associated with low-count genes in both dispersion and fold change estimation?
questions.expected_answer:
Both shrinkage steps follow one principle: empirical Bayes priors set the amount of shrinkage from the amount of information the data carry for the estimated quantity.

Dispersion: with two or three replicates, the dispersion estimates for each gene are highly variable. DESeq2 assumes that genes of similar average expression strength have similar dispersion. It first gets gene-wise maximum-likelihood estimates, then fits a smooth curve against average expression strength. It shrinks the gene-wise estimates toward the values predicted by the curve, combining the likelihood with the trended prior to give maximum a posteriori (MAP) dispersion estimates. The strength of shrinkage depends on how close true dispersion values tend to be to the fit, and on the degrees of freedom. It decreases as the sample size increases. The width of the prior is estimated from the data, and the fitted curve aids estimation in less information-rich settings. Estimates below the curve are raised, which helps avoid false positives from underestimated dispersion. A gene-wise estimate more than 2 residual standard deviations above the curve is used instead of the shrunken one. On low counts, the paper says that when μ ≲1/α the observed data provide little information on α, so the sampling variance of the estimator is large. Overestimating α in that low-count range has little effect on inference, because the Poisson component dominates the variance there.

Fold change: LFC estimates have strong variance for genes with low read count, because ratios are noisier when counts are low. DESeq2 fits ordinary GLMs to get maximum-likelihood estimates (MLEs) of the LFCs, then fits a zero-centered normal distribution to the MLEs over all genes. That distribution is the prior in a second round of GLM fits, and the MAP estimates are kept as the final LFCs. Shrinkage toward zero is stronger when a gene has little information, because counts are low, dispersion is high or there are few degrees of freedom. The amount of information is indicated by the observed Fisher information, not simply by the mean count. Such genes have flatter profile likelihoods, so the zero-centered prior pulls the high-uncertainty MLE closer to zero. This removes the problem of exaggerated LFCs for low counts. For genes with less than one read per sample on average, LFCs hardly deviate from zero. The paper describes this as a bias-variance trade-off: lower variance in exchange for a bias toward zero. As the degrees of freedom increase, the shrunken estimates converge to the unshrunken estimates.

questions.question: What is the specific purpose of the regularized logarithm (rlog) transformation, and how does its performance compare to an ordinary log transformation in terms of variance stabilization?
questions.expected_answer: Purpose: the rlog transforms RNA-seq data to render them homoskedastic. On the original count scale, results would be dominated by highly expressed, highly variable genes. With logarithm-transformed data, undue weight goes to weakly expressed genes, which show exaggerated LFCs. The rlog thus facilitates multivariate visualization and ordinations such as clustering or principal component analysis, heat maps, and machine-learning techniques that require homoskedastic input data. It uses the shrinkage approach of DESeq2. For genes with high counts it behaves similarly to a log2 transformation, and for genes with low counts it shrinks together the values for different samples. This avoids the standard logarithm's spreading apart of data for genes with low counts. Comparison: after the rlog, gene variances are stabilized (approximately the same, or homoskedastic); otherwise they would strongly depend on the mean counts. On the Hammer et al. dataset (Figure 5), the gene-wise standard deviation is variable across the range of the mean of counts under the ordinary logarithm with a pseudocount of 1, log2(Kij/sj + 1), while relatively stable using the rlog. The comparison is qualitative, with no numeric measure in the text.
expected_concepts: strongly depend on the mean counts
ordinary logarithm with a pseudocount of 1
variable across the range of the mean of counts

questions.question: How does SeqKit achieve stable memory usage and efficiency when processing datasets that are significantly larger than the human genome?
questions.expected_answer: Most SeqKit subcommands do not load all FASTA/Q records into memory. Removing duplicate sequences by content does need whole sequences in memory, so SeqKit uses an MD5 digest to represent sequence content, which greatly reduces memory usage. Some subcommands ("sample", "split", "shuffle" and "sort" on page 4; "subseq", "split", "sort" and "shuffle" on page 3) read the files twice in two-pass mode, which uses the FASTA index for rapid access of sequences and reduces memory usage (FASTA format only). The sequence parser uses a custom buffered file reading algorithm instead of Go's "bufio", which increased speed and significantly lowered memory usage. Most CPU-intensive processes are parallelized by multiple Goroutines. In tests on files made by repeating human chromosome 1 N times, memory stayed at approximately 780 Mb for reverse complement and duplicate removal, and peak memory stayed at approximately 750 Mb for shuffling and sorting with the FASTA index. The authors conclude that peak memory usage is determined by the length of the longest sequence record, so SeqKit can handle large FASTA and FASTQ files as data size grows.
expected_concepts: do not load all FASTA/Q records

questions.question: What specific technical optimization was applied to SeqKit's reverse complementation process, and what was the measured performance gain compared to using standard hash maps?
questions.expected_answer: SeqKit replaced Go's built-in map (a hash table), which is inefficient for byte keys and values, with a slice data structure. The slice stores the complementary sequences with the ASCII code of the byte as the indexing key (Algorithm 1). This gave a ~20× speedup relative to the map strategy (Table A in S1 File). Memory usage is also very low because the base alphabet is limited. Reverse complementation of long sequences is also parallelised, but the paper reports no gain figure for that.
expected_concepts: relative to the strategy of map
built-in map data structure of Go

questions.question: How does the implementation of Cutadapt balance the trade-off between user accessibility and computational efficiency?
questions.expected_answer: Cutadapt is mainly written in Python, but for speed the alignment algorithm is implemented in C as a Python extension module. On accessibility, it is a user-friendly, easy-to-use command-line program that supports a variety of file formats, automatically detects gzip compression of input or output files, has full documentation via "cutadapt --help", and should work on any platform for which Python is available. questions.question: In the study of the 2018 African Swine Fever Virus (ASFV) outbreaks, how many blood samples were collected in total and how many of those were confirmed positive for ASFV DNA?
questions.expected_answer: Sixty-two (62) blood samples were collected, and real-time PCR confirmed ASFV DNA in twenty (20) of them.
expected_concepts: confirmed ASFV DNA in twenty samples

questions.question: How did the researchers use multi-gene analysis to establish the genetic identity and classification of the ASFV strains responsible for the outbreaks?
questions.expected_answer:
The researchers characterised four gene targets: the partial P72, the complete p54, the partial CD2v and the partial B602L genes. They sequenced nineteen partial p72 and p54 genes, fourteen partial CD2v genes and twenty partial B602L, and aligned the sequences with MUSCLE in MEGA software version 7. Each gene gave a different level of classification.

Genotype (p72): they built a Neighbor-Joining tree in Mega 7 with the Maximum Composite Likelihood method and 1,000 bootstrap re-samplings. The dataset held 93 nucleotide sequences (398 characters): 19 from this study plus GenBank sequences, with at least one representative of each of the 24 known ASFV genotypes and historical samples from Burkina Faso and neighbouring countries. All 2018 Burkina Faso ASFV clustered within genotype I.

Subgroup (p54): they built a Minimum Evolution tree with the p-distance substitution model and the Close-Neighbor-Interchange (CNI) algorithm. The dataset held 63 taxa (453 characters), including 19 study sequences and representatives of the 18 p72 genotypes for which a p54 sequence is available. All isolates belong to the genotype Ia subgroup. The alignments split them further into two sub-groups by complete p54 length (552 bp and 564 bp).

Serogroup (CD2v): they built a maximum-likelihood tree of the partial CD2v amino acid sequences with the predetermined CpREV + G model. The dataset included representatives of the eight known serogroups and ASFVs clustering outside them. All sequenced isolates belong to serogroup 4. By the number of deleted PCPPPK units, the isolates fell into groups with 0, 2, 3 or 4 missing KPCPPP units. The Abstract and Conclusion instead give five variants based on deleted KCPPPK motifs.

CVR (B602L): each CVR was translated and its tetramers matched with previously reported codes. The 20 CVRs gave four TRS variants, with 32, 24, 23 and 12 TRS.

Combined result: ASFVs of genotype I, serogroup 4, caused four outbreaks in October 2018 in Burkina Faso. CD2v can serve as an additional tool for discriminating ASFV isolates.

questions.question: What specific software and phylogenetic methods were utilized for the analysis of the ASFV sequences, and what variation was found in the Central Variable Region (CVR)?
questions.expected_answer:
Software: the raw sequences were assembled and edited in Vector NTI 11.5 Software. Multiple sequence alignments were done with MUSCLE as implemented in MEGA software version 7.

Phylogenetic methods, one per gene:
- p72: a Neighbor-Joining (NJ) tree built in Mega 7 using the Maximum Composite Likelihood method.
- p54: a Minimum Evolution tree using the p-distance substitution model and the Close-Neighbor-Interchange (CNI) algorithm. The initial tree came from the Neighbor-joining algorithm, and all positions with less than 95% site coverage were removed.
- CD2v: a maximum-likelihood (ML) tree of the partial amino acid sequences using the CpREV + G model.
Each tree was tested with 1000 bootstrap replicates.

CVR: each CVR nucleotide sequence was translated into amino acids, and the tetramers were matched with previously reported codes. The 20 CVRs gave four variants of the tetrameric repeat sequence (TRS), with 32, 24, 23 and 12 TRS. Three of the four shared motifs beginning with "ABNAAA" and ending with "CBNAFA". Where each variant was found:
- 12 TRS: Saaba (the index outbreak), Nioko II and Kossodo.
- 24 TRS: only at Nioko II.
- 23 TRS and 32 TRS: Kossodo.

Tampouy: the Results say the Kossodo 23 TRS pattern was identical to Tampouy's. Table 2 lists the Tampouy isolates as 32 TRS, and the Discussion matches Tampouy to the 32 TRS Kossodo isolate.

All four variants differ from the ten found in samples from 2007 to 2010, which makes fourteen variants identified in the country.
expected_concepts: MUSCLE as implemented in MEGA software version 7
four variants of the tetrameric repeat sequence (TRS)

questions.question: What was the specific percentage increase in the distribution of HPAI outbreaks in meat-type poultry when comparing the 2014–2018 period to the 2020–2022 period?
questions.expected_answer: The paper does not state a single percentage increase. Meat-type poultry farms rose from 6.3% of HPAI-infected farms in 2014–2018 (1 of 16 farms) to 39.5% in 2020–2022 (30 of 76 farms). The change in the distribution of poultry types between the two periods was significant (Fisher's exact test p = 0.01).

questions.question: How do the clinical presentations and mortality detection thresholds of HPAI differ between chicken populations (Galliformes) and duck populations (Anseriformes) according to the study?
questions.expected_answer:
Clinical signs: ducks more often showed neurological (nervous) and locomotor signs and reproductive tract signs. Nervous and locomotor signs were seen on 67.7% of duck farms in the text (66.7% in Table 5), against 48.4% of meat-type and 15.0% of layer-type farms. Reproductive tract signs were seen in 100% of ducks, against 19.4% of layer-type and 28.6% of meat-type farms. Reduced feed intake was also seen mainly in ducks. Layer- and meat-type poultry more often showed mucosal membrane and skin signs, including cyanosis and hemorrhagic conjunctiva (55.0% and 67.8%, against 4.7% of duck farms). These signs were more frequent in juvenile than adult chickens. Respiratory signs were most frequent in meat-type poultry (61.3%, against 37.5% of layers and 23.8% of ducks). Gastrointestinal signs were more frequent in adult than juvenile chickens, and the opposite held in ducks.

Mortality: in both chickens and ducks, mortality increased exponentially within four days before notification. The trend fluctuated more in ducks and meat-type poultry than in layers, and duck mortality showed more peaks. Ducks reached a mortality ratio (MR) > 3 against the previous week's average less often than chickens. The day before notification, 54% of duck farms reached it, against 83% of layer-type and 80% of meat-type chicken farms, but these differences were not statistically significant. Adult ducks reached it least often (0 of 1 farm). In chicken flocks, high mortality was the main reason for notification. In ducks, mortality remained limited, and notifications were more often based on a decrease in feed or water intake or egg production.

Reporting thresholds: the Dutch rules require chickens to be reported at MR > 3, meaning mortality tripled for two consecutive days against the average of the week before. Ducks must be reported at daily mortality >0.15% for two consecutive days, or >0.5% for one day combined with a 5% decrease in feed intake. The literature suggested daily mortality thresholds of 0.13% for layers, >0.17% for broilers and 0.3% for ducks, and a >9% drop in egg production for breeder ducks. The authors conclude that reporting criteria should differ between poultry species and age groups.
expected_concepts: Neurological, locomotor and reproductive tract signs
reached less often than in chickens
decrease in feed or water intake

questions.question: How did the researchers define and calculate the Mortality Ratio (MR) metric used to assess early warning signals on the infected farms?
questions.expected_answer: The MR was calculated from NVWA farm production charts with daily mortality records, which were retrieved for 63 of 92 farms. The percentage of daily mortality was calculated per house. Then 0.1 was added to all percentages so that log10 could be taken, and log10(0.1) = −1 indicated no mortality (0%). For each flock, the MR of the day before notification was calculated using the method described by Gonzales and Elbers (2018). The MR compares mortality with the average mortality of the previous week. The method had also been used by Schreuder et al. (2021), but this study adjusted it slightly, using a threshold of >3 instead of >2.9. This threshold matches Dutch legislation, which requires notification when daily mortality is >3 times the average mortality of the preceding week for two consecutive days. Each farm was scored as increased (MR above the cut-off value of 3), not increased (MR < 3), or unknown/unclear (MR could not be calculated). The MR could not be calculated for 36 of 92 farms.
expected_concepts: average mortality of the previous week

questions.question: What were the overall morbidity, mortality, and case fatality rates recorded during the LSD outbreak in the study area?
questions.expected_answer: In the LSD outbreak in Nawalpur, the overall morbidity rate was 28.02% (431 of 1,538 animals), the mortality rate was 3.06% (47 of 1,538) and the case fatality rate was 10.90% (47 of 431 sick animals; given as 10.9% in the Results text).

questions.question: Based on the epidemiological data, which specific cattle group was most affected by the outbreak and what were the primary clinical manifestations observed?
questions.expected_answer: Dry cattle, including pregnant cows, were the most affected group by morbidity: 47.62% (90 of 189 sick). Cattle calves (33.33%) and heifers (32.73%) came next. The abstract names "dry cattle, including pregnant cows and cattle heifers" as the most affected. Cattle heifers had the highest mortality (5.09%) and case fatality (15.56%). The primary clinical manifestations were skin nodules, reduced milk production and lameness, seen in 97%, 87% and 55% of case farms respectively. Skin nodules were the most predominant sign, and the conclusions also list death.

questions.question: According to the multivariable logistic regression analysis, what was identified as the most significant risk factor for LSD transmission and what were its associated statistical metrics?
questions.expected_answer: Symptoms in neighbor farms (neighboring farms having sick animals) was the only variable significant in the final multivariable logistic regression model: odds ratio 88.45, 95% CI 13.27–589.36, p value <0.001. The other variables in the model were not significant (herd size p 0.434, introduced new animals p 0.143, use of vector control p 0.126, share feed p 0.086). The paper states that the univariable associations of herd size, introduction of new animals, and sharing of feed and water were overshadowed by the presence of symptoms in neighboring farms in the multivariable analysis.

questions.question: What were the specific bovine tuberculosis (bTB) prevalence estimates calculated in this study based on the different diagnostic tests and thresholds used?
questions.expected_answer:
The study tested 160 cattle. Its apparent prevalence estimates, from the Results text and Table-2, are:
- CIDT at a 3 mm threshold: 11 positive, 6.8% (95% CI: 4.35%–9.41%).
- Simple intradermal tuberculin test (SITT) at 4 mm: 3 positive out of 160, 1.8% (95% CI: 0%–3.6%).
- CIDT at 4 mm: 0.6% (95% CI: 0%–1.2%). Table-2 and the first Results sentence give 1 positive, but the Results paragraph and the Discussion give three.
The Abstract swaps the two 4 mm values. It gives 1.8% (0%–3.6%) for CIDT at 4 mm and 0.6% (0%–1.2%) for the simple test (IDT) at 4 mm.
expected_concepts: CIDT performed at a threshold of

questions.question: How does the choice of diagnostic method and skinfold thickness threshold impact the assessment of bTB exposure according to the study's findings?
questions.expected_answer: Both the test and the skinfold-thickness threshold change the estimated prevalence substantially. With CIDT at 3 mm, 11 of 160 cattle were positive, an apparent prevalence of 6.8% (95% CI: 4.35%–9.41%). At the 4 mm threshold (the WOAH positive decision threshold), CIDT gave 0.6% (95% CI: 0%–1.2%). The paper gives that count as 1 positive in Table-2 and as three positives in the prose. SITT at 4 mm found 3 positives out of 160, an AP of 1.8% (95% CI: 0%–3.6%). The Abstract reverses the two 4 mm figures. The authors conclude that the 3 mm threshold increased the sensitivity of bTB detection, and that AP at ≥3 mm was significantly higher than at ≥4 mm for CIDT. At the CIDT 3 mm threshold, body condition score significantly influenced prevalence. They cite an Ethiopian study in which CIDT performed best at a threshold strictly >2 mm, and they recommend applying thresholds of 3 mm in Cameroon rather than 4 mm.
expected_concepts: increased the sensitivity of bTB detection

questions.question: Which specific statistical software and metrics were employed to refine the logistic regression models and verify the independence of the identified risk factors?
questions.expected_answer: The univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were run in R 2.10.0 statistical software (R Core Team). Only variables with p < 0.2 entered the multivariate analysis. The model was refined by a top-down step-by-step analysis using the Akaike information criterion (AIC; the lower the AIC, the better the model): AIC fell from 85.07 in the original model to 45.83, and the procedure stopped when deleting any other variable would increase the AIC. Table-6 (identification of variables with significant effects on the initial model) also reports a likelihood ratio statistic (LRT) per variable, and all possible interactions with the final model were examined. Independence of the risk factors was checked as multi-collinearity with the variance inflation factor (VIF): all VIFs were close to one (forage reason 1, cattle herder 1.212942, age >10 years 1.106897, tuberculous organs seizure 1.172151). The multivariate model reported adjusted ORs (AORs) and p-values. Elsewhere the paper says Microsoft Excel 2010 was used to organize data and IBM SPSS Statistics (version printed as 20.0 and as 27.0) to analyze data.
expected_concepts: all VIFs were close to one

questions.question: How many human rabies deaths were recorded during the study period, and what was observed regarding their treatment status?
questions.expected_answer: 48 human rabies deaths were identified over January 2002 to December 2022, peaking at seven in 2011; deaths occurred every year until 2018, two more in 2019, and none thereafter. None of the 48 completed a full course of post-exposure vaccinations: 3 received one vaccination, 4 received two and the remaining 41 received none.

questions.question: Explain how spatial heterogeneity in vaccination coverage impacts the persistence of rabies even when average coverage targets are met.
questions.expected_answer: The spatial distribution of coverage matters, not only its average. For the same average prior non-focal (wider-district) vaccination coverage, increased heterogeneity in coverage among non-focal villages leads to increased focal incidence. In the power mean susceptibility model, p was estimated to be substantially larger than one. With p>1, the same total number of unvaccinated dogs gives a higher effective susceptibility when those dogs are distributed unevenly. Against homogeneous 40% prior coverage, a 30%/50% split is predicted to raise focal incidence 1.4 (95% CrI: 1.3-1.6) times. A 20%/60% split raises it 2.6 (95% CrI: 1.9-3.4) times. Outbreaks followed multi-year periods when clusters of villages remained unvaccinated. High coverage in a small area has only limited impact if the rest of the population is poorly vaccinated. Spatial heterogeneity in dog vaccination was detrimental for control, and vaccination interrupted endemic circulation only when implemented consistently. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell to <0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually, although mean district coverage stayed relatively low. Two caveats. The effect was seen only once the masking effects of prior non-focal incidence were removed. The estimated p lay beyond the range the authors expected a priori. The premise does not hold for this study: only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target, and vaccination controlled rabies without reaching it.
expected_concepts: masking effects of prior non-focal incidence
high coverage in a small area

questions.question: What methodological approach and software tool were used to distinguish between local rabies transmission and disease incursions, and how did the proportion of incursions change by 2022?
questions.expected_answer: The authors reconstructed transmission trees using the treerabid package in R. The algorithm probabilistically assigned a progenitor to each case with no known rabid biter. A possible progenitor had to have an earlier symptoms onset date, and its serial interval and distance from the case had to be smaller than a selected quantile of those distributions (the pruning threshold). The main analysis used the 97.5% pruning threshold. Where no progenitor qualified, the case was assumed to be an incursion. Probable incursions were the cases identified as an incursion more often than they were assigned to any other progenitor across 1,000 bootstrapped trees. The number of incursions stayed relatively constant (mean of 7 annual incursions). The proportion of cases identified as incursions sharply increased, from 3% pre-2018 to 26% post-2018 (>20% of cases since 2019), and peaked at 50% in 2022.

questions.question: How many total PPR outbreaks were recorded in the Borena Zone between 2018 and 2022, and which specific month saw the highest percentage of these outbreaks?
questions.expected_answer: 53 PPR outbreaks were recorded in the Borena Zone between 2018 and 2022 (9.6% of the 554 outbreaks recorded in Ethiopia). January had the highest share of outbreaks, at 20.8%, followed by December.

questions.question: Why does the study conclude that the current PPR herd immunity in the Borena Zone is insufficient according to international standards?
questions.expected_answer: Herd immunity measured in 128 vaccinated small ruminants was 68.8% (reported as the seroconversion rate). That is below the FAO-WOAH recommended threshold of 80% herd immunity, so the study concludes that herd immunity in vaccinated animals is inadequate. The authors suggest the shortfall may be due to logistical challenges in vaccination efforts: inadequate cold chain management, poor vaccine handling and distribution practices, and insufficient awareness and communication during vaccination campaigns.

questions.question: Using the multivariable logistic regression results, how do animal age and origin (gifted or purchased) quantify the risk of PPR seropositivity in nonvaccinated animals?
questions.expected_answer: In the multivariable logistic regression for the nonvaccinated population, older animals were 7.3 times more likely to be seropositive for PPRV (OR: 7.3; 95%CI: 2.7–19.4; P = 0.000). The text compares them with adult animals, but Table 4 gives Young as the reference, with Adult at 0.7 (0.2–1.7; P = 0.448). For origin, born small ruminants are the reference. The probability of being seropositive was 4 times higher in purchased animals (OR: 4; 95%CI: 1.4–11.3; P = 0.008) and 8.3 times higher in gifted small ruminants (OR: 8.3; 95%CI: 2.1–32.6; P = 0.003).

questions.question: What specific districts in the Somali Region of Ethiopia were included as study areas for this research?
questions.expected_answer: Three districts of the Somali region, all in Liban Zone: Goro Baqaqsa, Guradamole and Dolo Ado. They were purposively selected based on livestock populations and proximity to the road.

questions.question: Based on the study's findings, how does the clinical history of livestock relate to the likelihood of brucellosis seropositivity in both small ruminants and camels?
questions.expected_answer:
In both species, a history of retained fetal membranes (RFM) was the history factor significantly associated with Brucella seropositivity. Together with herd size, the paper names it a risk factor for brucellosis in animals.

Small ruminants: 33.3% of animals with a history of RFM were seropositive, compared with 1.5% of those without (univariable OR 8.2, 95% CI 2.4–29). For the multivariable model, the text gives OR 9 (95% CI 1.9–42) and Table 2 prints 8.2 (2.4–29). History of abortion was not significant (23% vs 3.1%, OR 3, 95% CI 0.9–9.7, p = 0.08).

Camels: in the univariable analysis, both history of abortion (10.2% vs 2.8%, OR 3.9, 95% CI 1.2–13) and RFM (35.7% vs 2.5%, OR 22) were significant. In the multivariable model only RFM stayed significant (OR 35, 95% CI 12.7–60, p = 0.004). Abortion did not (OR 0.7, p = 0.80). Even so, the Discussion says camel seropositivity was associated with both RFM and history of abortion.

The authors explain the link this way: when Brucella causes abortion, the placenta is frequently retained, so retained fetal membrane is a sequel of brucellosis.

questions.question: Describe the laboratory diagnostic sequence and the statistical methods used to identify significant risk factors for brucellosis in this study.
questions.expected_answer:
Laboratory sequence: the 1,000 serum samples were first screened for anti-Brucella antibodies with the Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT). Any visible agglutination counted as positive. Camels were tested with 30 μL of RBPT. Sheep and goats got a modified RBPT, one volume of antigen to three volumes of serum (e.g. 25 μL with 75 μL), to improve sensitivity. All RBPT-positive sera were then tested at Jigjiga Veterinary Diagnostic and Research Laboratory. The Methods say animal sera went to a commercial cELISA (Abbexa) and human sera to an IgG ELISA (Abbexa). The Discussion instead says RBPT and c-ELISA were used for camel and human sera. A sample was seropositive only if it tested positive on both RBPT and cELISA, and a flock or herd was seropositive if at least one animal was positive on both tests. The two tests were used serially. RBPT was the screening test for its high sensitivity, and competitive ELISA excluded false-positive cross-reactions to keep specificity at its maximum.

Statistics: data were entered into Microsoft Excel and analysed in R (version R-3.3.0). Univariate logistic regression first identified putative risk factors. Variables with p ≤ 0.2 in that step went into a multiple (multivariable) logistic regression, estimated by maximum likelihood. The candidate variables were age, sex, species, RFM, parity, abortion, physiological status, flock/herd size and migration. When two variables showed strong collinearity (p < 0.05), one was excluded on grounds of biological plausibility. Stepwise backward elimination selected the variables for the final model, and strength of association was assessed with odds ratios.
expected_concepts: positive for RBPT and cELISA methods

questions.question: According to the paper, what are the primary sites of FMDV infection in ruminants and pigs?
questions.expected_answer: Primary replication typically occurs in the upper respiratory tract (nasopharynx) of ruminants and in the upper gastrointestinal tract (oropharynx) of pigs. In cattle, the primary site is localized to the nasopharyngeal mucosa. In pigs, primary infection is in the oropharynx after oral exposure, specifically in the epithelial crypts of the oropharyngeal tonsils (the tonsil of the soft palate and the paraepiglottic tonsils). Caveats: the Figure 2 legend says sheep are infected via the respiratory tract (nasopharynx), but the text says no pre-viremic site has been published for sheep, and that both the nasopharyngeal mucosa and the oropharyngeal tonsil crypts are potential primary sites. In African cape buffalo, as in pigs, the primary site may not be located in the upper respiratory tract.
expected_concepts: epithelial crypts of the oropharyngeal tonsils

questions.question: How does the FMDV 'carrier state' differ between pigs and ruminants, and what biological evidence challenges the historical 28-day threshold for this state?
questions.expected_answer:
Pigs: no FMDV carrier state. Pigs efficiently clear FMDV from all tissues after recovering from the clinical phase.

Ruminants: FMDV can cause a prolonged persistent phase of subclinical infection, with continuous low-level virus replication in distinct epithelial compartments. In cattle these are in the upper respiratory tract; in sheep and African buffalo, the upper gastrointestinal tract. This is the carrier state. In ruminants, persistence follows either clinical or subclinical infection, regardless of vaccination or immune status.

The 28-day threshold: the carrier state is commonly defined as isolating FMDV from oropharyngeal fluid (probang) samples for more than 28 days after infection. Three points in the review undercut that threshold.
- It came from a single historical experimental study limited to 4 weeks, which assumed that cattle still virus-positive at the end of the study were carriers.
- Cattle that cleared infection had done so considerably earlier, a finding confirmed by more recent publications.
- A transitional stage, in which animals either clear the virus or become carriers, occurs at about 14–21 dpi in clinically affected cattle, and about 7–14 dpi in cattle clinically protected by vaccination.

The review concludes that the 28-day threshold holds no specific biological relevance, but may still be useful for practical purposes.
expected_concepts: no FMDV carrier state in pigs
continuous low levels of virus replication

questions.question: What are the specific quantitative estimates for preclinical transmission (theta) in pigs and cattle as identified in the research synthesis?
questions.expected_answer: Pigs: Arzt et al. estimated θ at 0.12 (95% CI 0.00083–0.27) using Bayesian modelling, meaning 12% of FMDV transmission occurs during the subclinical phase. Cattle: Charleston et al. estimated θ at 0.13 (approximately 0.13) from direct, observed transmission measures. With proxy measures (viral isolation from blood, nasal fluid or oropharyngeal fluid) their values were substantially higher: 0.43, 0.27 and 0.44 (up to ~0.44). Using similar data, Gubbins et al. estimated θ at 0.18 (95% CI 0.06–0.43) with nasal fluid as the proxy, and 0.32–0.45 with blood or OPF proxies.

questions.question: According to the epidemiological review of the 2022 H5N1 outbreak, how many birds were culled in Canada?
questions.expected_answer: Over 7 million birds have been culled in Canada. For comparison, the paper reports depopulation of more than 58 million in the United States.

questions.question: What are the common clinical presentations and relative frequency of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b infections when comparing mammals to humans?
questions.expected_answer: Mammals: clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 has infected multiple species, including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, porpoises, sea lions and dolphins. Most infected mammals presented with severe neurological signs and died from encephalitis or meningoencephalitis. Milder disease was likely also present (and likely more prevalent), because wildlife testing is biased towards severely infected or dead animals, and identified infections are assumed to represent only a minority of spillovers. Humans: this clade has been identified in less than 10 humans. Most cases have been mild or asymptomatic (the first case, in the United Kingdom, was mild; a second, in the United States in April 2022, was asymptomatic), but in recent months severe cases have occurred, all with direct exposure to poultry. The paper reports no symptom profile for the clade 2.3.4.4b human cases, but it advises clinicians to consider HPAI virus infection in any individual with acute febrile respiratory disease or unexplained neurological diseases after exposure to birds or sick wildlife in the previous 10 to 14 days; it notes that conjunctivitis and gastrointestinal symptoms have also been reported in humans infected with other avian H5 strains. Comparison: detected mammal infections span many species and are mostly severe neurological disease, while human infections are few (less than 10) and mostly mild or asymptomatic.

questions.question: Which specific viral mutations linked to mammalian adaptation were detected in the neurological tissues of carnivores in Canada and Europe?
questions.expected_answer: The PB2 mutations PB2-E627K, E627V and D701N. Viruses with these mammalian adaptations were found in the brain of various carnivores in Europe and Canada.
expected_concepts: various carnivores in Europe and Canada

questions.question: What is the reported efficacy of the homologous vaccine Lumpi-ProVacInd developed in India?
questions.expected_answer: According to ICAR scientists, the efficacy of the homologous vaccine Lumpi-ProVacInd is 100%.

questions.question: How does the clinical impact of Lumpy Skin Disease Virus (LSDV) differ in terms of its spread within a herd versus its lethality?
questions.expected_answer: LSD has significant morbidity but a low fatality rate: illness morbidity can reach 100%, while the mortality rate is typically less than 10%. The abstract calls it a "rapidly explorative, and sometimes fatal infection". In the current outbreak in India, morbidity rates cover a wide range and fatality rates among cattle a wider one.

questions.question: According to the comparative analysis of vaccinations, what is the specific cross-protection rate between LSDV and related poxviruses, and which viruses are involved?
questions.expected_answer: Approximately 96%. The three viruses of the Capripoxvirus genus, Sheep Pox Virus (SPPV), Goat Pox Virus (GTPV) and Lumpy Skin Disease Virus (LSDV), share a high cross-protection rate of approximately 96% when vaccinated against. Elsewhere the same paper is less positive. It says an attenuated sheeppox vaccine gives only partial cross-protection against the LSD field strain, and that the goat pox vaccine used in India gives 60 to 70% protection against disease.

questions.question: In cattle, which two bacterial phyla are the most abundant and what percentage of the gastrointestinal tract bacterial community can they represent?
questions.expected_answer: In cattle, Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes are the most abundant phyla. Together they may account for more than 90% of the entire GIT bacterial community.

questions.question: What are the primary biases currently existing in livestock gut microbiome research regarding breed selection and taxonomic focus?
questions.expected_answer: Breed selection: most studies focus on a few cosmopolitan and highly selected breeds. The available data are biased toward a small number of globally distributed and carefully chosen varieties. Local breeds from rural areas are largely neglected or frequently overlooked, despite their demonstrated resistance to harsh environmental circumstances. The paper names ovicaprine and chicken breeds from rural areas of developing countries as largely neglected. It says this focus lacks representativeness in terms of diversity and functionality. Taxonomic focus: research has mostly focused on bacteria, the most-studied microbial group. Other microorganisms (protists or protozoa, fungi, archaea and viruses) have received far less attention, and knowledge of them is scant. They usually get attention only when they are parasites of commercial relevance. Research on commensal protozoa and on the fungal component of the gut microbiome is still limited.

questions.question: Which specific bioinformatics tools and molecular sequencing techniques are utilized in the analysis of the livestock microbiome as described in the paper's methods?
questions.expected_answer:
The paper is a review and has no methods of its own. It describes these next-generation sequencing techniques and tools:
(1) Amplicon metabarcoding, a PCR-based method with dual indexing. It targets the V2-V3 and V3-V4 16S rRNA hypervariable regions for bacteria, the V4 and V9 18S rRNA regions for protists, and ITS1 and ITS2 for fungi. Its reference sequences come from GenBank, Greengenes v13_8, SILVA 138 and RDP18. QIIME does 16S-based taxonomic assignment, and Tax4Fun predicts functional profiles from 16S sequences.
(2) Shotgun sequencing, with BLAST+ for building customized reference databases.
(3) Metatranscriptomics, especially RNASeq, with the software HISAT and ABioTrans.
(4) Functional-profile prediction with PICRUSt, PICRUSt2, FaproTax, Tax4Fun and Tax4fun2, often combined with KEGG pathway analysis.
In passing, the review also names comparative metagenomic pyrosequencing (chicken studies) and nanopore technology (cow resistome).
expected_concepts: Quantitative Insights into Microbial Ecology pipeline (QIIME)
Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis

questions.question: What percentage of the recovered metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) were assigned to species without cultured representatives, and what does this suggest about the swine gut microbiome?
questions.expected_answer: 82% of the MAGs (938 of the 1,150 non-redundant MAGs) were assigned to archaeal or bacterial species that lack cultured representatives. The authors take this to indicate that a large portion of the swine gut microbiome is still poorly characterized and that a large fraction of it has yet to be cultivated (cultured).

questions.question: Based on the study's findings, how does the transition from nursing to weaning impact the taxonomic composition and relative abundance of specific bacterial groups in pigs?
questions.expected_answer:
The diet changes abruptly at weaning, from liquid and milk-based to solid and based on cereal grains. By 7 days postweaning, the relative abundance of a large number of MAGs had shifted significantly (MaAsLin2, immediately before weaning versus 7 days postweaning).

Decreases: 69 MAGs fell in relative abundance. The most differentially abundant were Limousia pullorum, B. fragilis, E. coli, P. hyovaginalis and P. vulgatus. C. coli and S. pasteurianus MAGs were also enriched in preweaned piglets. Six MAGs above 0.1% in nursing piglets were not detected in the same pigs 7 d later: B. thetaiotaomicron, Bulleidia sp., Enterococcus faecalis, Mediterraneibacter torques, Parvimonas sp. and P. hyovaginalis. One E. faecalis MAG was relatively abundant in nursing samples (0.25 ± 0.07%, printed '0.25 6 0.07%') and was not detected in any postweaning sample. It may represent a strain unique to nursing piglets.

Increases: 140 MAGs rose in relative abundance, including Copromorpha sp., Clostridium sp000435835, Fusicatenibacter saccharivorans, Intestinibacter sp., Oliverpabstia intestinalis, Phascolarctobacterium sp004558595, Prevotella sp002251295, Prevotella sp004556065 and Ruminococcus sp003011855. They also included uncultured potential butyrate producers (CAG-83 sp., Aphodosoma sp900769035, Copromorpha sp., Egerieousia sp004561775, UMGS1668 sp004556975).

Genus level: earlier studies (38-40) report that weaning lowers Bacteroides and Escherichia and raises Blautia, Prevotella and Roseburia. Many of this study's differentially abundant MAGs were assigned to these genera, but several belonged to taxa not known to be associated with weaning.

On an NMDS plot of Bray-Curtis dissimilarities, the preweaned samples appear separate from the postweaned samples of other studies.

questions.question: Describe the bioinformatic workflow and specific quality thresholds used to identify, assess, and dereplicate the non-redundant MAGs reported in this research.
questions.expected_answer: Reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic v. 0.38 (quality score threshold 15 over a sliding window of 4 bp, minimum length of 50 bp), which also removed sequencing adapters. Host reads were removed by alignment to the Sus scrofa genome (Sscrofa11.1) with Bowtie2 v. 2.4.2-1. MEGAHIT v. 1.29.0 co-assembled the metagenomes and also assembled each one individually. Before co-assembly, samples were normalized with BBNorm (BBTools v. 38.79). Reads were mapped back to the assemblies with Bowtie2, and contigs with a minimum length of 2,000 bp were binned with MetaBAT 2. CheckM v. 1.1.2 assessed the bins, and MAGs with greater than 90% completeness and less than 5% contamination were retained. This gave 2,327 MAGs from the individual assemblies and 85,145 from the co-assemblies, 87,472 in total, from 738 Gb of sequencing data. dRep v. 3.2.2 dereplicated these MAGs with primary clustering at 90% and secondary clustering at 99% ANI. The result was 1,150 non-redundant MAGs (potentially unique strains), which were used for all subsequent analyses. With 95% ANI for secondary clustering, 758 putative species were produced instead. Taxonomy was assigned with GTDB-tk 2.0.0 and GTDB release 207.

questions.question: How many bacterial colonies were isolated in total, and how many distinct sub-ASVs were identified within the Lactobacillus ASV5 group?
questions.expected_answer: A total of 1,299 colonies were Sanger sequenced (16S rRNA gene). Within ASV5 Lactobacillus, 100 isolates were identical in the V4 region, but their near-full-length 16S rRNA gene sequences (V3-V7 hypervariable regions) split them into 13 sub-ASVs.

questions.question: How does the microbial diversity identified by culture-dependent (CD) methods compare to culture-independent (CI) methods across the four growth stages, and what does this imply about the overlap between the two approaches?
questions.expected_answer:
The CD methods detected more ASVs than the CI methods at every stage: 415, 675, 808 and 823 ASVs against 378, 482, 565 and 555 at the lactation, nursery, growing and finishing stages. Diversity increased over successive growth stages under both methods, and Shannon diversity rose with age under both. Simpson evenness followed different patterns under the two methods.

The overlap is only partial. 171, 264, 301 and 313 ASVs were shared by CD and CI. On average, 45.2, 54.8, 53.3 and 56.4% of the CI-detected ASVs were observed on the plates, so approximately half of the ASVs were recovered by culture. About 44 to 54% of the CI-detected ASVs remain to be cultured. CD also found 244, 411, 507 and 510 new ASVs that CI did not detect. Each method therefore captures ASVs the other misses, and together they yielded 622, 893, 1,072 and 1,065 ASVs at the four growth stages.
expected_concepts: reveal more bacterial ASVs than CI
shared by both CD and CI
approximately half of the bacterial ASVs
undetected when using the CI methods
increased the recovery of microbial richness

questions.question: Based on the PERMANOVA analysis, what was the most significant factor influencing the culturable bacterial community composition, and what specific statistical result supports this?
questions.expected_answer: Oxygen was the top driver of the culturable community in the PERMANOVA (permutations=999; adonis function in the vegan package of R): F-scoremean = 142.1, R2 mean = 0.12, P value 0.001. The growth stage of donor pigs was the second influencing factor (F-scoremean = 35.51; R2mean = 0.09; P value, 0.001), followed by medium type (F-scoremean = 10.64; R2 mean = 0.27; P value, 0.001).
expected_concepts: Oxygen ranked as the top driver

questions.question: Based on the longitudinal occurrence analysis over the 42-day study period, how many microbial genera were classified into the 'colonization', 'disappearance', and 'core' categories?
questions.expected_answer: The 23 occurrence patterns that showed regular changes were sorted into three categories. Colonization: 107 genera in 15 patterns. Disappearance: 24 genera in seven patterns (22 fungal, 2 bacterial). Core: 18 genera in one pattern, present for the entire 42-day period.

questions.question: How does the choice between Relative Microbiome Profiling (RMP) and Quantitative Microbiome Profiling (QMP) affect the interpretation of microbial interactions and community variations?
questions.expected_answer:
RMP profiles the proportions of taxa, while QMP tracks changes in absolute abundance (AA) and shows the real community dynamics. Microbial loads changed over time and space in the gut. RMP ignored the absolute growth or decline of microbes, failed to detect real microbial changes, and biased both the developmental trajectory and the microbial interactions.

Community variation: AA was relatively stable over time compared with the RMP results. Firmicutes AA was relatively stable in the four gut segments, but its RA varied more, especially in the duodenum and cecum. Ascomycota showed the opposite development trend under QMP and RMP. QMP showed similar Lactobacillus numbers across segments after 7 DHP, whereas RMP showed its abundance as extremely low in the cecum. The same held for Candida. The correlation coefficients (Figure 2B) were only 0.622 (bacteriome) and 0.459 (mycobiome). RA exaggerated the proportion of variation explained by individual, segment and DPH, so RMP overestimated community structure variations and the influencing factors.

Microbial interactions: the comparison used genus-level Spearman's correlation. The QMP and RMP correlations were consistent in 82.1%, 66.0%, 78.7% and 86.8% of cases for the bacteriome (duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum) and in 81.1%, 73.8%, 78.6% and 56.0% for the mycobiome. RMP overestimated bacterial positive correlations: 402 vs. 196 (duodenum), 1164 vs. 678 (jejunum) and 1050 vs. 725 (ileum), but 668 vs. 683 in the cecum. RMP missed fungal positive correlations: 400 vs. 775, 997 vs. 1338, 865 vs. 1044 and 1048 vs. 2270. Overall, RMP missed many significant positive taxon–taxon interactions found in QMP, especially for the fungal community. The authors conclude that quantitative approaches are necessary.
expected_concepts: microbial loads changed over time and space
RA exaggerated the proportion of variation
missed positive correlations for the mycobiome
ignored the absolute growth or decline

questions.question: Using the ecological modeling metrics employed in the study, what are the primary assembly processes for bacterial versus fungal communities in the chicken gut?
questions.expected_answer: The study used a two-step procedure based on the β-nearest taxon index (βNTI) and the Bray–Curtis-based Raup–Crick Index (RCBray), calculated with the R package iCAMP (v1.3.4). It sorted assembly into five processes. Two are deterministic: heterogeneous selection and homogeneous selection. Three are stochastic: homogenizing dispersal, dispersal limitation and undominated. Bacterial communities were mainly deterministic (56.7% deterministic versus 43.3% stochastic). Fungal communities were mainly stochastic (55.1% stochastic versus 44.9% deterministic). Two processes governed assembly. Homogeneous selection accounted for 56.7% in bacteria and 44.0% in fungi. Homogeneous dispersal accounted for 32.7% in bacteria and 50.3% in fungi.
expected_concepts: homogeneous selection (56.7% for bacteria and 44.0% for fungi)
Homogeneous dispersal (32.7% for bacteria and 50.3% for fungi)

questions.question: Which specific genomic regions were identified as co-localizing the rumen microbiome and feed efficiency traits, and where was the cluster on BTA11 located?
questions.expected_answer: The paper found SNP co-localized between feed efficiency traits and rumen microbial traits on eight chromosomes (Table 1: BTA3, 7, 11, 13, 15, 16, 19 and 26). For RFI the regions are 116.5-117.3 Mb on BTA3, 28.1–30.5 Mb on BTA16 and 37.2 Mb on BTA19. For NESec there is a region at 16.5 Mb on BTA13, near a suggestive pQTL. BTA3 and BTA7 also carry co-localized pQTL and rmQTL, and some feed efficiency traits and rumen microbes share the same SNP on BTA11. The BTA11 cluster lies at 6.1–6.2 Mb. It holds two significant co-localized SNP between DMI and the rumen microbiome, Chr11:6,192,173 and Chr11:6,216,461.
expected_concepts: two significant co-localized SNP between DMI
co-localized regions on BTA3 and BTA7

questions.question: How does the host genome at Chr3: 116.5 Mb influence residual feed intake (RFI), and what role do microbes play in this relationship?
questions.expected_answer: The causal network was learned with the IAMB algorithm and Fisher's Z test. It shows that the cow genome at Chr3: 116.5 Mb (SNP Chr3:116,575,934) affects RFI indirectly. The effect is mediated by the abundance of rumen microbes: Syntrophococcus, Prevotella and an unknown genus of Class Bacilli. Results says the two BTA3 QTL (Chr3:116,575,934 and Chr3:117,335,980) were directly and indirectly associated with RFI, mediated by the rumen microbiome (ASV1047, ASV666 and ASV57). In the genomic scans, 116.5-117.3 Mb on BTA3 was an RFI pQTL and one of the regions with the strongest SNP effects on RFI. Prevotella ASV57, Syntrophococcus ASV666 and [Eubacterium] brachy group ASV2236 had significant SNP in the same region. So the microbes are mediators: the host genome affects their abundance, and through them it affects RFI. Prevotella can use starch, protein, hemicellulose and pectin to produce acetate, succinate and propionate. It interacts with other microorganisms and affects dairy cow feed efficiency.
expected_concepts: directly and indirectly associated with RFI

questions.question: What specific algorithm was used for causal structural learning in the study, and how was the stability of the resulting causal networks evaluated?
questions.expected_answer: Causal structure was learned with the Incremental Association Markov Blanket (IAMB) algorithm, used in conjunction with Fisher’s Z test for conditional independence (α = 0.10), with all network analyses in the R package bnlearn. Stability of the causal networks was evaluated using Jackknife resampling: leaving out one observation per time from the dataset, each edge of the original network was evaluated for presence (presence or absence in the resampled network) and direction (same direction as the original edge, opposite direction, or undirected arc), expressed as the frequency at which a given edge was presented and with the same direction in the resampled networks. Most edges were present in more than 65% of the resampled networks.
expected_concepts: leaving out one observation per time
more than 65% of the resampled networks

questions.question: Which specific bacterial genera are positively correlated with higher intramuscular fat (IMF) content in pigs according to the gut microbiome studies cited?
questions.expected_answer: Lei et al. (2021): higher relative abundances of Ruminococcaceae_NK4A214_group, Parabacteroides, Christensenellaaceae_R-7_group and Ruminiclostridium might correlate with higher IMF content (the review prints "corelate"). Wu et al. (2021): increased abundance of genus Romboutsia in colonic samples, together with an elevated ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes, was correlated with higher IMF content in pigs. Tang et al. (2020): in Enshi pigs, Prevotellaceae UCG-001 and Alistipes in the cecum and Clostridium sensustricto 1 in the jejunum were highly, positively correlated with IMF.

questions.question: How do short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) bridge the gap between dietary fiber intake and the regulation of host fat accumulation and metabolism?
questions.expected_answer:
Gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber (host-indigestible carbohydrates) into SCFAs, chiefly acetate, propionate and butyrate. Dietary fiber intake therefore influences SCFA levels and composition. Colonic cells absorb SCFAs through monocarboxylate transporters, passive diffusion or bicarbonate exchange. Inside these cells, SCFAs are converted to acetyl-CoA or propynyl-CoA, which produces ATP. SCFAs the colonic cells do not metabolize travel through the portal circulation to the liver, where they serve as an energy substrate. Only small amounts reach the systemic circulation. There they increase insulin secretion, maintain energy homeostasis and improve the function of the liver, skeletal muscles and adipose tissue.

The review cites four links from SCFAs to fat:
- Acetate-dependent GPR43 stimulation in white adipose tissue improved glucose and lipid metabolism.
- In rabbits, acetate reduced intramuscular triglyceride levels by increasing fatty acid uptake and fatty acid oxidation, and PPARα was associated with this reduction in fat.
- Low-fat pigs had more butyrate-producing bacteria and more SCFA formation, especially butyrate, which alleviated fat deposition.
- SCFA administration into the ileum of growing pigs inhibited mRNA expression of fatty acid synthase (FAS) and acetyl-CoA carboxylase in the longissimus dorsi.

The review concludes that through these effects on muscle and fat tissue, SCFAs influence meat quality.

questions.question: What metric is used to quantify the impact of the gut microbiome on rabbit finishing weight, and which specific host genes are highlighted as part of the microbial-influenced pathway for intramuscular fat accumulation?
questions.expected_answer: The metric is the share of variation in finishing weight explained by the gut microbiome: nearly 11% in rabbits. Among the SCFAs, butyrate level had critical impacts on rabbit finishing weight. In the rabbit intramuscular fat pathway, the paper names one host gene, PPARα. PPARα is associated with the acetate-reduced intracellular fat content. In that pathway, acetate reduces intramuscular triglyceride levels by increasing fatty acid uptake and fatty acid oxidation. The paper's explicit fat accumulation genes come from pigs. There, Prevotella copri acts through the TLR4 and mTOR signaling pathways and upregulates the lipogenesis and fat accumulation genes Fabp9, Scd1, Scd2 and Scd3. Mice that received Jinhua pig microbiota had elevated lipid and triglyceride levels and lipoprotein lipase activity, with reduced ANGPTL4 expression in the muscle.
expected_concepts: fatty acid uptake and fatty acid oxidation

questions.question: What are the names of the two specialized pipelines integrated into iNAP, and what specific types of microbial associations do they represent?
