questions.expected_answer: iNAP contains the molecular ecological network analysis pipeline (MENAP) and the interdomain ecological network analysis pipeline (IDENAP). MENAP corresponds to intradomain associations and IDENAP to interdomain associations of microbial species at multiple taxonomic levels; these relationships are shown with an adjacent network matrix (intradomain) and a bipartite network matrix (interdomain).
expected_concepts: intradomain and interdomain associations of microbial species

questions.question: How does the iNAP system facilitate the visualization and downstream interpretation of the generated ecological networks?
questions.expected_answer:
Whenever iNAP exports a network matrix (adjacent or bipartite), it also generates the files needed for visualization. These files can be imported directly into Cytoscape or Gephi, and the output format is chosen for one or the other.
- Cytoscape: a .sif file, which imports directly, plus a node attribute file (.txt) and an edge attribute file (.txt).
- Gephi: a node attribute file (.csv) and an edge attribute file (.csv).
The node attribute file holds node features. The edge attribute file shows the positive/negative association between nodes and the coefficient values.

A "Generate node attribute for visualization" step combines two sets of results into a formatted node property file for Cytoscape and Gephi:
- node-level properties: degree, betweenness and closeness;
- module results: within‐module connectivity (Z) and among‐module connectivity (P), which classify species into network hubs, module hubs, connectors and peripherals, plus an exported Z–P plot.
In Figure 3, nodes are coloured by taxonomic group (Cytoscape) or by module compartment (Gephi).

For further interpretation:
- Topological structure can reflect ecological implications, for example modular structure indicating similar functions.
- Mantel and partial Mantel tests relate network topological structure to environmental factors.
- Module‐EigenGene analysis outputs a web page of tables and plots covering each module's eigengene, the hierarchy structure and module correlations to environmental factors.
- Auxiliary tools convert a sif file exported from Cytoscape back into a bipartite or adjacent matrix for further analysis.

questions.question: Which specific algorithms and methods does iNAP recommend for constructing networks from non-temporal versus temporal microbial datasets?
questions.expected_answer: For nontemporal data sets, iNAP gives SparCC (sparse correlations for compositional data), SPIEC-EASI (sparse inverse covariance estimation for ecological association inference) and RMT-based Pearson's and Spearman's correlations as alternative options. For temporal (time series) data sets, it gives eLSA/LA (extended local similarity analysis and liquid association) and RMT-based Pearson's and Spearman's approaches as candidate methods to generate network matrices. In the RMT-based methods, a threshold based on random matrix theory filters the correlations. These methods appear in both lists, and when the data set is temporally dynamic they need a sample description file giving the replicates and time points.

questions.question: How many total taxa were identified in the full dataset by the OTU-based pipeline compared to the ASV-based pipeline prior to filtering?
questions.expected_answer: In the full dataset, before the 0.001% abundance threshold, Table 1 gives 67,015 taxa for the OTU-based pipeline on unrarefied data (50,065 when rarefied with vegan), against 8005 taxa for the ASV-based pipeline.

questions.question: How does the choice of bioinformatic pipeline influence the interpretation of microbial community diversity and composition across different sample types?
questions.expected_answer:
Comparing an OTU-based and an ASV-based pipeline, the paper finds that both gave comparable results that would generally allow the same interpretations, and phylum-level composition was overall in good agreement. Still, community composition differed between 6.75% and 10.81% per treatment on phylum level, based purely on the pipeline. Biologically driven variability between samples affected the two pipelines differently.

- Thermophilic AD reactors: diversity trends were similar, and the OTU pipeline typically reported slightly higher diversity. Inverse Simpson values were almost identical. Both pipelines allow the same interpretation of alpha diversity. Some genera (Firmicutes, Chloroflexota, Patescibacteria, Hydrothermae) still differed, and several genera were not picked up by one or the other pipeline.
- Psychrophilic PWASS: diversity indices diverged. The Shannon Wiener index was similar, but other estimators strongly differed, with a partial trend reversal for some (especially evenness). Inverse Simpson differed at times by a factor greater than two. Between-pipeline variability in composition was much greater than in the other treatments. Aeromonas differed by as much as 3% of the total community, or by 400% (4% ASV, 1% OTU).
- Statistics: on the AD-only dataset, NMDS and Permanova showed that the choice of pipeline significantly influences the reported composition. Pipeline differences were greater than treatment differences, even over more than 170 days. The ASV pipeline showed the time and co-substrate drift more clearly. On the whole dataset, pipeline alone was not significant, but it became significant once its interaction with treatment was included. With factors nested within pipeline, the null hypothesis could no longer be rejected. On the reduced dataset, this would suggest that pipeline affects composition more than any treatment, which has no foundation in experimental reality.
- Cause the authors propose: temperature was the prominent factor. The ASV algorithm calculates error rates on a subset of samples, mostly thermophilic AD samples, and applies them to every sample, including psychrophilic ones, where the results diverged.
- Consequence: pipeline-dependent differences in taxonomic assignment could lead to different conclusions and interfere with downstream analysis such as network analysis or predictions of ecosystem service. The differences were not limited to the PWASS.

questions.question: What specific software tools and clustering parameters were utilized to define the OTU-based and ASV-based pipelines in this research?
questions.expected_answer:
OTU pipeline: it follows the method of Dyksma et al. Cutadapt trimmed adapters (minimum adapter overlap of 6 bases, adapter error rate of 0.1). BBMerge merged reads at default merging strictness with a quality trim threshold of 10. VSEARCH did dereplication and chimera removal, then clustered sequences into OTUs at 97% similarity. The SINA classifier assigned taxonomy (minimum length 100 bp, quality score filter of 20 at the 3′ end) against the SILVA REF99 SSU reference database version 138.1.

ASV pipeline: DADA2 v1.18.0 under R version 4.1.0, following the DADA2 workflow for Big Data: Paired-End (1.4 or later). Changes to that workflow: reads trimmed left 17 bases to remove residual primers, truncQ lowered to 2, truncLen removed, and minFoldParentOverAbundance increased to 8 for chimera removal. Taxonomy came from the SILVA REF99 SSU reference database version 138.1. This pipeline does not cluster: a quality-based error correction mode replaces the 97% clustering.

Both pipelines: an abundance threshold of 0.001% was applied to the OTU and ASV datasets to remove rare taxa.

questions.question: What is the recommended target for raw read numbers per sample when starting a 16S rRNA gene sequencing study without prior pilot data?
questions.expected_answer: In the absence of any data on the sample matrix, 10,000 reads per sample is a good starting point for a raw read number target. With pilot samples, the most appropriate method to find a minimum target is a rarefaction curve. Some studies indicate as few as 2,000 reads allow characterization of a bacterial community, whereas others argue the number is closer to 10,000 to 15,000.
expected_concepts: In the absence of any data

questions.question: Why are Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) considered superior to Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) for modern microbiome comparative analyses?
questions.expected_answer:
OTUs are clusters of reads that differ by less than a fixed dissimilarity threshold (usually 3%). The clustering is done either de novo or against a reference database (closed-reference). OTUs have no innate biological meaning: each is a "cloud" of similar sequences, not a single species or genus. They are artifacts of either a subjective threshold (de novo) or the reference database (closed-reference). As a result, de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies, and closed-reference clustering loses any biological information that is not in the database.

ASVs can differ by as little as one nucleotide and have no fixed threshold. They are produced by a model-based approach that separates sequencing errors from bona fide biological variation without constructing OTUs. The paper gives these advantages:
- ASVs significantly reduce clustering artifacts, so ASVs generated independently from different samples can be validly compared (cross-study tractability).
- They capture unique biological sequence variation from all phylogenetic lineages, without the limits of closed-reference databases (database-independent biological veracity).
- They avoid the computationally intensive clustering step. Their time and memory requirements are relatively light and scale linearly, which suits routine large-scale microbial monitoring.

For these reasons, replacing OTUs with ASVs has been proposed. The paper notes one concern: ASVs may inflate diversity, because a single bacterial genome can produce multiple ASVs (Schloss, 2021).

questions.question: How does the technical approach of rarefaction differ from scaling normalization methods like TMM or DESeq2 in handling sample variance?
questions.expected_answer: Rarefaction randomly subsamples ASVs or OTUs within each sample without replacement to a preselected depth that is the same across all samples. Every sample ends with the same number of ASVs, and samples below the rarefaction level are removed. This discards valuable data and loses statistical power by removing sequences, and rarefying equalizes sample variance by adding artificial uncertainty. Scaling normalization does not subsample. It multiplies the ASV numbers by a value or proportion. In DESeq2 (median of ratios), the scaling factor is the median ratio of an ASV's count over its geometric mean across all samples. TMM (Trimmed Mean of M-values) uses one sample as a reference and compares the weighted mean of log ratios of an ASV within a sample with that reference. These methods have been shown to be robust to differences between samples and to maintain the differences in relative abundance.
expected_concepts: multiplied by a value or proportion

questions.question: What specific percentages of prokaryotes, eukaryotes, archaea, and viruses were identified using the shotgun metagenomics data?
questions.expected_answer: In the shotgun metagenomics data, prokaryotes made up 75.55%, eukaryotes 23.97%, archaea 0.24% and viruses 0.24%.

questions.question: How do the three sequencing approaches (16S rRNA, PacBio long-read, and shotgun metagenomics) differ in their contribution to the study's characterization of the microbial environment?
questions.expected_answer: 16S short-amplicon sequencing was adequate for community studies. It captured spatio-temporal dynamics and community composition at higher taxonomic levels. Primer choice and amplicon length changed some values, such as diversity measures and the number of assigned taxa, but had no impact on the spatio-temporal patterns between sample types, farms and time points. It cannot provide the resolution required for species or strain identification. PacBio long-read amplicons underperformed on the quantitative resolution of spatio-temporal patterns, because the low number of reads prohibited community statistics. Still, the 10,041 reads identified 204 species, and the approach was suited to identifying functional services (e.g. nitrification cycling) and detecting pathogens. Shotgun metagenomics corroborated the amplicon findings and extended the picture beyond prokaryotes (75.55%) to eukaryotes (23.97%), archaea (0.24%) and viruses (0.24%), including fungi and bacteriophages. The authors call it the most thorough approach. All datasets agreed on the major prokaryotic players (Actinobacteriota, Bacteroidota, Nitrospirota, Proteobacteria). The approaches gave overlapping and highly complementary results, and each contributed data the others could not provide.

questions.question: Based on the comparative analysis of the Earth (V4) and MiSeq (V3-V4) primers, what were the quantitative differences in alpha richness and how did this impact the interpretation of community structure?
questions.expected_answer:
Earth (V4) primers gave higher alpha richness than MiSeq (V3-4) primers, even though the MiSeq primers identified more taxa. Richness ranged 1070–2240 with Earth and 441–1962 with MiSeq.

Average richness, Earth vs MiSeq:
- Farm A biofilter water: 2166 vs 1504.
- Farm A tank water: 1934 vs 1477.
- Farm A young biofilm: 1135 vs 465.
- Farm A mature biofilm: 1497 vs 829.
- Farm B tank biofilm: tank1 1793 vs 1665, tank2 1805 vs 1815.

Farm B tank 2 is the one place where MiSeq was slightly higher. The paper's figure legend nonetheless says Earth was higher across all sample types.

The authors call these minor differences in ASV richness. They did not impact the spatio-temporal patterns or the biological conclusion. Amplicon choice did not affect community composition at higher taxonomic levels. Composition and spatio-temporal patterns were very similar between the two amplicons. Subtle phylum biases remained: Chloroflexi was favored by Earth, and Myxococcota and Plantomycetota by MiSeq. These biases did not affect the inferred overall community structure, which was virtually identical for both amplicons according to MDS analyses. With Earth primers the pattern was identical but sat in a distinct area of the morphospace. The authors conclude that relative differences in community composition can safely be compared across primers, but they recommend against comparing absolute statistics from different primers.
expected_concepts: Earth primers resulted in higher alpha diversity
did not impact the spatio-temporal patterns

questions.question: According to the World Health Organization's 2019 data, how many of the 32 antimicrobials in hospital development were classified as innovative?
questions.expected_answer: Six. Of the 32 antimicrobials in hospital development that the WHO identified in 2019, only six were classified as innovative.

questions.question: How does the metabolism and excretion of antimicrobials in animals contribute to environmental concerns within the One Health framework?
questions.expected_answer: Animals excrete a significant percentage (75%–90%) of antimicrobials without the drugs being metabolized, and these are dispersed into the environment. In aquaculture, antimicrobial residues can remain in aquatic environments for a long time through excreta, and they spread rapidly in water bodies, exerting selective pressure. Agriculture and aquaculture consume the largest amounts of antimicrobials globally. The paper therefore lists reducing the unnecessary use of antimicrobials in agriculture, and their dissemination to the environment, among its key strategies for addressing AMR from the One Health approach.

questions.question: Compare the recorded usage in tons of fluoroquinolones and third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins in animals between Europe (2017) and the USA (2018).
questions.expected_answer: Fluoroquinolones: approximately 216 tons were used in Europe in 2017, mainly in animals meant for human consumption (approximately 2.4% of all antimicrobials used in animals in Europe). The USA used approximately 23.3 tons in animals in 2018, so Europe's use was much higher. Cephalosporins: Europe used approximately 18 tons of third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins in 2017, mainly in animals intended for human consumption (approximately 0.2% of total antimicrobial use in animals in Europe). The USA's total cephalosporin use for animals was approximately 31.44 tons in 2018, which is the higher figure. However, the USA figure covers all cephalosporins, not only the third and fourth generations.

questions.question: What is the projected annual human mortality rate associated with antimicrobial resistance by the year 2050 if current trends continue?
questions.expected_answer: If current trends continue, there could be up to 10 million annual AR-associated (antibiotic resistance) deaths from a variety of untreatable infections by 2050.

questions.question: How do the interconnected domains of the One Health framework contribute to the cycle of antimicrobial resistance dissemination?
questions.expected_answer:
The review calls AR a One Health issue because livestock, humans and the environment are interconnected, which opens channels for transmission of antibiotic resistant bacteria (ARB). AR is linked to each domain through reckless and excessive antibiotic use in agriculture, livestock farming and human medicine. The interconnections create pathways for bacteria, mobile genetic elements (MGEs) and antibiotics themselves, and movement between compartments promotes the spread of AR. Each domain contributes:
- Humans: careless antibiotic use drives ARB and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), which pass to other humans through direct contact, food, water and environmental surfaces.
- Livestock: antibiotic use contributes to resistant bacteria, which reach humans through direct contact and food products. They reach the environment through livestock waste, and pathogens pass into the environment through air, slurry and feces from livestock, acting as a source of ARGs.
- Environment: environmental contamination is a major factor in dissemination. Residues from the pharmaceutical industry, livestock husbandry, hospitals, fecal waste from humans and animals, and agricultural runoff make it a hidden source of resistant organisms. ARB persist in soil and water and can potentially spread to animals and humans who contact contaminated sources.
The cycle closes when bacteria released in the feces of livestock and humans act as an environmental reservoir before reintroduction into the livestock-human cycle. At the human-animal-environment interface, AR bacterial clones, MGEs and ARGs carry the dissemination. MGEs (plasmids, transposons, integrons) act as vehicles, and together these components promote horizontal genetic exchange. Changes in one domain can have far-reaching effects on the others, and the Fig. 1 legend shows pathways running in every direction among the three domains. The review notes that it is not yet clear how much livestock-derived routes contribute compared with human-derived routes.
expected_concepts: the use of antibiotics in livestock

questions.question: Based on statistical modeling estimates, what was the estimated global antimicrobial usage in livestock for 2020 and what is the projected usage for 2030?
questions.expected_answer: Statistical models (Mulchandani et al., ref. 19) estimated antimicrobial usage at 99,502 tons in 2020. They projected an 8% increase to 107,472 tons, based on the latest trend. The paper's sentence gives no target year. The cited study covers food-producing animals from 2020 to 2030.

questions.question: What percentage of antibiotics administered to food animals is estimated to be excreted without being absorbed, and through what primary mediums does this occur?
questions.expected_answer: Approximately 75% of antibiotics are not absorbed by the animals and are excreted via feces and urine. Elsewhere (the Manure section) the paper gives this fraction as 70% ("the vast majority"), citing the same source, Mackie et al., 2006.

questions.question: How do antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) and genes (ARGs) originate in food animal farms and eventually reach the human population through different environmental and occupational pathways?
questions.expected_answer:
Origin: the misuse or overuse of antibiotics in animal production has led to ARB and ARGs. The animal gut microbiota is a reservoir of ARB and ARGs, and antibiotic use is the main cause of ARG prevalence. Insertions, integrations and transposons lead to horizontal transfer of ARGs among microbes, and spread between farm animals and humans is mostly attributed to the transfer of mobile ARGs. About 75% of antibiotics (70% in another passage) are not absorbed and are excreted via feces and urine, contaminating the surrounding environment. Manure used as fertilizer increases resistant bacteria and resistance genes in the environment.

Pathways to humans (three groups):
(1) Direct contact with farm animals. Farm workers have an increased risk and can transfer ARB and ARGs between persons; ESBL-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae were found in 9.8% of workers versus 5% of the Dutch population.
(2) Exposure to animal manure, wastewater or aerosol. Manure and wastewater are hotspots for animal-to-human transmission. Animal waste and slaughterhouses are an occupational risk to workers (MDR E. coli in up to 50% of butchers). Bioaerosols from swine confinement buildings carry zoonotic pathogens and ARGs from feces and may cause respiratory infections in pig farmers. Natural wind carries ARB and ARGs from farms to environmental dust, ARGs disperse up to 10 km, and MDR bacteria and ARGs reach workers and residents in the surrounding environment via inhalation into the respiratory tract.
(3) Consumption of uncooked or contaminated animal products (meat, eggs, milk), a key route of extraintestinal MDR pathogens, especially E. coli and Salmonella; the food chain is one of the important sources of transmission between animals and humans.

questions.question: Based on the findings regarding novel mitigation technologies, what is the specific mechanism and efficiency of using graphene oxide (GO) nanosheets for water treatment?
questions.expected_answer: The review cites Yu et al. (2017). Mechanism: GO nanosheets bind ARGs (such as tetA, ermB, ampC and sul2) nonspecifically through π-stacking interactions. Efficiency: approximately 80% of ARGs were removed from water samples taken from feedlots, fishponds and wastewater treatment plants. After 5 regeneration cycles, removal efficacy was reduced by <40%, which the paper calls excellent stability and reusability. The paper says GO nanosheets may be a desirable candidate for treating ARGs in animal wastewater or other water.

questions.question: What are the estimated annual public health and economic benefits of the PulseNet laboratory network according to the paper?
questions.expected_answer: PulseNet, a US-based domestic and international network of food, animal and public health laboratories, is estimated to have averted 270,000 foodborne illnesses and saved US $507 million each year by identifying enteric disease clusters of increasing incidence.

questions.question: How does the Generalized One Health Framework (GOHF) aim to improve zoonotic disease programming?
questions.expected_answer: The GOHF gives recommendations for using a One Health approach to improve multisectoral collaboration, and thereby enhance the prevention and control of zoonotic diseases. It is a five-step framework: engagement, assessment, planning, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation. A visualization (Fig. 2) sets out the steps and their corresponding activities, which give countries a structure for developing the capacity to coordinate zoonotic disease programming across sectors. Users may enter at any step based on their current capacity. A toolkit (Supplementary Tables S1–5) compiles available resources matched to each step and activity, so users can identify their progress on the visualization and then use the toolkit to advance. The GOHF is applied across technical domains: laboratory, surveillance, joint outbreak response, prevention and control, preparedness, communication, and government and policy. It is not intended to be prescriptive. It is meant to be broadly applicable to common zoonotic diseases, in high-income and low-middle income countries, from the local to the international level. Its intended outcome is improved capacity to control zoonotic diseases and other threats at the human–animal–environment interface. Instead of building independent programs for priority zoonotic diseases, it is intended to deepen One Health capacity throughout the system. Ideally this leads to a gradual transition towards a comprehensive One Health system that can combat a diversity of health threats.

questions.question: According to the paper, what is the specific threshold for dog vaccination coverage required for rabies control, and how does smartphone-based H5N1 detection compare to traditional methods?
questions.expected_answer: Rabies: the paper cites previous research showing that vaccination coverage of 70% or higher in dog populations can reduce human dog-bite injuries, the use of post-exposure prophylaxis and human rabies cases. H5N1: a smartphone-based system for detecting H5N1 avian influenza in clinical patient samples has a "two-folder" (as printed) higher detectability than traditional fluorescent strip readers. The paper says this makes it a sensitive and portable system for field-based diagnostics.

questions.question: What are the five distinct levels of evaluation defined in the Integrated Surveillance System Evaluation (ISSE) framework?
questions.expected_answer: The ISSE framework has five evaluation levels, which follow the hierarchy of a generic logic model: (1) Integration of a OH Approach; (2) Production of OH Information and Expertise; (3) Generation of Actionable Knowledge; (4) Influence on Decision-Making; (5) Contribution to Desirable Outcomes. The abstract describes the same five as the capacity of the system to integrate a OH approach, produce OH information and expertise, generate actionable knowledge, influence decision-making, and positively impact outcomes.
expected_concepts: Production of OH Information and Expertise

questions.question: Why did the authors conclude that existing evaluation tools like ATLASS and NEOH were insufficient for assessing the full value of integrated surveillance systems?
questions.expected_answer: None of the 12 tools examined, ATLASS and NEOH included, was developed specifically to evaluate OH integration into AMR and AMU surveillance systems, and none covers all the information required at all five levels of the ISSE framework. ATLASS was developed for national AMR surveillance in the food and agriculture sectors. It mostly addresses the animal components of surveillance systems and gives no guidance on how to evaluate integration with the other sectors (human and environment). Table 4 shows it covering parts of Levels 1, 2, 3 and 4. NEOH was developed for OH evaluation: it measures the degree of OH implementation (knowledge integration) in projects or programs. Its metrics were not developed specifically to evaluate OH integration into surveillance systems, but they can be applied to surveillance systems as a complementary approach. Table 4 shows it covering Level 1 and parts of Levels 2 and 4. Several tools mention the importance of measuring impacts, but none includes specific guidance for evaluating the global health and economic impact of OH integration. The authors found it difficult to link the existing tools to the ISSE levels, most likely because none was designed to evaluate OH surveillance systems, and the tools' metrics and methods were only partially relevant to most ISSE evaluation questions.
expected_concepts: none covers all the information required
integration with other sectors (human and environment)

questions.question: How does the ISSE framework technically measure the level of One Health integration across different surveillance activities?
questions.expected_answer:
Integration is measured at the first evaluation level, which evaluates the integration of a OH approach across the different components of the surveillance system. The evaluator first answers three questions with a descriptive qualitative methodology: focus groups or individual interviews with key informants from the surveillance team, external end-users and AMR/AMU experts. That information is then used to assess the overall level of integration on a semi-quantitative scale (Table 3). Integration is treated as a continuum (multiple levels of integration), not a dichotomy. The scale defines six levels of OH integration, 0 to 5, for each of four surveillance activities: data collection, analyses, interpretation and dissemination. The levels are defined with respect to the type of information integrated, the integration into operations and processes (e.g., standardization of measures), and the integration of multiple institutions, disciplines and perspectives. Table 3 gives criteria for each level, for example the lowest and highest:
- Data collection: level 0 means the system does not collect data from sources other than humans. Level 5 means AMR data in >1 bacteria species from >1 animal source including retail food, AND from at least one collection point in the environment, AND AMU data in ≥1 animal species and humans.
- Data analysis: level 0 means separate, non-standardized analyses by different analysts in ≥2 organizations. Level 5 means conjoint analysis by a team of analysts, with formal statistical testing and multivariable statistical approaches or modeling.
- Data interpretation: level 0 means there are no formal integrated analyses. Level 5 means a team with multispecies/multidisciplinary/multiperspective expertise, including external collaborators/stakeholders from different sectors.
- Information dissemination: level 0 means animal and human information goes separately to animal and human health stakeholders. Level 5 means conjoint reporting by one organization, with means of dissemination adapted to different end-users.
expected_concepts: data collection, analyses, interpretation, and dissemination

questions.question: How many integrated surveillance systems for ABR were identified in the review, and what is their geographic distribution?
questions.expected_answer: The review identified 14 integrated surveillance systems (from 59 records). All of them operate exclusively in high income countries, with domestic funds: 11 in Europe, two in North America and one in Asia. The systems by country are BELMAP (Belgium), ONERBA (France), the Japan surveillance system (Japan), NethMap/MARAN (Netherlands), ANRESIS / ARCH-Vet (Switzerland), the surveillance system in the United Kingdom, DANMAP (Denmark), NORM/NORM-VET (Norway), SWEDRES/SVARM (Sweden), NARMS (USA), the Canadian CIPARS, the Scottish SONAAR, the German ZoMo and the Finnish FINRES-Vet. The Discussion instead says that 11 were established in the member countries of the European Union (EU).
expected_concepts: exclusively operate in high income countries
member countries of the European Union

questions.question: Based on the study's findings, what is the current state of knowledge regarding the outcomes and impacts of integrating ABR surveillance systems?
questions.expected_answer: Knowledge is limited. The outcomes of integration are poorly described and evidenced, and information on them is rarely available in the literature. A few papers describe some outcomes. Immediate outcomes: improved knowledge about ABR, surveillance capacity to detect correlation in ABR across sectors and between ABU and ABR, and level of awareness on ABR and ABU. Intermediate outcomes: a more responsible use of antibiotics by prescribers (Swedres-Svarm), a decrease in the quantity of antibiotics used in animals and humans (CIPARS, DANMAP, NethMAp/MARAN), new research projects with a One Health perspective (NethMap/MARAN), and the One Health perspective in sectoral or intersectoral policies (DANMAP, NARMS). To a lesser extent, ultimate outcomes were identified as changes in ABR levels (CIPARS). In the example, CIPARS detected a strong correlation between ceftiofur-resistant Salmonella Heidelberg from retail chicken and human infections across Canada. As a result, the poultry sector stopped using ceftiofur, and resistance to this antibiotic in salmonella decreased. Where outcome information exists, the direct causal link with integration is difficult to establish. The information is usually provided by people in charge of the surveillance system, who may lack objectivity. Reliable information was found only for systems at an advanced stage of maturity that have undertaken external evaluations. For less performant and more recent systems, outcome claims seem more aspirational than based on observed facts. Few systems have been formally evaluated for effectiveness and impacts, partly because of a lack of adapted tools and methods. Better integration does not systematically bring greater surveillance performance. The authors call for more evaluation of the impacts of integrated surveillance systems, and of the outcome of the integration models.
expected_concepts: aspirational than based on observed facts
lack of adapted tools and methods
decrease the quantity of antibiotics used

questions.question: Describe the statistical methodology and the number of variables used to generate the typology of the identified surveillance systems.
questions.expected_answer: The typology came from a multiple-correspondence analysis (MCA) followed by a hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA). The MCA used a subset of variables of the full database, which has 39 variables. Variables were selected if information could be retrieved for most of the systems and if they could discriminate between the systems. A Fisher exact test was applied to variables suspected of being highly correlated. "Collection points" was excluded from the MCA because it correlated too closely with "populations/commodities under surveillance". The HCA was applied to the Euclidean distance matrix of the first three axes of the MCA, which represent 44% of variance. A k-means clustering algorithm was used to check the robustness of the HCA. Table 2 marks 16 of the 39 variables as selected for the MCA: variables 2, 4, 8, 10, 14, 15, 18, 24, 25, 28, 30, 31, 32, 37, 38 and 39. The 14 systems grouped into four distinct clusters.
expected_concepts: first three axes of the MCA

questions.question: According to the World Bank, what specific percentage of operational savings can be achieved by co-locating human and animal health laboratories?
questions.expected_answer: 26% savings in operational cost, from hosting national human and animal health laboratories under one roof. The figure is in Table 1 under the Infrastructure domain and is cited to World-Bank [15], the report "People, Pathogens and Our Planet: The Economics of One Health" (2012).
expected_concepts: national human and animal health laboratories

questions.question: How does the One Health multisectoral framework theoretically reduce disease incidence and economic damage during a zoonotic spillover event?
questions.expected_answer: Infection is transmitted and amplified in people after a pathogen from wild animals moves into livestock and causes an outbreak there, and that outbreak amplifies transmission to people (Figure 1A). Early detection and control efforts reduce disease incidence in people and animals (Figure 1B). A One Health approach supports early detection through local, national and global surveillance of zoonotic disease events, with prompt sharing of data for a coordinated response. Sustainable collaboration across all sectors and disciplines lets countries prepare for, detect, assess and respond to these diseases. A coordinated One Health surveillance system can also project disease progression and predict the magnitude and time of a potential outbreak. On economic damage, the paper gives four routes. Improving the efficiency and effectiveness of disease management can reduce cost. Strengthening systems and coordination across the human, animal and environment interface can save costs by preventing duplication of activities and providing a positive return on investment. Analytically driven approaches can predict potential outbreaks at a much lower economic cost than responding after the pathogens might have emerged. Reduced risks from zoonotic diseases also reduce indirect societal losses, such as poorer nutrition and restriction of tourism and trade.

questions.question: Regarding the machine learning modeling referenced from Mollentze et al., what features were used for zoonotic risk prediction and what was the reported accuracy for high-potential viruses?
questions.expected_answer: Mollentze et al. developed machine learning models that use viral and human genome sequence features to predict the probability that an animal virus might jump into humans. The model correctly identified 70.8% of human viruses with high or very high zoonotic potential.
expected_concepts: viral and human genome sequence features
high or very high zoonotic potential

questions.question: What is the reported case fatality rate for bat-originated viral zoonotic diseases in Africa according to the paper?
questions.expected_answer: 61%. The paper reports a 61% case fatality rate for bat-originated viral zoonotic diseases in Africa and attributes it to a meta-analysis (reference 22, Khan et al., a systematic review and meta-analysis of major bat-borne zoonotic viral epidemics in Asia and Africa).

questions.question: How does the paper justify the 'business case' for the One Health approach in the context of zoonotic disease prevention?
questions.expected_answer: The paper makes the case with one cost comparison, cited from reference [4]: zoonotic disease prevention actions cost less than 1/20th the value of lives lost each year. It says this presents a business case to address the heavy burden of emerging, re-emerging and endemic zoonoses in the continent and globally. The argument sits within the context of scarce resources in Africa, where the multiplicity of players needs to address risks at the interface of human, animal and environmental health. The burden is described as economic. Zoonotic outbreaks have caused billions of dollars lost and indirect losses affecting economies, with impacts reaching the tourism, agricultural and financial sectors. Across the continent they cause massive economic losses for both the government and private sector.
expected_concepts: the value of lives lost each year

questions.question: According to the disease burden metrics provided, what percentages of existing and emerging infectious diseases in humans are zoonotic, and what is the resulting impact in low- and middle-income countries?
questions.expected_answer: About 60% of existing and 75% of newly emerging infectious diseases in humans are zoonotic, and most of these diseases originate from wildlife. In many low- and middle-income countries, zoonotic diseases are estimated to cause 2.5 billion cases of human illness and 2.7 million deaths each year.

questions.question: According to the study's findings, what was the reported seroprevalence of Japanese encephalitis in pigs in Vietnam in 2009?
questions.expected_answer: 100% positive by ELISA (sample size 43 pigs, sampled in Vietnam in 2009, 95% CI 89.8–100), from Lindahl et al. 2013 as listed in Table 2.

questions.question: How does the research focus on different pathogen types (viral, bacterial, and parasitic) compare across the reviewed literature, and which countries were identified as high priority for pig and poultry zoonoses?
questions.expected_answer: Of the 358 full-text articles, parasitic pathogens were studied most, at 52% (187/358). Bacterial pathogens came next at 34% (120/358), and viral pathogens last at 14% (51/358). Cambodia and Vietnam stand out for both pigs and poultry. For poultry, the paper says the few zoonotic diseases identified as high priority in Southeast Asia stem mainly from Cambodia and Vietnam: Vietnam had 5 studies (50%) and Cambodia 4 (40%, all on Campylobacter). For pigs, the paper does not use "high priority". It says the data highlight the importance of pig zoonoses, with Cambodia and Vietnam having the highest numbers of studies: Vietnam 14 (39%, the largest number) and Cambodia 9 (30%).
expected_concepts: mainly stemming from Cambodia and Vietnam
Cambodia and Vietnam having the highest numbers

questions.question: Describe the systematic methodology used to select the final 95 publications from the initial search results, including the databases and criteria involved.
questions.expected_answer:
The authors searched the PubMed, Web of Science and Science Direct databases. Only articles in English and from online databases were considered, and the time span was 2011–2022. The last search was on 11 March 2022. The search combined three groups of terms with AND: (i) animal terms (livestock, swine, pig, cattle, poultry, pets, dogs, cats, rats and others); (ii) the Southeast Asian countries or "Southeast Asia"; and (iii) "zoonoses OR zoonotic diseases". It retrieved 2,329 articles: PubMed n = 1043, Web of Science n = 994 and Science Direct n = 292. These were imported into Endnote (version X7), where duplicates were manually identified and removed. The authors also checked that known key articles were in the results.

First screening (titles and abstracts):
- Inclusion: original English research articles (peer-reviewed), published 2011–2022 (by 11th March), presenting prevalence or outbreak data on zoonotic/livestock diseases.
- Exclusion: study not conducted in Southeast Asia, articles about avian influenza, and review articles.
- 674 duplicates were removed and 1,302 publications were excluded: not conducted in Southeast Asia (n = 339), focusing on influenza (n = 145), review articles (n = 91), book chapters (n = 4) and not related to the targeted diseases (n = 723).
- 358 articles went to full-text assessment.

Second screening (full text):
- Inclusion: cross-sectional study, random selection of individuals, and clear description of methods and results.
- 263 articles were excluded: full text unavailable (n = 23), animal selection procedure unclear (n = 156) or results not presented clearly (n = 84). The stated reasons were missing information on how farms and individuals were selected, and poor random selection, such as targeted sampling of animals showing symptoms.
- Grey literature on the articles' reference lists was cross-checked against the search results.

All four authors (TTN, TNM, XSD and HSL) worked independently and classified each article 'Yes' or 'No' for inclusion. Conflicts were settled by discussion among the four reviewers. This left 95 publications in the final qualitative synthesis.
expected_concepts: PubMed, Web of Science and Science Direct
358 articles were included in the full-text assessment

questions.question: What percentage of all human pathogens and emerging diseases affecting humans are estimated to be zoonotic in origin?
questions.expected_answer: An estimated 60% of all human pathogens and 75% of emerging diseases affecting humans are zoonotic.

questions.question: How does animal agriculture facilitate the development and transmission of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) from farms to the human population?
questions.expected_answer:
Development: misuse and overuse of antimicrobials happen on a far greater scale in agriculture than in human medicine, and use in animal agriculture vastly outstrips medical use in humans. Agricultural overuse has been directly linked to the rise of AMR. The drivers named are: group antimicrobial treatment, which causes overuse and inconsistent dosing; use for disease prevention and growth promotion; metaphylactic and prophylactic use; and delivery in feed and water, which gives suboptimal dosing and environmental residues. Under antimicrobial selection, bacteria acquire resistance genes and mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Animal bacteria are one of the most important reservoirs for the horizontal transfer of resistance genes and share most of these genes and MGEs with human pathogens. Some genes (tetX, cfr, optrA) give cross-resistance to protected human last-resort antimicrobials.

Transmission to humans happens by three routes. (1) Direct infection with resistant bacteria, most commonly through consumption of contaminated meat, eggs and dairy. For example, as resistant Campylobacter spp. increase in chickens, many Campylobacter spp. from diarrhea patients are quinolone-resistant. Some resistant hospital bacteria can be traced back to animals. (2) Direct exposure to the farm environment, which shapes the human gut microbiota and resistome. Resistant plasmids spread from chicken to handlers. (3) The environment. Farm waste carrying antimicrobial residues and resistant bacteria creates new resistance reservoirs. Manure used to fertilize crops can move ARGs from animals to soil and crops and then to the human microbiome, and manured soil holds approximately 28,000 times more ARGs than un-manured soil. Animal waste contaminates water sources around farms. More than 70% of administered veterinary antibiotics are excreted into the environment, where residues select resistant environmental bacteria, and plants can absorb and accumulate them. The paper notes that the direct contribution to human infections is debated.
expected_concepts: direct exposure to the farm environment

questions.question: Based on the paper's findings, what are the specific projected global health and economic impacts of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) by the year 2050?
questions.expected_answer: The paper states that by 2050 AMR is predicted to cause 10 million human deaths a year and global healthcare costs of more than $1 trillion USD a year (citing reference [26]). From the same reference, and without naming a year, it also says rising AMR is expected to cut global livestock production by 2.6% to 7.5% a year, with serious consequences for food security.
expected_concepts: in excess of $1 trillion USD per year

questions.question: Which specific beta-lactam resistance gene was most commonly identified in Salmonella isolates from imported chicken, and what was its prevalence?
questions.expected_answer: The plasmid encoded blaCMY-2 was the most common β-lactam resistance gene in Salmonella from imported chicken, found in 124 of the 231 chicken isolates (54%). In total, 170 isolates (74%) had determinants conferring β-lactam resistance.

questions.question: Based on the findings, how do the antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiles and serovar distributions differ between Salmonella found in imported raw chicken versus imported edible leaves?
questions.expected_answer: AMR: resistance was rare among Salmonella from imported edible leaves but common, including MDR, among those from imported raw chicken. Of the 115 leaf isolates, three (3%) had AMR determinants, all from three curry leaf samples, and two (2%) were MDR. 97% of leaf isolates had a genotypic profile in line with the typical intrinsic resistance to aminoglycosides. Of the 231 chicken isolates, 214 (93%) had at least one mutation or resistance gene determinant, most commonly to β-lactams, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines or sulphonamides, and only 17 (7%) had none. 164 (71%) were MDR, and these came from all four countries of origin. In chicken, 170 (74%) had β-lactam resistance determinants (blaCMY-2 the most common, 54%) and 222 (96%) had at least one QRDR mutation. Serovars: leaves showed a larger diversity of serovars than chicken. The paper gives the leaf count as 33, 29 or 30 in different places; chicken has 16 throughout. Curry leaves had the most diversity (23). The most common leaf serovars were S. Virchow (20.9%), S. Newport (11.3%) and S. Bareilly (7.8%). Chicken was dominated by S. Heidelberg (138, 60%), all from Brazil except one isolate of unrecorded origin, followed by S. Minnesota (9%) and S. Enteritidis (7%). All S. Heidelberg isolates had resistance genes for fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and sulphonamides, and the paper reports S. Heidelberg from Brazil as resistant to three or more antimicrobial classes. The authors say antimicrobials are less likely to be used in farming edible leaves, which may account for the larger serovar diversity in leaves.
expected_concepts: two (2%) of which were multidrug resistant

questions.question: What bioinformatics pipeline and specific quantitative threshold did the researchers use to establish genetic relatedness between Salmonella isolates?
questions.expected_answer: SNP typing was derived from the genomic data as described previously (Chattaway et al., 2019; Dallman et al., 2018). The Dallman et al. (2018) reference is SnapperDB. Within an eBG or ST, relatedness was assessed by pairwise SNP differences. Isolates with ≤5 SNPs difference were considered indistinguishable and to have a recent common ancestor. Isolates in the same ≤5 SNPs single linkage cluster were therefore considered genetically related. The Discussion describes this as a 5 SNP cluster.

questions.question: Which specific sequence type was identified as the most prominent in the study, and what was the assigned number for the novel sequence type discovered?
questions.expected_answer: The most prominent sequence type was ST 2274 (5 isolates, 19.2%). The novel sequence type, found in one C. coli isolate, was assigned the number ST 13540 by PubMLST.

questions.question: Based on the findings, how do the genotypic markers for resistance in C. jejuni relate to its observed phenotypic resistance against fluoroquinolones?
questions.expected_answer: Genotype and phenotype correspond closely for fluoroquinolones. All 21 C. jejuni isolates were phenotypically resistant to ciprofloxacin, enrofloxacin and nalidixic acid (CIP, ENR, NAL). The genotypic marker, the gyrA T86I mutation (associated with quinolone resistance), was detected in 95.2% of C. jejuni and was among the most consistently identified resistance markers in C. jejuni. Across all Campylobacter isolates, gyrA T86I was found in 96% of the isolates with phenotypic quinolone resistance. The authors call this a correspondence between fluoroquinolone resistance and gyrA mutations (T86I) (96%) and conclude that phenotypic and genotypic resistance correlate.
expected_concepts: resistant to CIP, ENR, and NAL

questions.question: Describe the bioinformatic tools and methods used for the de novo assembly and the subsequent identification of antimicrobial resistance genes and virulence factors.
questions.expected_answer: Illumina MiSeq paired-end reads were quality-checked with FastQC (Galaxy version 0.74, default parameters) and trimmed with Trimmomatic (Galaxy version 0.36.6; quality cut-off 20, minimum percentage 90%). They were de novo assembled with SPAdes (Galaxy version 3.15.4). Assembly quality was checked with QUAST (Galaxy version 5.2.0), and assemblies with sequence identity > 95% were kept for further analyses. These steps ran on Galaxy at https://usegalaxy.org.au. The assemblies were then analysed with web-based tools. Antimicrobial resistance genes were detected with ResFinder version 4.1, using its default thresholds of 90% sequence identity and 60% minimum length; the paper describes these thresholds as being "to identify chromosomal point mutations". MobileElementFinder V1.0.3 was used to identify mobile genetic elements and their relationship to ARG and VF. Virulence genes were detected with the Virulence Factor Database, using a conservative threshold of blastp E-value 1e-10 and query coverage > 40%.

questions.question: What are the reported annual figures for infections and deaths attributed to ESBL-producing E. coli in the European public health sector?
questions.expected_answer: A study in Europe, cited by Ramos et al. (2020), documented approximately 300,000 infections and 9000 deaths attributed to ESBL-producing E. coli. The paper does not say these figures are annual.

questions.question: How does the paper support the claim that ESBL-producing E. coli transmission constitutes a cycle between animals, the environment, and humans?
questions.expected_answer:
The paper never calls it a cycle. Instead it describes a "transmission continuum" (Figure 1 legend), a "complex web" of transmission pathways that runs in both directions. All of it comes from cited studies.
1. Animals to the environment. Discharge from bovine and poultry slaughterhouses and farms introduces ESBL-producing microorganisms into aquatic ecosystems, which helps them spread among animal and human populations. Stored dairy cow manure can serve as a reservoir for resistance genes. Antimicrobial use in food-producing animals indicates AMR in the environment.
2. Animals and the environment to humans. Multidrug-resistant pathogens reach humans through the consumption of animal-derived foods. Fish and shrimp are reservoirs that threaten human health through raw seafood. blaCTX-M transfer suggests a role in transfer to human gut E. coli after contaminated fish is eaten. The paper also cites the zoonotic potential of ESBL-producing bacteria.
3. Humans back to the environment and to food. Effluent contaminated with human feces, and wastewater from hospitals and healthcare facilities, spread ESBL producers. The Figure 1 legend describes the aquatic ecosystem as a reservoir fed by farm, industrial and hospital sewage. Food handlers can contaminate animal-origin foods.
4. Shared genetics. Plasmid backbones are nearly identical among chickens, cattle and swine and are similar to plasmids from humans. ST10 is found in meats, in healthy individuals and in human blood cultures, and also in animals and animal-origin food. Resistance patterns of isolates from UTI patients resemble those of isolates from meat and animals.
The paper concludes that clonal lineages found in humans, animals and environments call for surveillance within a One Health framework. It also reports a Reunion Island study suggesting animals might not be the primary reservoir of ESBL E. coli in humans.

The paper frames ESBL E. coli spread as a web or "transmission continuum" linking farms, food industries, food handlers and an aquatic reservoir fed by farm, industrial and hospital sewage [9, 10, 11, 12]. Animals and farms release resistant bacteria into the environment through manure and through slaughterhouse and farm discharge, and antimicrobial use in food animals indicates AMR in the environment [3, 6, 13]. From there the bacteria spread to animal and human populations [6], including through raw seafood and contaminated fish [4, 5]. Animals also pass them to humans through animal-derived foods, and the paper cites their zoonotic potential [14, 19]. Humans feed them back into the environment through effluent contaminated with human feces and hospital wastewater [7, 8], and back into food through food handlers and human carriers [17, 18]. Shared genetics tie the compartments together: isolates from animals and food resemble those from human infections [0], plasmids are nearly identical across chickens, cattle and swine and similar to plasmids from humans [1], ST10 occurs in meats, healthy people, human blood cultures and animals [15, 16], and resistance patterns of UTI isolates resemble those from meat and animals [20]. The paper concludes that lineages across humans, animals and environments require One Health surveillance [21]. It also notes a Reunion Island study suggesting animals might not be the primary reservoir for human ESBL E. coli [2].

questions.question: According to the modeling studies reviewed, what specific reduction in ESBL-producing E. coli prevalence within poultry parent stock is necessary to impact human prevalence?
questions.expected_answer: Furusawa et al. (2024), based on modeling studies in poultry farms, proposed reducing the presence of ESBL-producing E. coli in parent stock and broiler farm environments to less than one percent through improved farm management. They proposed that this could effectively reduce their subsequent prevalence in humans.
expected_concepts: parent stock and broiler farm environments

questions.question: According to the 2022 data for human Salmonella cases, what was the specific resistance percentage observed for S. Kentucky against ciprofloxacin?
questions.expected_answer: 72.7% of S. Kentucky isolates from human cases in 2022 were resistant to ciprofloxacin, which the report calls an extremely high proportion. For comparison, overall ciprofloxacin resistance in Salmonella from humans was 18.7%.

questions.question: Based on the reported resistance levels in 2021-2022, what is the clinical implication regarding the use of fluoroquinolones for treating human Campylobacter infections?
questions.expected_answer: In 2021–2022, C. jejuni and C. coli from humans and animals showed high to extremely high resistance to fluoroquinolones. In human isolates in 2022, overall ciprofloxacin resistance was 69.1% in C. jejuni and 70.6% in C. coli. The abstract gives a range of 33.1% (lower in Iceland and Norway) to 100%, and the key findings give 20.6% to 96.6% for human C. jejuni among EU countries. The implication is that fluoroquinolones can no longer be recommended for treating Campylobacter infections in humans. Ciprofloxacin is not advised because of the risk of treatment failure, unless prior testing can confirm susceptibility. Fluoroquinolones are no longer an obvious option for severe human campylobacteriosis in Europe, and macrolides are now the main first-line treatment. As a result, even low levels of resistance to other critically important antimicrobials are a cause for concern in public health.

questions.question: From 2021 onwards, what method was authorized as an alternative to the supplementary (panel 2) phenotypic testing for Salmonella and indicator E. coli isolates showing resistance to extended-spectrum cephalosporins and/or carbapenems?
questions.expected_answer: Whole genome sequencing (WGS). From 2021, WGS was authorised as an alternative method to supplementary (panel 2) phenotypic testing of Salmonella and indicator E. coli isolates with resistance to extended-spectrum cephalosporins and/or carbapenems, and for presumptive ESBL-/AmpC-/CP-producing isolates from the specific monitoring.

questions.question: How does the OHAMRS architecture enable a One Health approach to antimicrobial resistance surveillance?
questions.expected_answer:
OHAMRS integrates human and animal health AMR data at Kenya's national AMR data repository, the Central Data Warehouse (CDW), and collates the data in a single digital platform. It has two core digital components:
(1) interoperability middleware (Open Interop), which integrates data from various sources and connects the CDW to the OHAMRS portal;
(2) a DHIS2 web portal, which analyses and visualises AMR surveillance data from the human and animal health sectors.
Animal health data flow from SILAB into the CDW. The customisable dashboards show data from both sectors and update in near real time as new data are submitted to the CDW. There are 42 dashboards, including 17 for human and animal health priority pathogens, a One Health intersectoral analysis dashboard and a One Health AWaRe classification dashboard. The components are scalable for future inclusion of other One Health sectors (environment, food/feed, aquaculture). Environmental data are not yet included, and the paper proposes adding them.

questions.question: What are the three specific methods used by the 17 human health surveillance sites to submit data to the system, and what is the percentage breakdown for each method?
questions.expected_answer: The 17 surveillance sites report AMR data to the CDW in three ways. (1) A LIMS linked to the CDW, which transmits data directly in near-real-time: 43% of sites. (2) The national standard MS-Excel tool developed by NPHL, with files sent monthly to NPHL for upload to the CDW: 38% (the "MS-Excel template"). (3) WHONET data files sent to NPHL on a weekly or monthly basis: 19%.
expected_concepts: sending WHONET data files to NPHL

questions.question: According to the performance metrics, how many human promoters can methylPipe profile in approximately 50 seconds using a single core?
questions.expected_answer: 100 human promoters in a sample, in about 50 s with one core (max 1GB RAM peak usage), once the data processing step is done.

questions.question: What statistical algorithms does the system use for identifying Differentially Methylated Regions (DMRs), and what are the resource requirements for genome-wide identification?
questions.expected_answer: methylPipe's findDMR function identifies DMRs with paired non-parametric tests: Wilcoxon to compare two groups of samples, and Kruskal-Wallis to compare multiple samples. The tests run inside a dynamic sliding window. Each window is seeded by a cytosine that the binomial test calls methylated and that meets user-defined cutoffs for sequencing depth and methylation difference. The consolidateDMRs function then applies a multiple-testing correction to the p-values. It merges significant regions that lie closer than a user-adjustable threshold and combines their p-values with Fisher's method. A genome-wide DMR identification between 2 WGBS samples took 45 min with 10 cores, with a max 28GB RAM peak on a cluster. On chromosome 1 alone, the same two-sample analysis took 20 min with 1 core (max 4GB RAM peak). DMR identification among 8 WGBS methylomes took 40 min on chromosome 1 with a single core (max 4.9GB RAM peak), and a similar time on a cluster with 10 cores. Parallelization adjusts automatically to the available number of cores and RAM.

questions.question: What are the five critical issues identified by the authors for effective NGS data management?
questions.expected_answer: The abstract lists the five key issues as follows. (1) Adopting a laboratory management system (LIMS) and safeguarding the resulting raw data structure in downstream analyses. (2) Monitoring the flow of the data and standardizing input and output directories and file names, even when multiple analysis protocols are used on the same data. (3) Ensuring complete traceability of the analysis performed. (4) Enabling non-experienced users to run analyses through a graphical user interface (GUI) acting as a front-end for the pipelines. (5) Relying on standard metadata to annotate the datasets and, when possible, using controlled vocabularies, ideally derived from biomedical ontologies. The main-text section headings for the same five issues are: Structuring the raw data; Monitoring the analysis flow; Automatizing and documenting tools; Ease of use; Data reproducibility.
expected_concepts: complete traceability of the analysis performed

questions.question: How does HTS-flow balance the trade-off between user accessibility and analytical flexibility compared to platforms like Galaxy?
questions.expected_answer: According to the paper, HTS-flow offers a web interface (GUI) designed for users without bioinformatics skills, the typical wet-lab scientist. It gives them enough control by choosing a few critical parameters, for example the maximum number of mismatches in alignment or the significance threshold for the peak caller, while leaving the rest as defaults. In Table 1, HTS-flow has "default parameters provided" and the "possibility to tweak some parameters". HTS-flow also runs predefined, easily customizable modular scripts and builds in standard Bioconductor annotation (TxDb, BSgenome). The authors say its automation is higher than in the other tools, mainly because of the integration with the SMITH LIMS and the optional parameter tweaking. Galaxy offers the "possibility to tweak all the parameters". The paper says this high flexibility decreases a lot the automation and limits Galaxy to an audience with a good knowledge of the tools and good IT skills. Galaxy is intended also for non-programmers but is mainly restricted to skilled bioinformaticians for complex tasks. Its pipeline output is not standardized, and expert users must add annotation libraries by modifying pipelines. At the other extreme, QuickNGS achieves high automation at the expense of flexibility, because parameters cannot be set.

questions.question: Which specific software libraries and packages does HTS-flow utilize to ensure genomic reproducibility and perform secondary analysis of mRNA kinetics?
questions.expected_answer: Reproducibility: HTS-flow is based entirely on standard Bioconductor metadata libraries, the TxDb and BSgenome packages, to annotate transcripts and reference genomes. Table 1 lists "TxDB, Bsgenome, compEpiTools" for data reproducibility. The main text instead names compEpiTools as an R/Bioconductor package for further analysis of HTS-flow's output R data objects. mRNA kinetics: HTS-flow integrates nascent and total RNA-seq data and quantifies mRNA synthesis, processing and degradation rates with the INSPEcT Bioconductor package.
expected_concepts: mRNA synthesis, processing and degradation rates

questions.question: How many primary MYC-induced and repressed genes were identified via RNA-seq following a 16-hour inactivation of MYC?
questions.expected_answer: The text gives the counts only approximately: RNA-seq on tumors 16 hours after tet-MYC shutdown defined primary, MYC-dependent genes in equivalent numbers of MYC-induced and repressed genes, ca. 1,200-1,400 each. The Discussion puts each group at over 1,000 genes, close to half of all genes deregulated in tumors relative to normal tissue.

questions.question: Based on the findings regarding the V394D mutant, what is the functional significance of the MYC-MIZ1 interaction in the context of liver tumor development?
questions.expected_answer: The V394D mutant (MYC-VD), a MYC mutant defective in MIZ1 binding, shows that the MYC-MIZ1 interaction is required for MYC to transform liver cells and thus for initiation of liver tumorigenesis, and not for MYC-driven proliferation, for transcriptional activation, or for the aggressiveness of tumours once formed. (1) Tumour onset: tet-MYC-VD animals showed delayed tumorigenesis, with median survival 13 weeks against 5 weeks for tet-MYC-WT, and tet-MYC-VD in the liver showed significantly reduced tumorigenic potential relative to wild-type MYC; once formed, MYC-WT- and MYC-VD-induced tumours appeared equally aggressive, with comparable liver weights and tumour load. (2) Cellular level: MYC-WT and MYC-VD led to similar increases in the number of fetal hepatoblasts recovered per embryo, suggesting equivalent proliferative activities, but MYC-VD showed marked defects in cellular transformation, in vitro by sphere formation in methylcellulose and in vivo by subcutaneous tumour growth in CD1-nude mice, and MYC-ER VD cells showed a marked decrease in sphere-forming ability. Knockdown of MIZ1 with either of two different shRNAs (#8 and #9) decreased sphere-forming efficiency of MYC-ER WT to levels comparable with MYC-ER VD, so the deficit in cellular transformation of the VD mutant was entirely attributable to its interaction with MIZ1. The authors conclude that while retaining normal proliferative activity, MYC-VD is defective in cellular transformation, affecting most likely the frequency of tumour initiation in vivo. (3) Transcriptional mechanism: the defect is selective for repression. Secondary response genes were similarly deregulated in both genotypes, and MYC-VD is as effective as WT in transcriptional activation, whereas primary MYC-repressed genes showed weaker downregulation in MYC-VD tumours, with 285 genes repressed with a 2-fold lower efficiency in MYC-VD relative to MYC-WT tumours, enriching for functional categories including cell adhesion/response to wounding. Already at a pretumoral stage, in tet-MYC-WT and tet-MYC-VD fetal hepatoblasts purified by magnetic cell sorting, the two populations showed comparable activation of the MYC-induced gene Smpdl3b but defective repression of Cdkn1a by MYC-VD. Hence MIZ1-dependent repression plays an important role in MYC-induced liver tumorigenesis, and the requirement for the MYC-MIZ1 interaction differs among tumour types: suppression of TGFb-mediated senescence in T-cell lymphomas, maintenance of stemness in medulloblastoma, and tumour initiation in the liver in this work.

questions.question: How does MYC activity influence RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII) across different gene categories, and how does this relate to the predictive power of MYC-binding profiles?
questions.expected_answer: MYC influences RNA Pol II loading on both activated and repressed genes. Up- or downregulation of gene expression is paralleled by equivalent changes in RNA Pol II binding at promoters. During the C→T transition, primary and secondary genes (classes 2/5 and 1/4) show similar variations in Pol II binding. During the T→Toff transition, only primary MYC-dependent genes (classes 2,3/5,6) are affected. Pol II abundance changes consistently on gene bodies as well as on promoters, but stalling indices are not consistently affected in any regulatory category. Whether regulated by MYC in a primary or secondary manner, activated and repressed genes show generally consistent changes in Pol II loading and elongation. MYC-binding profiles, by contrast, are not predictive of MYC-dependent regulation. Peak presence, localization relative to the TSS and binding intensity do not distinguish primary from secondary MYC-responsive genes. Increases in binding neither discriminate MYC-dependent from -independent responses nor correlate with the extent of changes in mRNA levels. Enhancer recruitment does not discriminate them either. Primary repressed genes are less frequently and more weakly bound than nonregulated genes, and primary induced genes show the opposite. So genome-wide MYC binding alone does not discriminate primary from secondary targets and no simple rule links it to regulation, whereas changes in RNA Pol II activity correspond to the DEG categories.
expected_concepts: MYC inﬂuences RNA Pol II loading
paralleled by equivalent changes in RNA Pol II binding
stalling indices were not consistently affected
did not allow distinguishing primary from secondary
no simple rule could be drawn

questions.question: What specific Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) and Positive Predictive Value (PPV) did PDBinder achieve on the holo (bound) test set of 239 complex pairs?
questions.expected_answer: On the holo test set (LigASite, 239 apo/holo structure pairs), PDBinder achieved an MCC of 0.313 and a PPV of 0.413.

questions.question: How does PDBinder's performance on apo proteins compare to its performance on holo proteins, and what does this suggest about the method's robustness?
questions.expected_answer:
PDBinder does only slightly worse on apo (unbound) structures than on holo (ligand-bound) structures:
- MCC: 0.313 holo, 0.271 apo
- PPV: 0.413 holo, 0.372 apo
- Sensitivity: 0.295 holo, 0.251 apo
- Specificity: 0.983 holo, 0.984 apo
- ROC AUC (Figure 1 legend): 0.780 holo, 0.767 apo

That is a 13% drop in MCC and a 10% drop in PPV. Q-SiteFinder drops 35% in MCC and 28% in PPV.

On robustness, the authors say performance "suffers only a modest decrease" from holo to apo and that apo performance is "quite similar" to holo. Their explanation is that the method considers the conformation of groups of three residues only. The ligand can alter the overall structure of the binding pocket, but the local conformation of these small subsets of residues is mostly preserved. They call this extremely important for real-world applications, where the location of the binding site is unknown because the protein has been crystallized without a ligand.

questions.question: Explain the role of 'Spatial Clustering' in the PDBinder methodology and the specific parameters used for this step.
questions.expected_answer: Spatial clustering filters PDBinder's predictions. On the training set the propensity value alone gave about 40% correct predictions. Binding sites are contiguous regions of the surface, so PDBinder discards spatially isolated predictions: any prediction without at least one other prediction within a defined radius is dropped. The authors tested radii from 1.0 Å to 20.0 Å in increments of 1 Å. The best clustering radius was 10.0 Å, close to the mean binding-site radius in the training set (8.97 ± 0.20 Å, 99% confidence interval). This threshold raised the positive predictive value by 5.4% and the MCC by 0.018, with a loss of 1.4% in sensitivity. The Table 1 results use a single propensity threshold for all amino acids together with spatial clustering at a 10 Angstrom threshold. With residue-specific thresholds, adding spatial clustering did not recover the slightly worse average performance (data not shown).
expected_concepts: at least another prediction in a defined radius

questions.question: According to the paper's subsampling analysis, what is the minimum number of cis-mapped reads required to generate reproducible 4C profiles?
questions.expected_answer: The subsampling analysis shows that roughly 50,000–100,000 cis-mapped 4C reads are sufficient to generate reproducible 4C profiles. The paper gives this range, not one exact minimum. Separately, the authors routinely aim for ~1 million reads per experiment.

questions.question: How does the distribution of sequencing reads across the genome serve as an indicator of a successful 4C-seq experiment?
questions.expected_answer: A successful 4C-seq experiment should always show a strong enrichment of contacts with DNA fragments flanking the viewpoint on the linear chromosome, in particular fragments co-occupying the same TAD. Preferably >60% of the reads map to the chromosome containing the viewpoint (the cis chromosome), with most reads mapping within 1 Mb of the viewpoint. Self-ligation of the viewpoint fragment and undigested DNA can heavily skew these metrics, so they should be assessed after exclusion of the top fragments (fragMappedCisCorr and cov1Mb). The viewpoint should also capture many different fragments: >40%, preferably >60%, of mappable fragment ends within 100 kb of the viewpoint should be captured at least once (capt100Kb > 40%). Low-complexity libraries (capt100Kb < 40%) often result from bad template quality rather than insufficient sequencing depth. With (previously frozen) primary tissue, the cis percentage frequently drops to ~50%. That drop indicates random ligations, but the local coverage around the viewpoint is often still good enough to draw reproducible conclusions.

questions.question: What is the function of the 'motifPosperc' metric within the pipe4C data processing pipeline, and what value indicates high specificity?
questions.expected_answer: motifPosperc is a data quality metric in the pipe4C report file, used for quality assessment of individual 4C-seq experiments. It is the percentage of reads in the FASTQ file in which the first RE motif position is equal to the most occurring first RE enzyme motif position. To compute it, reads are scanned from the 5′ side for the first primary RE motif. The pipeline then trims all reads from their 5′-end to that fixed location, leaving the RE motif intact. In a good 4C experiment, with no a-specific amplification from undesired genomic locations, the value should typically be >90%. A lower percentage might indicate off target binding of the primer to the genome or low sequence quality reads.
expected_concepts: most occurring first RE enzyme motif position
off target binding of the primer

questions.question: How do the storage and cost-efficiency optimization strategies in the nf-core framework compare to the scheduling and transparency features of the Snakemake workflow system?
questions.expected_answer:
The two papers address different layers, and neither compares itself with the other.

nf-core (here the nf-core/sarek 3 pipeline) saves storage and cost through pipeline design and cloud set-up:
- Storage: intermediate files are CRAM instead of BAM. CRAM stores only differences to the reference, and work-directory storage for pre-processing dropped by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB), at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage. The default number of interval groups is set to 21, because more scattering gave no runtime benefit but increased storage. Together the two changes cut storage requirements by two-thirds plus a further factor of 5.
- Cost: the abstract credits the 70% cost reduction to the CRAM format (less storage) and more intra-sample parallelization (less runtime) together. Input FastQ files can be split and mapped in parallel, which cut the median mapping runtime to 37% at a plateau of 12 shards. Costs were evaluated on AWS Batch using spot instances. The saving is stated four ways: a 70% cost reduction (abstract), a 69% reduction (introduction), costs reduced to approximately 30% (Results) and to 50% (Discussion). Table 2 gives $68.04 per normal sample for 2.7.2 against $20.82 for 3.1.1, about $20 per germline analysis. Users can cut costs further by choosing cheaper AWS regions and capping the spot price.

Snakemake offers engine-level features:
- Scheduling: a mixed integer linear program (MILP) replaced the earlier greedy scheduler. It runs at the start of execution and whenever a job finishes, and selects jobs without exceeding resources such as hard drive space, I/O capacity and CPU cores. Its goals are fast execution, preferring high-priority jobs and quickly deleting temporary output files. The MILP's four criteria are job priority, number of used cores, deleting temporary files as soon as possible, and reducing the lifetime of temporary files that cannot yet be deleted.
- Transparency: the ability to judge whether an analysis is methodologically valid. Snakemake tracks input files, output files, parameters, software and code of each job and makes them available in self-contained, interactive HTML based reports that show provenance and runtime statistics and are portable and archivable.

Comparison: both act on disk storage, sarek through file format and scattering defaults, Snakemake through scheduling that deletes temporary files early. Only sarek reports measured cloud cost savings; only Snakemake describes provenance reporting for transparency.

The nf-core/sarek paper reduces storage at the pipeline level by adopting CRAM, which stores only differences to the reference and cut work-directory storage by 65%, from 170.4 TB to 59.7 TB, at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage [0, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. It sets the default number of interval groups to 21, because more scattering did not reduce runtime further but increased storage, and the two changes together cut storage by two-thirds and a further factor of 5 [9, 10, 11, 12]. It also shortens runtime by intra-sample parallelization, splitting input FastQ files and mapping them in parallel, which cut the median mapping runtime to 37% at a plateau of 12 shards [0, 39, 40], and the abstract credits the 70% cost reduction to the storage and runtime gains together [0, 1]. It evaluated costs on AWS Batch with spot instances [13, 15], and states the saving as a 70% reduction, a 69% reduction, a reduction to approximately 30% and a reduction to 50% [1, 2, 14, 17], with $68.04 against $20.82 per normal sample in Table 2 and about $20 per germline analysis [3, 16]. Users can reduce costs further through cheaper AWS regions and a spot price cap [18].
