Snakemake instead schedules jobs with a mixed integer linear program, which replaced a greedy scheduler [24, 30], run at the start of execution and whenever a job finishes [20], within resources including hard drive space, I/O capacity and CPU cores [19]. It aims for fast execution, high-priority jobs and quick deletion of temporary files [21, 22, 23], and its MILP criteria are priority, used cores, deleting temporary files as soon as possible and shortening the lifetime of temporary files not yet deletable [25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. For transparency, the ability to judge whether an analysis is methodologically valid [31, 32, 33], Snakemake tracks each job's inputs, outputs, parameters, software and code and presents them in self-contained, interactive HTML reports that show provenance and runtime statistics and are portable and archivable [34, 35, 36, 37, 38]. Both address disk storage, sarek through file format and scattering defaults [6, 11], Snakemake through scheduling that deletes temporary files early [23, 28]; only sarek reports measured cloud cost savings [14, 16], and only Snakemake describes provenance reports [34, 35, 36].
expected_concepts: default number of interval groups to 21
temporary output files should be quickly deleted

questions.question: How does the 'all-in-one' preprocessing approach of fastp complement the visualization and quality control capabilities of MultiQC in a bioinformatics pipeline?
questions.expected_answer:
Neither paper mentions the other, so the complementarity is inferred from what each paper says about its own tool. In the past, multiple tools were used for FASTQ quality control and preprocessing, and reading and loading the data multiple times made preprocessing slow and I/O inefficient. fastp is an all-in-one FASTQ preprocessor. It performs quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering, per-read quality pruning and other operations in a single scan of the FASTQ data. For each run it writes HTML and JSON reports. The HTML report shows quality control for pre- and post-filtered data on a single page, and the JSON holds all the data visualized in the HTML report. MultiQC fills a different gap. Nearly all logs and reports are produced on a per-sample basis, so MultiQC scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and creates a single report visualizing output from multiple tools across many samples. Its shared plots allow comparison between samples. It supports 22 common tools (aligners, processing tools and QC programs) and functions as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines. In a pipeline, then, fastp provides the preprocessing and a per-run QC report, and MultiQC provides the cross-sample, cross-tool view. Neither paper states that MultiQC parses fastp output.

fastp combines quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering, per-read quality pruning and other operations into a single scan of the FASTQ data [1,2,7], which avoids the multi-tool approach that had to read and load the data multiple times [0,16]. For each run it generates HTML and JSON reports [3,5]. A single HTML page shows quality control reports for pre- and post-filtered data, which allows direct comparison of quality statistics altered by preprocessing [4,6], and the JSON contains all the data visualized in the HTML report [5]. MultiQC addresses the fact that logs and QC reports are produced on a per-sample basis [9]: it scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and creates a single report visualizing output from multiple tools across many samples, with shared plots for comparison between samples [8,10,11,14]. It exports parsed data and functions as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines [13,15]. Read together, fastp supplies the preprocessing and a per-run QC report, and MultiQC supplies the aggregation and visualization across samples and tools [3,4,8,10,15]. The MultiQC paper gives only a count of 22 supported tools [12], and neither paper names the other tool or states that MultiQC reads fastp's reports.
expected_concepts: single scan of the FASTQ data

questions.question: What common technical methodologies do Sarek, Snakemake, and the nf-core framework share to ensure reproducibility and portability across different computing environments?
questions.expected_answer:
All three provide software through Conda (Bioconda) environments or Docker and Singularity containers, and all three run across platforms including clusters/HPC schedulers and cloud. Sarek installs all its tools in Conda and pushes them to DockerHub, so they are available from a Conda environment or as Docker or Singularity containers "to ensure reproducibility"; containers let it install on all POSIX compatible systems, and through Nextflow it runs on Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF, Kubernetes, Google Cloud and AWS. Snakemake deploys a software environment per rule via the Conda package manager, or pulls a container image and runs the job using Singularity, which makes the environment portable across operating systems and increases reproducibility; it scales to cluster middleware, grid computing and cloud computing. In nf-core, module tools are typically accessible through (bio)conda with corresponding Docker and Singularity containers from Biocontainers, enabling portability and reproducibility for each module; nf-core/sarek, written in Nextflow, is portable to cloud vendors and common HPC schedulers.

The shared method is software deployment through Conda environments (Bioconda in Sarek and nf-core), with Docker or Singularity containers as the alternative: Sarek installs all its tools in Conda and pushes them to DockerHub [0, 1, 2], Snakemake deploys an environment or container per rule [5, 6, 7] and nf-core provides one per module [10]. Each paper credits this with reproducibility and/or portability [1, 3, 8, 10]. All three also run across cluster and cloud environments: Sarek and nf-core/sarek through Nextflow [4, 11], and Snakemake through cluster middleware, grid and cloud computing [9].

questions.question: How could integrating fastp and the nf-core framework's data management optimizations improve the performance and resource usage of the Sarek WGS workflow?
questions.expected_answer:
Baseline: the original Sarek WGS run on a 90x/90x tumour/normal dataset took 48 hours and 21 minutes and 1790 CPU h, of which mapping, merging and deduplication took 1081 CPU h. Total storage including temporary data was 3.7 TB. The paper recommends 16 cores, 128 GB RAM and at least 4 TB of free storage.

fastp: it does quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering and per-read quality pruning in a single scan of the FASTQ data. It is 2–5 times faster than Trimmomatic or Cutadapt and can split its output into multiple files for parallel processing.

fastP in nf-core/sarek 3 (introduced with release v3.0) shards the FastQ files with optional adapter trimming in one step:
- Alignment can run on smaller machines, and the computation is faster.
- Median mapping runtime fell to 37%, reaching a plateau at 12 shards.
- Storage rose because sub-FastQs are written to disk, and mapping CPU hours stayed about the same.
- Running the split as a dedicated process in place of splitFastq() gives resource assignment, automatic retries on job failure and resume.
- Doing trimming, QC and sharding in one step, together with more tailored interval splitting, reduced the needed CPU hours by 66%.

Data management:
- CRAM intermediates cut pre-processing work-directory storage by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB).
- Average pre-processing CPU hours were 3252.37 with CRAM against 3,761.07 with BAM, at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage.
- Runtime gains stop beyond 21 interval groups, and reducing scattering cuts storage by a further factor of 5.

Overall on AWS:
- One normal sample went from $68.04, 46h8m and 1118.4 CPU hours (2.7.2) to $20.82, 12h4m and 342.5 CPU hours (3.1.1).
- The results text reports single-sample CPU hours reduced by approximately 70%, runtime by 84%, and costs to approximately 30%.
- Elsewhere the paper gives the cost saving as 70%, 69%, or costs reduced to 50%.

The original Sarek WGS workflow was recommended to run on 16 cores, 128 GB RAM and at least 4 TB of free storage [0]. A 90x/90x tumour/normal run took 48 hours and 21 minutes and 1790 CPU h, mapping, merging and deduplication took 1081 CPU h, and total storage including temporary data was 3.7 TB [2, 3, 29]. That workflow already used scatter-gather to spread load across CPU cores [1]. fastp performs quality control, adapter trimming and filtering in a single scan, avoiding the slow, I/O-inefficient repeated reading of data [4, 5]. It is 2–5 times faster than Trimmomatic or Cutadapt and can split its output for parallel alignment [6, 7, 8, 9]. In nf-core/sarek 3, fastP shards FastQ files with optional adapter trimming in one step, so alignment runs on smaller machines and computation is faster [10, 11]. Median mapping runtime fell to 37%, with a plateau at 12 shards [12]. Sharding increased storage and left CPU hours about the same [13, 14]. Running the split as a dedicated process gives resource assignment, automatic retries and resume [16]. Together with tailored interval splitting, the single fastP step reduced CPU hours by 66% [15]. Storing intermediates as CRAM cut pre-processing work-directory storage by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB) and lowered average CPU hours from 3,761.07 to 3252.37, at the cost of a 34% increase in memory [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Scattering gives no runtime benefit beyond 21 interval groups, and reducing it cuts storage by a further factor of 5 [22, 23]. On AWS, one normal sample went from $68.04, 46h8m and 1118.4 CPU hours to $20.82, 12h4m and 342.5 CPU hours [30]. The paper reports the overall effect as approximately 70% fewer CPU hours and 84% less runtime [25]. It gives the cost saving variously as costs reduced to approximately 30%, a 70% or 69% reduction, or costs reduced to 50% [24, 26, 27, 28].
expected_concepts: reduction of the median runtime to 37%
reduces the needed CPU hours by 66%

questions.question: In the context of scaling large-scale genomic analyses, how do the parallelization strategies of the nf-core framework differ from the job scheduling approach of Snakemake?
questions.expected_answer:
nf-core/sarek, a Nextflow pipeline from nf-core, gets its parallelism by splitting the data. The FastQ files are split into shards with fastP and mapped in parallel. Mapping runtime plateaus at 12 shards, with the median runtime reduced to 37%. Genomic regions are processed in parallel after duplicate marking, and small regions are grouped to reduce the number of jobs. Scatter/gather across genomic regions is used for BQSR and variant calling, and the variant calling tools all run in parallel. Interval-group parallelization has clear limits: there is no further benefit beyond 21 interval groups. Job execution is left to Nextflow, which runs on several cloud vendors and common HPC schedulers. Splitting runs as a dedicated process, so it gets regular job submission with resource assignment, automatic retries and resume.

Snakemake does the job scheduling itself. At the start of execution, and whenever a job finishes and new jobs become pending, it selects the subset of jobs to run without exceeding resources such as hard drive space, I/O capacity and CPU cores. It does this by solving a mixed integer linear program (MILP), which replaced the greedy scheduler of its first releases. Four criteria are applied in lexicographical order: job priority first, then the number of used cores (the extent of parallelization), then deleting temporary files as soon as possible, then reducing the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass. By default all jobs have the same priority, so the MILP maximizes used cores while removing as many temporary files as possible. On a cluster or cloud, Snakemake passes resource requirements to the middleware. By default it submits each job separately, but it can partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs submitted together as a single cluster or cloud job. Scaling to a platform only requires changing command line parameters.

nf-core/sarek parallelizes by splitting the data inside the pipeline. It shards FastQ files with fastP and maps them in parallel, with runtime gains plateauing at 12 shards [0, 1, 2]. It processes genomic regions in parallel, grouping small ones to reduce job count, with scatter/gather for BQSR and variant calling [3, 4, 5, 6], and it runs the variant callers in parallel [7]. Interval-group parallelization gives no further benefit beyond 21 interval groups [8, 9]. Job execution is handed to Nextflow and the cloud vendors or HPC schedulers beneath it, and splitting runs as regular job submission with resources, retries and resume [10, 11]. Snakemake instead solves scheduling in its own engine. Each time jobs become pending, it selects which ones to run within resource limits by solving a MILP, which replaced an earlier greedy scheduler [14, 15, 16, 17]. The MILP ranks four criteria: priority, then used cores (parallelization), then temporary file deletion, then the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass, and by default maximizes used cores while removing temporary files [18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. On clusters and clouds it passes resource requirements to the middleware [25]. It submits jobs separately by default but can partition the DAG into subgraphs submitted as one job [26, 27]. Scaling to another platform only changes command line parameters [12, 13].
expected_concepts: maximize the number of used cores

questions.question: How do the implementation languages and performance-optimization strategies of fastp, SeqKit, and Cutadapt differ in addressing computational bottlenecks in sequence data processing?
questions.expected_answer:
fastp is developed in C/C++ (printed "Cþþ" in the text layer) with multi-threading. It says earlier tools were slow because most were written in Python or Java with limited multi-threading, and because they read and loaded data multiple times. Its strategies:
- multi-threaded parallel processing, with reads packed in groups of N = 1000 and each pack consumed by one thread in a pool
- all operations in a single scan of the FASTQ data
- a duplication array and a counting array in place of a hash table, for faster access

fastp reports being 2–5 times faster than other FASTQ preprocessing tools such as Trimmomatic or Cutadapt (abstract). In its speed evaluation, with all tools run on a single thread, the other tools take 3–5 times longer than fastp (Results). In Table 1, fastp SE takes 6 min (129397.9 reads/s) and Cutadapt SE 18 min (43132.6 reads/s).

SeqKit is implemented in Go. It names file I/O, and sequence record parsing, as the main bottleneck. Its strategies:
- its own parsing package, bio, with performance similar to klib (kseq.h)
- a custom buffered file reader instead of Go's "bufio", which increased speed and lowered memory use
- CPU-intensive processes parallelized by Goroutines, with a default of two threads (three or more gave no further significant improvement)
- a slice indexed by ASCII code instead of a map for reverse complement, a ~20× speedup
- lower memory use by not loading all records into memory, by MD5 digests, and by a two-pass read mode with a FASTA index

Cutadapt is mainly written in Python, but for speed its alignment algorithm is implemented in C as a Python extension module. In theory its run time is dominated by alignment, O(nk). In practice, reading and parsing the input files take more than half of the time. It trims about 1 million reads per minute (0.06 ms per read) on a single core of a 2.66 GHz Intel Core 2 processor.

The three tools use different languages: fastp is developed in C/C++ [3, 5], SeqKit in Go [13], and Cutadapt mainly in Python, with its alignment algorithm in C as a Python extension module for speed [27]. fastp and SeqKit both parallelize. fastp uses a thread pool that consumes packs of 1000 reads [6, 7, 8]. SeqKit runs CPU-intensive processes as Goroutines [16] and defaults to two threads, because three or more gave no further significant improvement [25, 26]. Cutadapt reports its speed on a single core [30]. They target different bottlenecks. fastp blames high-level languages, limited multi-threading and repeated loading of data [0, 1], answers with a single scan of the data [2], and uses arrays in place of a hash table for faster access [9]. SeqKit names file I/O and record parsing as the bottleneck [14, 24]. It answers with its own parsing package [15], a custom buffered reader [17, 18], a slice in place of a map with a ~20× speedup [19, 20], and memory savings from streaming, MD5 digests and an indexed two-pass mode [21, 22, 23]. Cutadapt's time is dominated by alignment in theory, O(nk), and that is the part moved into C [27, 28], yet in practice reading and parsing input take more than half of the time [29]. fastp reports being 2–5 times faster than tools including Cutadapt [4]. In its Results, with all tools run on a single thread, the other tools take 3–5 times longer [10, 11], and in its Table 1 Cutadapt SE takes 18 min against fastp's 6 min [12].
expected_concepts: single scan of the FASTQ data
implemented in the Go programming language
implemented in C as a Python extension module
reading and parsing the input files

questions.question: In the context of RNA-seq analysis, how do the mapping and quantification methods of STAR and Salmon address technical challenges before downstream differential expression analysis in DESeq2?
questions.expected_answer:
STAR (mapping) targets the non-contiguous transcript structure, relatively short read lengths, increasing sequencing throughput and multiple copies of related genomic sequences. Its method is a sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, followed by seed clustering and stitching. This detects splice junctions in a single alignment pass without a priori knowledge of junctions. MMPs serve as anchors that are extended, which allows alignments with mismatches. Poly-A tails, library adapter sequences and poor sequencing quality tails are identified. The search finds all distinct genomic matches for multimapping reads, and STAR reports every alignment scoring within a user-defined range below the highest score.

Salmon (quantification) targets technical biases from fragmentation, amplification and sequencing, which, uncorrected, can lead to high false positive rates in differential expression studies. It quantifies either by quasi-mapping raw reads to a transcriptome index, without intermediate alignment files, or from pre-computed alignments in SAM or BAM format. Its model accounts for positional biases in coverage, 5′ and 3′ sequence-specific biases, fragment-level GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution, with parameters learned in the online phase. It estimates the conditional probability that a fragment came from each transcript to which it multimaps. It also estimates abundance uncertainty due to random sampling and multimapping. The paper says GC bias correction improves the reliability of subsequent differential expression analysis. In DE testing, Salmon's estimates gave 53% to 250% higher sensitivity at the same FDRs and fewer false-positive calls.

DESeq2 (downstream) starts from a count matrix of reads unambiguously mapped to a gene, that is, per-gene counts. Size factors estimated by the median-of-ratios method account for differences in sequencing depth. Gene-specific normalization factors for technical biases such as GC content or gene length, or estimates of average transcript length, can be supplied. DESeq2 contrasts its per-gene counts with algorithms that use probabilistic assignments of reads to transcripts. None of the papers describes STAR or Salmon output being passed to DESeq2.

STAR addresses non-contiguous transcripts, short reads, high throughput and multicopy sequences [0, 1]. It uses sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, followed by seed clustering and stitching [2], and detects splice junctions in a single alignment pass without prior junction knowledge [3]. It extends MMP anchors to allow mismatches and identifies poly-A tails, adapters and poor-quality tails [5, 6]. It finds all genomic matches for multimapping reads and reports alignments within a user-defined score range of the best [4, 7]. Salmon targets the technical biases of fragmentation, amplification and sequencing, which, uncorrected, can cause high false positive rates in differential expression studies [8, 10]. It quantifies from quasi-mapping of raw reads, without intermediate alignment files, or from pre-computed SAM/BAM alignments [14, 15]. It models positional, 5′/3′ sequence-specific, fragment-level GC, strand-specific and fragment-length effects [16]. It assigns multimapping fragments to transcripts probabilistically and estimates the resulting abundance uncertainty [11, 17]. The paper reports that GC correction improves the reliability of subsequent DE analysis [9]. In DE testing its estimates gave 53% to 250% higher sensitivity at the same FDRs and fewer false-positive calls [12, 13]. DESeq2 starts from a count matrix of reads unambiguously or uniquely assigned to genes [18, 19, 23]. It normalizes for sequencing depth with median-of-ratios size factors [20, 21]. It accepts supplied gene-specific normalization factors for GC content, gene length or average transcript length [22, 25]. It contrasts its per-gene counts with probabilistic read-to-transcript assignment [24].
expected_concepts: probabilistic assignments of reads to transcripts

questions.question: How do the methodological approaches of Cutadapt and Salmon differ in their treatment of technical artifacts in RNA-seq data, and what are the specific implications for downstream analysis?
questions.expected_answer:
Cutadapt edits the reads themselves, before read mapping.
- What it targets: in small RNA sequencing the reads are longer than the RNA, so they contain parts of the 3' adapter.
- How it finds the adapter: error-tolerantly, using 'regular' or slightly modified semi-global alignments.
- What it does with the read: it can either trim or discard reads in which an adapter occurs. It trims the read when the error rate is below the allowed maximum, and reads must be discarded entirely when the adapter is a sign of contamination.
- Other trimming: it can also trim low-quality read ends using the same algorithm as BWA.
- Colour space: it also removes the colour preceding the adapter.
- Stated implications: only the relevant part of the read is passed on to further analysis, and removing that colour avoids a spurious mismatch during read mapping.

Salmon (in quasi-mapping mode) takes raw, unaligned reads and performs quantification directly, without generating intermediate alignment files. It handles artifacts inside quantification.
- What it models: positional biases in coverage, sequence-specific biases at the 5′ and 3′ ends of fragments, fragment-level GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution.
- How: these models are learned in the online phase, including a foreground and background GC-bias model, and are used to re-estimate the effective length of each transcript.
- Read errors: when alignments are the input, it models substitution and indel rates in bins along each read.
- Stated implications: uncorrected biases can confound downstream analyses and lead to high false positive rates in differential expression. GC-bias correction improves the accuracy of abundance estimates and the reliability of DE analysis.

Salmon's reported DE results:
- Sensitivity 53% to 250% higher at the same FDRs. The Figure 1c legend instead gives 53%–450% over kallisto and 210%–250% over eXpress.
- Fewer false-positive DE calls. The Figure 1d legend says fewer than half as many.
- A ~2.6-fold decrease in genes called DE.
- Isoform switching seen under kallisto or eXpress estimates is eliminated.

The two tools handle different artifacts at different stages, and neither paper compares itself with the other.

Cutadapt acts on the reads themselves, before read mapping. The artifact is 3' adapter sequence in reads that are longer than the small RNA [0, 1, 5]. Cutadapt finds the adapter error-tolerantly with semi-global alignments and trims the read when the error rate is below the allowed maximum [5, 9, 10]. It can instead discard reads in which an adapter occurs, as when the adapter signals contamination [4, 6], and it can also trim low-quality ends [7]. Its stated downstream consequences are that only the relevant part of the read goes on to further analysis and that, in colour space, removing the preceding colour avoids a spurious mismatch during read mapping [2, 3, 8].

In quasi-mapping mode, Salmon takes raw, unaligned reads and quantifies them directly, without intermediate alignment files [16]. During its online phase it learns models of positional, 5′/3′ sequence-specific and fragment GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution [14, 15, 18]. It corrects for these biases by re-estimating effective transcript lengths [19]. With alignments as input, it models substitution and indel rates in bins along each read [20]. Its stated motivation is that other quantifiers lack rich bias models, and that uncorrected biases cause high false positive rates in differential expression and confound downstream analyses [12, 13, 17].

With GC-bias correction, Salmon reports more accurate abundance estimates and more reliable DE analysis [11]. DE sensitivity at the same FDR is 53% to 250% higher in the main text, and 53%–450% over kallisto and 210%–250% over eXpress in the Figure 1c legend [21, 22]. Salmon also reports fewer false-positive DE calls (fewer than half as many in the Figure 1d legend), a ~2.6-fold decrease in genes called DE, and elimination of the isoform switching seen under kallisto or eXpress estimates [23, 24, 25, 26].
expected_concepts: high false positive rates in differential expression

questions.question: How do the quality control and preprocessing capabilities of fastp and Cutadapt integrate with the visualization goals of MultiQC in high-throughput sequencing pipelines?
questions.expected_answer:
None of the papers describes a direct integration. Each describes a complementary role.

fastp: performs quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering and per-read quality pruning in a single scan of the FASTQ data. It generates its own reports in HTML and JSON formats, with statistics for pre-filtering and post-filtering data. The JSON contains all the data visualised in a standalone HTML report.

Cutadapt: a command-line adapter trimmer. It finds and removes adapters, can trim or discard reads in which an adapter occurs, and can trim low-quality read ends. It solves a small but important task within sequencing pipelines. In the older multi-tool combination it was used for adapter trimming, alongside FASTQC for quality control.

MultiQC: targets the problem that logs and QC reports are produced on a per-sample basis. It scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and creates a single summary report visualising results across all samples, through submodules that contribute only when they find logs. At the time of writing it supported 22 common bioinformatics tools, including processing tools and QC programs, and it functions as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines.

None of the papers states that MultiQC parses fastp or Cutadapt output specifically.

fastp does quality control and preprocessing in a single scan of the FASTQ data [0]. Cutadapt finds and removes adapters, trims or discards reads that contain one, and trims low-quality ends, a small but important task within sequencing pipelines [1, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. fastp also writes its own per-run HTML and JSON reports covering pre-filtering and post-filtering data, and the JSON holds all the visualised data [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. MultiQC addresses the fact that tool logs and QC reports are produced per sample [12]. It scans directories for log files and QC reports and combines output from multiple tools across all samples into a single summary report, through submodules that contribute when they find logs [13, 14, 15]. Its 22 supported tools include processing tools and QC programs [16], and it serves as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines [17]. The papers do not state that fastp or Cutadapt output is among what MultiQC parses [16].
expected_concepts: single scan of the FASTQ data
reports in HTML and JSON formats

questions.question: Contrast the algorithmic approaches used by STAR and SeqKit to manage large-scale genomic sequence data efficiently.
questions.expected_answer:
STAR trades memory for speed. It runs a sequential maximum mappable seed (MMP) search in uncompressed suffix arrays, applied only to the unmapped portions of each read, then a clustering/stitching/scoring step. The binary SA search scales logarithmically with reference genome length. Uncompressed SAs are faster than compressed SAs but use more memory: STAR requires 27 GB of RAM for the human genome. One SA is shared among all threads, so RAM does not grow with thread count, and throughput scales close to linearly with the number of cores. Its sparse-SA option cuts peak RAM to 15.6 to 16.0 GB (Table 1) at the cost of a 25% decrease in mapping speed.

SeqKit treats file I/O as the bottleneck and keeps memory use low. It parses FASTA/Q with its own lightweight bio package, using a custom buffered file reader in place of Go's bufio, which increased speed and lowered memory usage. It parallelises CPU-intensive processes with Goroutines, though more than two threads gave no significant further gain. It stores complementary sequences in a slice indexed by the byte's ASCII code instead of a map, a ~20× speedup. Most subcommands do not load all records into memory. Deduplication represents sequences by an MD5 digest, and sample, split, shuffle and sort read files twice in two-pass mode with a FASTA index. Its peak memory is determined by the length of the longest sequence record.

STAR gets its speed from a sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, applied only to unmapped portions of the read and followed by clustering and stitching, with binary search scaling logarithmically with genome length [0,1,2,3,4]. It accepts higher memory use for that speed: uncompressed SAs beat compressed ones, but STAR requires 27 GB of RAM for the human genome, and sparse SAs lower peak RAM to 15.6 to 16.0 GB at a 25% speed cost [5,6,7,9,10]. Its threads share one SA, and throughput scales close to linearly with cores [8,11]. SeqKit instead treats file I/O as the bottleneck and optimises parsing and memory, with its own bio package and a custom buffered reader that increased speed and lowered memory usage [12,13,15,16]. It avoids loading all records, uses MD5 digests for deduplication, and reads files twice in two-pass mode with a FASTA index, so peak memory is determined by the longest sequence record [19,20,21,22,23,25]. For CPU-bound work it uses Goroutines, with no significant gain beyond two threads, and a slice lookup table to store complementary sequences that gave a ~20× speedup over a map [14,17,18,24].
expected_concepts: only to the unmapped portions of the read
logarithmic scaling of the search time

questions.question: Compare the diagnostic methodologies and biological markers used to determine the prevalence of bovine tuberculosis (bTB) and Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) as described in studies from Cameroon and Ethiopia.
questions.expected_answer:
Cameroon (bTB): 160 live cattle were tested with the comparative intradermal tuberculin test (CIDT) and the simple intradermal tuberculin test (SITT), as described in the WOAH Manual. The initial skin thickness was measured, and then bovine PPD (AN5 strain, 20,000 IU/mL) and avian PPD (D4 ER strain, 25,000 IU/mL) were injected intradermally in the cervical region. Results were read 72 h later. The marker is the variation in skinfold thickness with bovine tuberculin (DB) and with avian tuberculin (DA). Under the WOAH grid, DB >2 mm with DB–DA >4 mm is positive, 1–4 mm inconclusive and <1 mm negative. SITT is positive at >4 mm. A 3 mm threshold was also applied. CIDT at 3 mm found 11 positives (6.8%, 95% CI 4.35%–9.41%), and the 3 mm threshold increased detection sensitivity compared with the WOAH 4 mm threshold. At 4 mm the paper is inconsistent. Table-2 and the Results give SITT 1.8% (3/160) and CIDT 0.6% (1 positive in Table-2, "three" in the text). The abstract gives CIDT 1.8% and simple IDT 0.6%. Ethiopia (PPR): 384 serum samples from sheep and goats were obtained from jugular blood. They were tested for PPRV antibodies by competition ELISA (ID Screen PPR Competition ELISA, ID.vet; sensitivity 94.5%, specificity 99.4%). ODs were read at 450 nm and expressed as S/N%: ≤50% positive, 50%–60% doubtful, >60% negative. Seroprevalence was 32.1% in nonvaccinated, 68.8% in vaccinated (seroconversion) and 45.5% in animals of unknown vaccination status.

The Cameroon bTB study tested 160 live cattle with the comparative intradermal tuberculin test under the WOAH Manual, and also with the simple intradermal test [0, 1, 6]. It measured initial skin thickness, injected bovine and avian PPD intradermally in the neck and read the result 72 h later [2, 3, 4]. Its marker was the variation in skinfold thickness to bovine versus avian tuberculin, against mm cut-offs (DB–DA >4 mm positive for CIDT, >4 mm for SITT), with a 3 mm threshold also applied [5, 9]. CIDT at 3 mm gave 6.8% (11/160) [11, 13, 14]. At 4 mm the values 1.8% and 0.6% are assigned to SITT and CIDT differently in the abstract and in the Results and Table-2 [7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14]. The 3 mm threshold increased sensitivity [15]. The Ethiopia PPR study instead used serology: 384 sheep and goat sera, separated from jugular blood, were tested for PPRV antibodies by competition ELISA [16, 17, 18]. The ID Screen kit had 94.5% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity [19]. OD at 450 nm was expressed as S/N%, with ≤50% positive, >60% negative and 50%–60% doubtful [20, 21, 22]. Seroprevalence was 32.1% nonvaccinated, 68.8% vaccinated and 45.5% unknown status [23, 24, 25]. So the bTB study reads a skin reaction to tuberculin in live cattle, and the PPR study measures antibodies in serum [5, 16].

questions.question: How do the challenges of disease control identified in the Serengeti rabies vaccination campaigns relate to the vaccine efficacy findings for Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD)?
questions.expected_answer:
Neither paper links the two diseases, so the answer is a comparison of what each reports. In the Serengeti, the rabies control challenges concerned delivering the vaccine, and the paper gives no efficacy figure. Campaign coverage ranged from 8-37% (mean 22%), and only 3% of village campaigns reached the recommended 70% target. Campaigns missed villages and lapsed due to logistical constraints, and increased heterogeneity in coverage led to increased incidence. Fast demographic rates mean many dogs must be vaccinated annually. Incursions reached 50% of cases in 2022 and are now a major driver of continued transmission, so elimination will require expanded vaccination. Once heterogeneity in coverage was reduced, vaccination controlled rabies despite not reaching the 70% target. The LSD review reports how well the vaccines protect. The goat pox vaccine gives 60 to 70% protection, and ICAR scientists report 100% efficacy for Lumpi-ProVacInd. The attenuated sheeppox vaccine gives only partial cross-protection, and SPPV vaccines had varying success. The capripoxviruses share approximately 96% cross-protection. On delivery, the review gives only 15 million doses for around 200 million cattle in India, ring vaccination within a 5-km radius of outbreaks, and an annual vaccination schedule with a booster dose. It does not discuss heterogeneity in coverage, but it does address disease entry: ring vaccination was prioritized in border areas of different states to limit the spread to surrounding states, and the review calls vaccination the singular means to thwart the onset, recurrence and infiltration of the disease and asks for genomic data from various points of incursion.

The rabies paper finds that control in the Serengeti was limited by how vaccination was delivered: campaigns missed villages and increased heterogeneity in coverage raised incidence [0, 1, 8]; coverage was low (8-37%, mean 22%) and only 3% of village campaigns reached 70% [3, 4]; campaigns lapsed due to logistical constraints [5]; fast demographic rates require annual vaccination [7]; and incursions (50% of cases in 2022) drive residual transmission, so elimination will require expanded vaccination [2, 8, 9]. Once heterogeneity was reduced, vaccination controlled rabies below the 70% target [0, 6, 8]. The rabies paper reports no vaccine efficacy figure. The LSD review reports vaccine protection: goat pox vaccine 60 to 70% [10], Lumpi-ProVacInd 100% according to ICAR scientists [11], sheeppox vaccine only partial cross-protection with varying success [12, 13, 14], good protection against virulent field strains in general [15], and approximately 96% cross-protection among capripoxviruses [16]. On delivery, it reports only 15 million doses for around 200 million cattle in India [17], ring vaccination within 5 km of outbreaks to limit spread to surrounding states [18] and an annual vaccination schedule with a booster dose [19], and it calls vaccination the singular means to thwart the onset, recurrence and infiltration of the disease [20], with LSDV genomic data from various points of incursion guiding vaccine strategies [21]. Neither paper states a link between the two diseases, so the papers support a comparison: the LSD review reports how well the vaccines protect, and the rabies paper reports coverage and delivery problems (low and heterogeneous coverage, missed villages, fast demographic turnover, incursions). The LSD review touches two of these only briefly, vaccine supply short of demand (15 million doses for around 200 million cattle, and vaccine makers asked to increase output) [17, 22] and spread between states (ring vaccination prioritized in border areas) [18], and it does not discuss heterogeneity in coverage.

questions.question: How do the clinical manifestations and species-specific impacts of HPAI Clade 2.3.4.4 outbreaks compare between the intensive poultry sector in the Netherlands (2014-2022) and the broader ecological crisis observed in Canada during 2022?
questions.expected_answer:
Netherlands (92 commercial poultry farms; H5N8, H5N6 and H5N1 of clade 2.3.4.4): the clinical picture differed by poultry type and age.
- Ducks: neurological, locomotor and reproductive tract signs were common. Nervous and locomotor signs were seen on 67.7% of duck farms (66.7% in Table 5), against 48.4% of meat-type and 15.0% of layer-type farms. Reproductive tract signs were seen on 100% of duck farms. Egg production fell in all five breeder duck flocks, and reduced feed and water intake was seen mainly in ducks.
- Chickens: mucosal membrane and skin signs, including cyanosis and hemorrhagic conjunctiva, were seen on 55.0% of layer-type and 67.8% of meat-type farms, against 4.7% of duck farms. Respiratory signs were most frequent in meat-type poultry: 61.3%, against 37.5% in layers and 23.8% in ducks.
- Age: juveniles (chickens and ducks) showed neurological and locomotor signs more often than adults. Diarrhea occurred more often in adult chickens and juvenile ducks.
- Mortality: it increased exponentially within four days before notification. An MR > 3 was reached on 83% of layer-type, 80% of meat-type and 54% of duck farms (82.6/80.0/53.8% in Table 6), and these differences were not statistically significant. Mortality remained limited in ducks, where notification relied more on drops in feed or water intake or egg production.
- Over time: outbreaks in ducks decreased in 2020–2022 against 2014–2018, and outbreaks in meat-type poultry increased.

Canada, 2022 (HPAI H5N1): the paper reports scale and species range, not clinical signs in poultry. It names clade 2.3.4.4b only for the UK outbreaks and for genotypes found in mammals.
- Birds: millions of wild and farmed birds were infected. Seabird mortality was particularly severe on the Atlantic Coast. Infected wildlife was found in all provinces and territories, with mass mortality events in a broad range of wild bird species. Over 7 million birds were culled.
- Mammals: skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, porpoises, sea lions and dolphins were infected. Most infected mammals had severe neurological signs and died from encephalitis or meningoencephalitis. Mammalian-adaptation mutations (PB2-E627K, E627V, D701N) were found in the brains of carnivores in Europe and Canada.

Comparison: the Dutch study measures differences in clinical signs between poultry types and age groups. The Canadian commentary describes infection and mortality across wild birds, farmed birds and mammals, and its only clinical picture is severe neurological disease in mammals.

In the Dutch commercial poultry sector, the clinical manifestation of clade 2.3.4.4 HPAI depended on poultry type and age [0, 1]. Ducks most often showed nervous and locomotor signs and reproductive tract signs [2, 3, 6], along with drops in egg production and reduced feed and water intake [7, 8, 9]. Chickens mainly showed mucosal membrane and skin signs, and respiratory signs were most frequent in meat-type poultry [1, 4, 5]. Juveniles showed neurological and locomotor signs more often than adults [10, 11], and diarrhea was more frequent in adult chickens and juvenile ducks [12]. Mortality rose exponentially within four days before notification [13]. Ducks reached MR > 3 less often than chickens (54% against 83% and 80%), but these differences were not statistically significant [14, 15, 16]. Mortality remained limited in ducks, so notification relied more on drops in feed or water intake or egg production [17, 18]. Over time, duck outbreaks decreased and meat-type poultry outbreaks increased [19]. The Canadian commentary instead describes HPAI H5N1 in 2022 across wild and farmed birds [21]. It reports severe seabird mortality on the Atlantic Coast, mass mortality in a broad range of wild bird species in all provinces and territories, over 7 million birds culled, and a substantial impact on both wildlife and the poultry industry [22, 23, 24, 25]. It also reports infection in many mammal species. Most infected mammals had severe neurological signs and died from encephalitis or meningoencephalitis, and mammalian-adaptation PB2 mutations were found in carnivore brains [26, 27, 28, 29]. Neurological disease appears in both papers: in ducks and juvenile poultry in the Netherlands [2, 10], and in infected mammals in the Canada paper [28]. The Canada paper gives no clinical signs for birds by poultry type, so it offers nothing to set against the Dutch data on that point [21, 24].
expected_concepts: mass mortality events in wild birds
Over 7 million birds have been culled

questions.question: How do the risk factors identified for brucellosis in Ethiopian camels and small ruminants compare to the risk factors for Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) in the same region?
questions.expected_answer:
Herd or flock size is the only risk factor the two studies share.
- Brucellosis: small ruminants from a large herd were 5.01 times more likely to be infected (OR 5.01, 95% CI 1.2–21.4).
- PPR: sheep and goats in medium-sized flocks were more likely to be seropositive (OR 15.4, 95% CI 3.1–77.3). Large flocks were not significant (OR 1.5, p = 0.551).
- Camel brucellosis: herd size was not significant (OR 1.9, p = 0.33).

The other brucellosis risk factor is reproductive: a herd history of retained fetal membranes (RFM).
- Sheep and goats: OR 9 (95% CI 1.9–42) in the text, but 8.2 (2.4–29) in Table 2.
- Camels: in the multivariable model, history of RFM was significantly associated with seropositivity, OR 35 (12.7–60). In the univariable analysis, pregnancy, history of abortion and RFM were all significant.

The other PPR risk factors, in nonvaccinated sheep and goats, are age, animal origin and veterinary services status.
- Age: older animals had OR 7.3.
- Origin: purchased animals had OR 4 and gifted animals OR 8.3, compared with animals born in the flock.
- Veterinary services: OR 2.6. The text says poor access raised the risk, but Table 4 lists Poor as the reference category, so the direction is unclear.

The PPR study did not sample camels. The two studies were not in the same region: the PPR study was in the Borena zone of Oromia Regional State, southern Ethiopia, and the brucellosis study was in the Liban Zone of the Somali region.

Herd or flock size is the only risk factor the two studies share. For brucellosis, small ruminants from a large herd had OR 5.01 [9, 10, 11]. For PPR, medium-sized flocks had OR 15.4, and large flocks were not significant [1, 4, 7]. Herd size was not significant for camel brucellosis (OR 1.9, p = 0.33) [17].

The other brucellosis risk factor is reproductive: a history of retained fetal membranes. In small ruminants the text gives OR 9 and Table 2 gives 8.2 [12, 13]. In camels, history of RFM was significant in the multivariable model, with OR 35 [15, 16]; pregnancy, abortion and RFM were significant in the univariable analysis [14].

The PPR risk factors with no counterpart in the brucellosis study are age, animal origin and veterinary services status [0, 1]:
- older animals, OR 7.3 [2, 6];
- purchased animals, OR 4, and gifted animals, OR 8.3 [3];
- veterinary services status, OR 2.6, with the text and the tables pointing in opposite directions [5, 8, 21].

The studies were done in different regions: the Borena zone of Oromia for PPR and the Liban Zone of the Somali region for brucellosis [19, 20].
