questions.question: Contrast the epidemiological findings of the 2022 Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) outbreak in Nawalpur, Nepal, with the general disease characteristics and prevention strategies outlined in global systematic reviews.
questions.expected_answer:
Nawalpur 2022 outbreak (13_lsd_nepal): morbidity was 28.02% (431/1,538) and mortality 3.06% (47/1,538). Case fatality was 10.90% (47/431); the Results text gives it as 10.9%. The predominant signs were nodules in the skin (97% of case farms), reduced milk production (87%) and lameness (55%). Dry cattle had the highest morbidity (47.62%), and dry cattle, including pregnant cows, and cattle heifers were the most affected. Case fatality was highest in heifers (15.56%) and milking cattle (12.95%). In univariable analysis, outbreaks were linked to importing animals from disease prevalent regions, sharing feed and water, herd size and clinical signs in neighbouring farms. In the multivariable model only symptoms in neighbouring farms remained significant (odds ratio 88.45, 95% CI 13.27–589.36, p <0.001). Vectors (mosquitoes, houseflies, tabanus flies, ticks) were found on almost every farm, and the movement of animals between farms spread the infection. The animals were not yet vaccinated against LSD. The study recommends animal movement control and quarantine (the government mandates a 21-day quarantine), biosecurity protocols during nearby outbreaks, a practical vector control strategy, and vaccination of susceptible animals with more than 80% coverage.

Review (20_lsd_review, Kaur et al.): LSD has significant morbidity but a low fatality rate. Mortality is typically less than 10%, and morbidity can reach 100%. The disease is characterised by fever, lymph node enlargement, anorexia, depression, agalactia, emaciation and skin nodules of 10–50 mm, which can cause a significant decrease in milk output, abortion in pregnant heifers and sterility in bulls. Vectors are the most common mode of transmission (blood-sucking arthropods). Breed, age and gender do not appear to have a significant impact on severity, though Bos taurus may be more prone to severe disease and calves often show more severe signs than adult cattle. Larger farms with intensive housing and shared feeding and watering facilities can contribute to transmission. Prevention relies on vaccination, movement management, quarantine, tick management and biosecurity through vector control. The review calls vaccination the singular means to prevent the disease.

Contrast: Nawalpur's mortality of 3.06% is within the review's typical range of under 10%. Its morbidity of 28.02% is well below the review's ceiling of 100%. Nawalpur shares the review's skin nodules and drop in milk production, and Nawalpur reports lameness in 55% of case farms. Morbidity was highest in dry and pregnant cattle, whereas the review singles out calves and Bos taurus for more severe disease. Shared feed and water and herd size, the farm-level risks the review lists, were associated only in the univariable analysis. In the multivariable model they were overshadowed by symptoms in neighbouring farms. Both papers point to vectors and recommend the same prevention measures: movement control, quarantine, biosecurity, vector control and vaccination. The review calls vaccination the singular means of prevention, yet the Nawalpur animals were not yet vaccinated.

The Nawalpur outbreak had 28.02% morbidity, 3.06% mortality and 10.90% case fatality [0, 5], which the authors summarise as morbidity below 30% with a low mortality rate [13]. This fits the review's profile of significant morbidity with a low fatality rate, where mortality is typically below 10% [18, 19]. Nawalpur's morbidity is well below the review's statement that morbidity can reach 100% [0, 19]. Skin nodules and reduced milk production appear in both papers [1, 3, 20], and Nawalpur also reports lameness in 55% of case farms [3]. In Nawalpur, morbidity was highest in dry cattle (47.62%), and dry cattle, including pregnant cows, and heifers were the most affected [2, 4]. The review instead says breed, age and gender do not appear to significantly affect severity, and it singles out Bos taurus and calves for more severe disease [23, 24]. The review lists larger farms and shared feeding and watering facilities as contributors to transmission [25]. In Nawalpur, herd size and shared feed and water were associated with outbreaks only in the univariable analysis [6, 8]. In the multivariable model they were overshadowed by symptoms in neighbouring farms (odds ratio 88.45, p <0.001) [7, 8, 9, 10]. Both papers point to vectors: vectors were present on almost every Nawalpur farm and acted as a predisposing factor [11, 12], and the review calls vectors the most common mode of transmission [21, 22]. The prevention strategies coincide (movement control, quarantine, biosecurity, vector control and vaccination) [14, 16, 26, 27, 29]. The review calls vaccination the singular means of preventing the disease [28]. The Nawalpur animals were not yet vaccinated against LSD, and the study calls for vaccine coverage above 80% [15, 17].
expected_concepts: mortality rate is typically less than 10%

questions.question: Using a One Health perspective, compare the identified zoonotic risk factors and surveillance priorities for HPAI H5N1 in Canada versus brucellosis in the Somali region of Ethiopia.
questions.expected_answer:
HPAI H5N1 in Canada (19_hpai_canada, a commentary)

Human risk factors:
- All severely affected human cases had direct exposure to poultry.
- Clinicians should consider HPAI after exposure to birds or sick wildlife in the previous 10–14 days.

Animal-side risks:
- Wild birds are a source of novel influenza viruses.
- Avian infections create abundant opportunities for spillover to mammals, particularly wild mammals.
- Mutations in the HA, PB2 and NA genes are linked to mammalian adaptation. PB2-E627K, E627V and D701N were found in the brains of carnivores in Europe and Canada.
- The spillover raises the risk of reassortment with swine or human influenza viruses.

Surveillance priorities:
- Enhanced surveillance among humans, by strengthening public health and laboratory capacity to detect, report and investigate cases.
- Coordination of surveillance and reporting among the human and animal health sectors.
- Strategic surveillance with the animal health sector, focused on the regions and populations at highest risk.
- Continued in vitro and in vivo analysis of circulating strains.
- Reporting suspect cases to local public health.
- Awareness among frontline practitioners.

Gaps: surveillance of sick and dead wildlife is limited, and preparedness in the human health care sector is limited. The animal health sector is already engaged in surveillance, and CFIA, PHAC and provincial authorities monitor the disease.

Brucellosis in the Somali region of Ethiopia (17_brucellosis_ethiopia, a serosurvey)

Animal risk factors are herd size and herd history of retained fetal membranes (RFM):
- Small ruminants from a large herd: OR 5.01 (95% CI 1.2–21.4).
- RFM in small ruminants: OR 9 in the text, 8.2 in Table 2.
- RFM in camels: OR 35 in Table 4.

Human risk factor: disposing of RFM, or handling and disposing of aborted fetal materials (p = 0.001). The Discussion calls this a 26-fold higher risk. Table 5 gives OR 26 and Table 6 gives OR 37.4.

Factors that were not significant or are reported inconsistently:
- Raw milk consumption (76.4% of participants; OR 5.7, p = 0.06) was not significant.
- Seropositivity was seven times higher in households with seropositive animals, but p = 0.72.
- Assisting calving or birthing is called significant in the Discussion (OR = 8), but Table 6 gives p = 0.11.

Environmental drivers: drought driven by climate change moves livestock, which concentrates animals, facilitates spillover and is expected to sustain endemicity.

Priorities:
- Molecular detection of the prevalent Brucella spp. strains before any vaccination programme.
- One Health epidemiological studies to isolate and characterise circulating Brucella spp. in humans and livestock.
- A coordinated One Health control strategy that respects the sociocultural dynamics of pastoral communities.

Comparison

Both papers place human risk in contact with animals: poultry, birds and wildlife for HPAI, and reproductive material from livestock for brucellosis. HPAI's priority is coordinated human and animal surveillance. Brucellosis's priorities are characterising the circulating strains and One Health control adapted to pastoral communities.

Both papers place human risk in contact with animals or their material. For HPAI in Canada, all severely affected human cases had direct exposure to poultry, and exposure to birds or sick wildlife in the previous 10–14 days is the clinical flag [0, 1]. For brucellosis in the Somali region, disposing of retained fetal membranes, or handling and disposing of aborted fetal materials, was significantly associated with human seropositivity [17, 27, 39]. The Discussion reports this as a 26-fold higher risk; Table 5 gives OR 26 and Table 6 gives 37.4 [28, 29, 34]. The paper also links close human-animal contact to the public health risk [42].

Other brucellosis exposures did not reach significance or are reported inconsistently. Raw milk consumption was common (76.4%) but not significant [25, 35]. The sevenfold higher seropositivity in households with seropositive animals had p = 0.72 [24, 37]. Assisting calving or birthing is called significant in the Discussion but has p = 0.11 in Table 6 [26, 29, 36].

The animal-side risks differ. For HPAI they are wild birds as a source of novel viruses, spillover to mammals, HA, PB2 and NA mutations linked to mammalian adaptation, and the risk of reassortment with swine or human influenza viruses [2, 3, 4, 5, 9]. For brucellosis they are herd size and herd history of retained fetal membranes [16, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 38]. The paper attributes the herd-size risk to stock density [30]. Livestock mobility driven by drought concentrates animals, facilitates spillover and is expected to sustain endemicity [31, 32, 40].

The priorities differ as well. The HPAI commentary calls for:
- enhanced surveillance among humans, with stronger public health and laboratory capacity, and coordination of surveillance and reporting between the human and animal health sectors [14];
- strategic surveillance focused on the highest-risk regions and populations [15];
- continued analysis of circulating strains [7];
- reporting of suspect cases [8];
- frontline practitioner awareness [13].
It notes that wildlife surveillance and human-sector preparedness are limited [6, 12], while the animal health sector and CFIA, PHAC and provincial authorities already conduct surveillance and monitoring [10, 11].

The brucellosis study calls for:
- molecular detection of the prevalent strains before any vaccination programme [33];
- One Health epidemiological studies to isolate and characterise circulating Brucella spp. in humans and livestock [41];
- a coordinated One Health control strategy that respects the sociocultural dynamics of pastoral communities [18, 43].
expected_concepts: exposure to birds or sick wildlife
Herd size and herd history of retained fetal membranes

questions.question: How do the data management capabilities of MultiQC and SeqKit contrast with the data collection requirements for zoonotic disease studies in Ethiopia and Cameroon?
questions.expected_answer:
MultiQC and SeqKit are tools for data that already exists as sequencing analysis files. MultiQC scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and creates a single summary report across all samples. It saves parsed data as tab delimited text, YAML or JSON, parses data for thousands of samples within minutes, and through plugins can insert LIMS metadata and store summary results in a database. This lets it act as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines. SeqKit has nineteen subcommands for FASTA/Q manipulation (converting, searching, filtering, deduplication, splitting, shuffling, sampling). They take plain or gzip-compressed inputs and outputs from standard streams or local files, and SeqKit converts FASTA/Q to and from tabular format.

The two zoonotic disease studies had to collect their data in the field from people and animals. In Cameroon (bovine TB), an interviewee-administered questionnaire gathered data from 90 cattle professionals. It was pre-tested and closed-ended, written in English and French, and could be translated into the participant's local language. It covered sociodemographics, herd management, cattle-wildlife interaction, knowledge of zoonotic TB and farm bTB status. Sex, age and body condition score were recorded for each tested animal at the time of the test. Data were organised in Microsoft Excel and analysed in IBM SPSS Statistics. In Ethiopia (brucellosis), a structured questionnaire collected biodata on tested animals and animal attendants: sex, age, herd size, animal movement, parity, herd history of abortion and RFM, and physiological status. Blood samples and exposure information (raw milk consumption, assisting calving, disposing of aborted fetuses) were collected from animal owners. In total 450 camel, 300 small ruminant and 250 human samples were collected. A bar code system, built from the first letters of region, zone, district and PA, labelled human and animal samples to minimise error. Field and laboratory data were entered into Microsoft Excel and analysed with R-3.3.0. None of the papers states this contrast itself.

MultiQC works on existing analysis output. It aggregates log files and QC reports into a single summary report [0], exports parsed data as tab delimited text, YAML or JSON [1], parses thousands of samples within minutes [2], links to a LIMS and a database through plugins [3] and serves as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines [4]. SeqKit converts, searches, filters, deduplicates, splits, shuffles and samples FASTA/Q files [5] with nineteen independent subcommands [6] that read and write plain or gzip-compressed streams or files [7], and it converts FASTA/Q to and from tabular format [8]. The field studies instead collect their data from people and animals. In Cameroon, a pre-tested closed-ended questionnaire in English and French, translatable into local languages, gathered sociodemographic, herd management, wildlife interaction and zoonotic TB knowledge data from 90 cattle professionals [9, 11, 12]. Animal sex, age and body condition score were recorded at testing [10], and the data were organised in Excel and analysed in SPSS [13]. In Ethiopia, a structured questionnaire collected animal and attendant biodata [14, 15], and blood samples and exposure information were collected from animal owners [16]. There, 450 camel, 300 small ruminant and 250 human samples were collected [17] and labelled with a bar code system built from region, zone, district and PA letters to minimise error [18, 19], and field and laboratory data were entered into Excel and analysed in R [20].
expected_concepts: tab delimited text, YAML or JSON
converting FASTA/Q to and from tabular format

questions.question: How do the implementation strategies for NGS workflow management and reproducibility differ between Nextflow-based systems like Sarek, the Snakemake system, and the HTS-flow platform?
questions.expected_answer:
Sarek is implemented in Nextflow, a workflow language designed for bioinformatics. Nextflow supports Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF and Kubernetes, with native support for Google Cloud and AWS. To ensure reproducibility, all Sarek required tools are installed in Conda and then pushed to DockerHub, so Sarek and its dependencies are available from a Conda environment or as Docker or Singularity containers. Nextflow downloads the specified pipeline version from GitHub, together with its container and the reference files from AWS-iGenomes. Sarek follows the nf-core portability and documentation guidelines, restarts incomplete runs from any stage and ships with a suite of tests to verify the installation. A complete run was executed by a single command.

Snakemake specifies workflows as rules in a domain specific language (DSL). Its DSL extends Python, while Nextflow's extends Groovy. Dependencies between jobs are inferred automatically. Software stack management is integrated into Snakemake itself: each rule can declare a Conda environment, or a container image run with Singularity. Snakemake can also automatically generate a containerized version once a workflow is production ready. It tracks the input files, output files, parameters, software and code of each executed job and makes them available in self-contained, interactive, HTML based reports. Scaling to a specific platform needs only a change of command line parameters, using execution plugins (e.g. SLURM, LSF, Kubernetes, Amazon AWS Batch).

HTS-flow is designed to work together with a LIMS (SMITH), so raw NGS data become visible in it automatically. Analyses run through a web interface designed for users without bioinformatics skills (the typical wet-lab scientist). It works with predefined, easily customizable modular scripts, deposited to Github for versioning. It allows complete traceability of datasets, accompanying metadata and analysis scripts. Reproducibility rests on standard Bioconductor metadata libraries (TxDb and BSgenome), outputs in standard locations as Bioconductor R data objects, and identical workflows for data from various sources.

Sarek and Snakemake both define workflows in code. Sarek is implemented in the Nextflow workflow language [0], and Nextflow and Snakemake both specify workflows in a DSL, built on Groovy and Python respectively [8, 9]. Snakemake decomposes workflows into rules and infers dependencies between jobs automatically [10, 11]. HTS-flow instead couples a LIMS to a web interface for users without bioinformatics skills [20, 21, 24, 29]. The interface sits over predefined, easily customizable modular scripts [25]. Both code-based systems get reproducibility by packaging software, at different levels. Sarek encapsulates all its dependencies in Docker or Singularity containers or a Bioconda-built Conda environment [2], and pulls a specified pipeline version from GitHub with its container and reference files [5]. Snakemake builds software stack management into the engine, with a Conda environment or a Singularity-run container for each rule [12, 13, 14], and can generate a containerized version of a workflow [15]. HTS-flow instead bases reproducibility on standard Bioconductor annotation packages (TxDb, BSgenome) and Bioconductor R data objects [27, 28]. It versions its scripts on Github [26] and analyses data from various sources with identical workflows [23]. For traceability and robustness, Sarek relies on nf-core portability and documentation guidelines, error reporting with restart from any stage, and installation tests [3, 4, 6]. Snakemake tracks the files, parameters, software and code of every job and reports them in self-contained, interactive, HTML based reports [16, 17]. HTS-flow provides complete traceability of datasets, metadata and analysis scripts, with raw data made visible automatically from the LIMS [20, 22]. For execution, Nextflow supports Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF, Kubernetes, Google Cloud and AWS [1]. Snakemake scales through execution plugins and needs only a change of command line parameters [18, 19]. HTS-flow's automation comes mainly from integration with the SMITH LIMS [29].
expected_concepts: automatically deployed via the Conda package manager

questions.question: How does Kenya's One Health AMR Surveillance System (OHAMRS) align with the Integrated Surveillance System Evaluation (ISSE) framework's levels of surveillance?
questions.expected_answer:
Neither paper makes this comparison, so the alignment is inferred from the two papers. ISSE evaluates a One Health surveillance system at five levels: (1) integrate a OH approach, (2) produce OH information and expertise, (3) generate actionable knowledge, (4) influence decision-making, (5) positively impact outcomes. Level 1 also scores six levels of OH integration for data collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination. Mapped onto these: Level 1, OHAMRS integrated human and animal health AMR data, through interoperability middleware and a DHIS2 web portal. Level 2, the portal analyses and visualises those data, but the environment, food/feed and aquaculture sectors are only planned for future inclusion, and antimicrobial consumption and use data still need to be incorporated; ISSE Level 2 asks whether data are collected from animals, humans and the environment, and the top data-collection integration levels require environmental or AMU data. Level 3, 42 dashboards (17 for priority pathogens, 8 for drug-resistance indicators, plus a One Health intersectoral dashboard) present, interpret and disseminate actionable information at national, county and surveillance site levels. Level 4, OHAMRS is meant to inform policymaking, and its success will be gauged by use in evidence-based decision-making, so this is expected, not shown. Level 5, the Kenya paper reports no outcome impacts. ISSE suggests focusing on evaluation levels 1 and 2 in the first 3–5 years of a new or recently integrated system.

ISSE evaluates a One Health AMR/AMU surveillance system at five levels: integrating a OH approach, producing OH information and expertise, generating actionable knowledge, influencing decision-making and positively impacting outcomes [0, 1, 4, 6, 7, 8]. Level 1 also scores six levels of OH integration for data collection, analyses, interpretation and dissemination [2]. OHAMRS integrated human and animal health AMR data through interoperability middleware, which is what ISSE Level 1 examines [1, 10, 11]. It analyses and visualises those data in a DHIS2 web portal, relevant to ISSE Level 2 [4, 11]. Its data coverage does not yet include the environment, food/feed or aquaculture sectors, or antimicrobial consumption and use data [12, 19], whereas ISSE Level 2 asks whether environmental data are collected and the higher data-collection integration levels require environmental or AMU data [3, 5]. Its 42 dashboards, including a One Health intersectoral dashboard, present, interpret and disseminate actionable information at national, county and surveillance site levels, the subject of ISSE Level 3 [6, 13, 14, 16]. OHAMRS is meant to inform policymaking, and its success will be gauged by use in evidence-based decision-making, the subject of ISSE Level 4 [7, 15, 17, 18]. The Kenya paper reports no impacts on AMR or AMU, the subject of ISSE Level 5 [8]. For a new or recently integrated system, ISSE suggests focusing on evaluation levels 1 and 2 in the first 3–5 years [9].
expected_concepts: integrated human and animal health AMR data
the environment, food/feed, and aquaculture sectors

questions.question: Contrast the impact of using Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) versus Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) on microbial community interpretation as discussed in recent microbiome studies.
questions.expected_answer:
28_otu_vs_asv ran the same data through VSEARCH (clustering into OTUs) and DADA2 (error correction into exact ASVs). Both pipelines gave comparable results that generally allow the same interpretations. Even so, community composition differed by 6.75% to 10.81% at phylum level, based purely on the pipeline.

Findings in 28_otu_vs_asv:
- **Spurious OTUs.** OTU approaches overestimate diversity and produce spurious OTUs. The study saw this too, but relative abundance thresholds easily mitigated it: a cutoff as little as 0.001% removed enough spurious or rare taxa to fall within the ranges produced by the ASV pipeline. The ASV pipeline outputs fewer to no spurious variants and is precise to a single base.
- **Alpha diversity.** Trends were similar, and the OTU pipeline typically reported slightly higher diversity. The two pipelines diverged for the psychrophilic PWASS samples, where the inverse Simpson index differed at times by a factor greater than two.
- **Community composition.** Pipeline choice significantly influenced reported composition. Over more than 170 days, the dissimilarity between pipelines was greater than the dissimilarity between treatments. The ASV pipeline showed the influence of time and co-substrate more clearly.
- **Consequences.** These differences could lead to different conclusions and could interfere with downstream analyses such as network analysis. On the reduced dataset they would suggest that the pipeline affects composition more than any treatment, a conclusion with no foundation in experimental reality.
- **Comparability.** OTUs are analysis-specific and give no direct comparability with other studies. ASVs are directly comparable between studies.

Findings in 29_16s_best_practices (a review):
- OTUs are clustered at an arbitrary threshold (often 3%) and have no innate biological meaning.
- De novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies, and closed-reference clustering loses information that lies outside the database.
- ASVs significantly reduce clustering artifacts, allow valid comparison, are not restricted by reference databases and need relatively light computation.
- One concern with ASVs is possible diversity inflation from multiple ASVs generated from a single bacterial genome.

23_swine_cultivation does not compare the two approaches.

Both papers say OTUs come from clustering, are analysis-specific and cannot be compared directly between studies [0, 4, 5, 23, 26]. They also say ASVs come from error correction, resolve single-base differences and are directly comparable [0, 6, 13, 22, 27, 28]. 29 adds that OTUs have no innate biological meaning and that clustering affects biological interpretation [24, 25]. 28 measured the effect on interpretation. Overall, the two pipelines allow the same interpretations [1, 14], but phylum-level composition differed by 6.75% to 10.81% [2, 9]. Diversity estimates diverged for the PWASS samples [8, 15]. Pipeline choice significantly influenced composition, and the dissimilarity between pipelines exceeded the dissimilarity between treatments [17, 18, 20]. These differences could lead to different or unfounded conclusions [3, 21]. The papers place the diversity bias differently. 28 reports that OTU approaches overestimate diversity with spurious OTUs and that abundance thresholds mitigate this [7, 10, 11, 12]. 29 records the concern that ASVs may inflate diversity through multiple ASVs per genome [30]. 29 also says ASVs need lighter computation [31].
expected_concepts: de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies

questions.question: How do the strategies for managing large-scale NGS data efficiency compare between the nf-core framework, the fastp preprocessor, and the methylPipe epigenomics package?
questions.expected_answer:
The three papers tackle efficiency at different levels.

nf-core/sarek 3 (the pipeline in the paper filed as nf-core), at the workflow level:
- Uses the CRAM format instead of BAM to reduce storage. Work-directory storage drops by 65%, from 170.4 TB (BAM) to 59.7 TB (CRAM), at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage.
- Increases intra-sample parallelization. FastQ files are split into shards with fastP, which combines sharding and adapter removal into one step, so alignment can run on smaller machines. Mapping runtime plateaus at 12 shards, with the median runtime reduced to 37%. Genomic regions are processed in parallel, with no further runtime benefit beyond 21 interval groups.
- Is written in Nextflow, so it is portable to several cloud vendors and common HPC schedulers.
- Single-step preprocessing plus tailored interval splitting reduces the needed CPU hours by 66%.
- The paper states the cost effect four ways: a 70% cost reduction in commercial clouds (abstract), a 69% reduction in compute costs (Introduction), cloud computing costs reduced to approximately 30% (Results) and costs reduced to 50% compared with previous releases (Discussion).

fastp, inside one preprocessing tool:
- Avoids reading and loading data multiple times, which is slow and I/O inefficient, by doing quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering and per-read quality pruning in a single scan of the FASTQ data.
- Is designed for multi-threading parallel processing: each pack of reads is consumed by one thread in the pool.
- Can split output into multiple files for parallel processing, by file lines or by file numbers.
- Is 2–5 times faster than tools such as Trimmomatic or Cutadapt. With a single thread it took 6 min (SE) and 13.3 min (PE).

methylPipe, at the data-storage level:
- Keeps WGBS data on disk as Tabix-indexed compressed files that are accessed directly from disk. This reduces disk space (269 MB and 380 MB compressed versus 372 MB and 554 MB uncompressed for IMR90 and H1) and saves memory.
- By contrast, BiSeq and M3D upload the entire dataset into memory and failed even with 80 GB.
- Parallelizes demanding tasks such as DMR identification and adjusts automatically to the available cores and RAM. DMR identification between 2 WGBS samples took 20 min with 1 core on chromosome 1 (max 4GB RAM) and 45 min with 10 cores genome-wide (max 28GB RAM).

The direct link between the tools: sarek uses fastp to shard FastQ files and remove adapters in one step.

All three papers use parallel processing, at different levels. nf-core/sarek increases intra-sample parallelization by sharding FastQ files and processing genomic regions in parallel, on cloud or HPC infrastructure made portable by Nextflow [0, 3, 4, 6]. fastp is designed for multi-threading inside one tool and can split its output into multiple files for parallel processing [18, 19, 20, 23]. methylPipe parallelizes demanding tasks such as DMR identification and adjusts to the available cores and RAM [25, 30]. Both sarek and fastp cut repeated passes over the data. fastp performs all operations in a single scan, avoiding slow, I/O-inefficient repeated reading [15, 16]. sarek adopted fastP because it combines FastQ sharding and adapter removal in one step, and single-step preprocessing with tailored interval splitting reduced CPU hours by 66% [5, 12]. On storage, sarek moved to CRAM files, cutting work-directory storage by 65% at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage [7, 8, 9]. methylPipe instead keeps data on disk as Tabix-indexed compressed files read directly from disk, saving both disk space and memory [24, 26, 27, 28], unlike BiSeq and M3D, which load the entire dataset into memory and failed with 80 GB [29]. Reported gains: for sarek, the median mapping runtime fell to 37% [10] and the cost reduction is given as 70%, 69%, to approximately 30% and to 50% in different sections [1, 2, 11, 14]. fastp is 2–5 times faster than other FASTQ preprocessing tools [17, 21, 22]. methylPipe ran a genome-wide 2-sample DMR analysis in 45 min with 10 cores [31].
expected_concepts: single scan of the FASTQ data

questions.question: In what ways do quantitative microbiome profiling (QMP) and culturomics address the biases of traditional relative microbiome profiling (RMP) in livestock research?
questions.expected_answer:
QMP (broiler chicken study): QMP combines high-throughput sequencing with a microbial load quantification assay. It turns the sequencing data into an absolute microbiome abundance matrix, so it follows changes in absolute abundance (AA), meaning whether a species thrives or withers over time. This minimizes the compositionality effects of relative analyses. Compared with QMP, RMP:
- ignored the absolute growth or decline of microbes and biased the developmental trajectory (by QMP, absolute numbers were relatively stable across segments and over time);
- exaggerated the variation explained by individual, segment and DPH;
- overestimated positive correlations in the bacteriome (e.g. 402 vs. 196 in the duodenum) and missed positive correlations in the mycobiome (e.g. 1048 vs. 2270 in the cecum).

Culturomics (swine study): the paper does not frame culture-dependent (CD) profiling as correcting RMP. It recovers taxa that culture-independent (CI) sequencing missed, and it gives the likely causes as low relative abundance below the detection limits of sequencing depth, incomplete lysis of bacterial cells during DNA extraction, or unfavorable PCR amplification. CD methods found 244, 411, 507 and 510 new ASVs at the four time points, including core ASVs and novel species. In one case Bacteroides relative abundance fell below CI detection, but culture suggested its absolute abundance might not decrease, because other taxa may have proliferated more.

Review: the livestock review says only that combining culturomics with shotgun metagenomics may give a more exhaustive picture of the gut in pigs.

QMP addresses RMP bias directly: it combines sequencing with a microbial load assay and produces an absolute abundance matrix [0, 3], so it follows whether taxa thrive or wither and shows real community dynamics [1, 2], minimizing compositionality effects [9]. Against QMP, RMP ignored absolute growth or decline and biased trajectories [4, 7, 8, 10], exaggerated the variation explained by individual, segment and DPH [5, 11], and overestimated or missed taxon–taxon correlations [6, 12]. Culturomics works on a different limitation of sequencing-based profiling: it recovers taxa missed for low relative abundance, shallow sequencing depth, incomplete lysis or unfavorable PCR amplification [14, 16], adding 244, 411, 507 and 510 ASVs across the four time points [15] and isolating core ASVs and novel species [20], which shows a more diverse microbiota [13]. Its Bacteroides example touches the compositional problem: relative abundance fell below detection while culture suggested absolute abundance might not decrease, as other taxa may have proliferated more [17, 18, 19]. The livestock review adds only that culturomics combined with shotgun metagenomics may give a more exhaustive picture of the gut [21].
expected_concepts: RA exaggerated the proportion of variation
lower relative abundance and shallow sequencing depth
Bacteroides absolute abundance might not decrease

Heidelberg isolates had resistance genes for fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and sulphonamides. Five of six S. Agona isolates from Thailand were resistant to five classes of antibiotics, while S.
