questions.question: Compare the organizational models and economic benefits of integrated One Health surveillance systems as discussed in global reviews and regional case studies.
questions.expected_answer:
Organisational models.
- Global review (integrated antibiotic-resistance surveillance): 14 integrated antibiotic-resistance surveillance systems, all operating in high-income countries; the review found no operating integrated system in LMICs. It sets out integration along two dimensions, information integration and structural integration, and groups the systems into four distinct clusters:
  - Group 1 (six systems) mainly operates in silos, with data analysed separately by each sector.
  - Group 2 (four systems: DANMAP, NORM/NORM-VET, SWEDRES/SVARM, NARMS) has a high level of integration at both structural and informational levels.
  - Group 3 (CIPARS, SONAAR) is supervised solely by the human health sector.
  - Group 4 (ZoMo, FINRES-Vet) is supervised by the food safety sector, with the animal health sector for ZoMo.
  At governance level, four systems are supervised by a multi-sectoral body and five separately by each sector. Some authors consider governance more effective when there is an intersectoral committee (DANMAP) or a single supervising organisation (CIPARS). The level of resources and the regulatory framework appeared to play a major role in how integrated surveillance was set up and organised.
- The data-driven One Health paper describes:
  - an inter-agency technical working group set up after the 2008 Hendra virus outbreak in Australia;
  - multisectoral partnerships, in contrast to preparedness and surveillance plans that in most countries are often developed by a single sector;
  - data-driven coordinated surveillance with machine learning modelling capability.
- The One Health in Africa paper describes the African Union's interagency One Health Coordinating Group on Zoonotic Diseases, the Africa CDC Framework for One Health Practice in National Public Health Institutes (coordinated surveillance and data sharing), and a continental strategy at national, regional and continental levels. It notes gaps in political commitment, skilled workforce, domestic financing and legal frameworks, and that many countries lack formal and funded One Health programs.

Economic benefits.
- The review reports no monetary benefit. Integration is associated with a financial and social cost; intersectoral coordination remains costly and funding is usually lacking; integration outcomes are poorly described and rarely available. The outcomes it reports are non-monetary: less antibiotic use in animals and humans, and the poultry sector stopped using ceftiofur, after which resistance to it in salmonella fell.
- The data-driven One Health paper cites returns of over €1 million in savings from integrated West Nile virus surveillance and response, and 26% savings in operational cost from hosting human and animal health laboratories under one roof. It says coordination can save costs by preventing duplication and provides a positive return on investment, that analytically driven prediction costs much less than response, and that the Ebola economic losses in Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia could have been prevented by a more resilient and integrated health system. It also says data on financing and cost projections are limited.
- The One Health in Africa paper says zoonotic disease prevention costs less than 1/20th the value of lives lost each year (a business case), set against outbreak losses of billions of dollars.

The organisational models differ in scale and detail. The global review classifies 14 high-income-country antibiotic-resistance systems by information and structural integration into four clusters: siloed (Group 1), highly integrated (Group 2), and led by the human health sector (Group 3) or the food sector (Group 4) [0, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. It found no operating integrated system in LMICs [19]. Resources and the regulatory framework shape how systems are organised [1], and governance is seen as more effective with an intersectoral committee or a single supervising organisation [13]. Paper 37 describes an inter-agency working group, multisectoral partnerships set against single-sector planning, and data-driven surveillance with machine learning [20, 21, 25, 26]. Paper 38 describes a continental model: an AU coordinating group, an Africa CDC framework in national public health institutes, and a multi-level strategy [32, 36, 37, 38, 39]. It also notes gaps in financing and funded programmes [31, 35]. On economics, the review stresses the costs of integration (a financial and social cost; costly, underfunded coordination) and finds outcomes poorly documented, reporting only non-monetary benefits [3, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. Paper 37 cites over €1 million in West Nile virus savings and a 26% cut in laboratory operating cost, and argues for a positive return on investment, cheaper prediction and avoided losses [22, 23, 24, 28, 29, 30], while noting that cost data are limited [27]. Paper 38 makes a prevention business case (less than 1/20th the value of lives lost) against outbreak losses of billions of dollars [33, 34].
expected_concepts: less than 1/20th the value of lives lost
One Health Coordinating Group on Zoonotic Diseases

questions.question: How do tools for analyzing DNA methylation and chromatin structure complement traditional transcriptomic analysis of oncogene targets?
questions.expected_answer:
The papers do not state the link, so the answer comes from reading them together. In the MYC liver carcinoma model (48), chromatin immunoprecipitation was combined with gene expression profiling. MYC binding at a locus was insufficient to predict gene regulation. RNA-seq analysis following tet-MYC shutdown, more than DNA binding, narrowed down the genes primarily regulated by MYC. Neither MYC binding nor recruitment to enhancers (assigned by nearest-neighbor analyses) discriminated primary from secondary targets, and no simple rule linked promoter/enhancer association by MYC with gene regulation. The stalling index alone was insufficient in assessing RNA Pol II dynamics. The determinants of which MYC-bound genes are deregulated largely remain to be understood, and likely include promoter-dependent cues. methylPipe/compEpiTools (46) add DNA methylation, which is often combined with RNA-seq and TF ChIP-seq. They accommodate any combination of DNA methylation data, histone marks, TF binding and RNA-seq expression. They identify enhancers and RNAPII stalling/elongation dynamics, compute the stalling index, and match enhancers to the most proximal genes. Variation in methylation at intermediate or high-CpG density promoters is associated to differential expression of the downstream gene. 4C-seq (50) adds chromatin structure. It identifies regulatory chromatin loops between enhancers and promoters, through which enhancers regulate expression of distal target genes. It has been used to study enhancer hijacking in disease, and its tracks can be displayed together with ChIP-Seq and RNA-Seq data. None of the papers applies methylation or 4C-seq data to MYC targets.

In the MYC-driven liver carcinoma model, chromatin immunoprecipitation was combined with gene expression profiling [0], and RNA-seq after tet-MYC shutdown, more than DNA binding, identified the genes primarily regulated by MYC [3]. MYC binding alone was insufficient to predict gene regulation [1]. Binding at promoters or at enhancers (assigned to genes by nearest-neighbor analyses) did not discriminate primary from secondary targets [5, 6]. The stalling index alone was insufficient to assess RNA Pol II dynamics [7]. What decides which MYC-bound genes are deregulated largely remains to be understood and likely includes promoter-dependent cues [2, 8]. The study's chromatin data were ChIP-seq profiles of MYC, RNAPII, H3K4me3 and H3K27ac [4]. methylPipe/compEpiTools add DNA methylation, which is often combined with RNA-seq and TF ChIP-seq [9], and integrate it with histone marks, TF binding and RNA-seq expression [13]. They identify enhancers and RNAPII stalling/elongation dynamics [10, 11] and match enhancers to the most proximal genes stratified by TF binding [14]. Their promoter CpG-content concept links methylation at intermediate or high-CpG promoters to differential expression of the downstream gene [12]. 4C-seq adds chromatin structure: it identifies regulatory loops between enhancers and promoters [16], through which enhancers regulate distal target genes [15]. It has been applied to enhancer hijacking in disease [17], and its tracks can be displayed with ChIP-Seq and RNA-Seq data [18]. None of the three papers applies methylation or 4C-seq data to MYC targets. That rests on reading all three papers, not on any one sentence.
expected_concepts: no simple rule could be drawn
regulatory chromatin loops between enhancers and promoters
regulate expression of distal target genes

questions.question: What are the shared methods and technical considerations for identifying antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) in different food animal environments?
questions.expected_answer:
Shared methods: all three papers detect resistance genes by sequencing.
- Pig gut (22): Illumina NovaSeq shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic and assembled into MAGs, and the MAGs were screened against the comprehensive antibiotic resistance database (CARD) with CARD-RGI v. 5.2.0. ARG co-location with integrase/transposase sequences was checked, using Proksee and Prokka.
- Salmonella from raw chicken and edible leaves (41): whole genome sequencing on the Illumina HiSeq 2500. Reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic, and AMR genes and chromosomal mutations were called with a customized algorithm, Genefinder. Efflux pump genes were identified by a separate method.
- Review (33): cited studies used metagenomic methods (cattle faeces, shrimp, compost), plasmid metagenomics, next-generation high-throughput sequencing (pig farm bioaerosols), PCR and qPCR (manure, swine manure wastewater, shrimp), direct culturing (compost) and whole-genome sequencing of isolates (poultry farms).
The two primary studies share Illumina short-read sequencing and Trimmomatic trimming.

Technical considerations:
(a) Binning ARGs into MAGs from short reads is extremely challenging, because ARGs are often flanked by repeat sequences and located on mobile genetic elements such as plasmids. MAG-detected ARGs are therefore assumed to be chromosomal. Only 115 ARGs were found, against 250 in a previous study of the same short reads and 897 in the co-assembly. Long-read sequencing would likely increase the number binned and improve resolution of their genomic context.
(b) WGS detects AMR determinants with a high level of concordance with phenotypic tests, but it is not without limitations and cannot totally replace phenotypic methods.
(c) Insertions, integrations and transposons drive horizontal transfer of ARGs. Plasmid metagenomics focusing on mobile genetic elements (MGEs) may have great potential to identify ARGs in complex environments.

All three papers detect resistance genes by sequencing. Shotgun metagenomics with MAGs is used for the pig gut [0, 2]. Whole genome sequencing of Salmonella isolates is used for raw chicken and edible leaves [10]. The review reports metagenomic methods [16, 19, 23], high-throughput sequencing [18], PCR and qPCR [19, 21, 22, 23], direct culturing [23] and whole-genome sequencing of isolates [24, 25] across cattle, pig, shrimp, manure, wastewater, compost and poultry settings. The two primary studies share an Illumina short-read workflow [2, 11] with Trimmomatic trimming [3, 12]. Each then calls genes with its own tool: CARD/CARD-RGI for pig MAGs [0, 1] and the customized Genefinder algorithm for Salmonella, with efflux pump genes identified separately [13]. Mobile genetic elements are a shared concern. The pig study checks ARG co-location with integrase/transposase sequences [4, 5]. The review links transposons and integrations to horizontal ARG transfer [17] and notes plasmid metagenomics focusing on MGEs may have great potential in complex environments [20]. Binning ARGs from short reads is extremely challenging because they are often flanked by repeat sequences and located on mobile genetic elements such as plasmids [6]. MAG-detected ARGs are therefore assumed chromosomal, and fewer are found (115 versus 250 and 897) [7, 8]. Long-read sequencing is proposed as the remedy [9]. For isolate WGS, results show a high level of concordance with phenotypic tests [14], but WGS cannot totally replace phenotypic methods [15].
expected_concepts: mobile genetic elements such as plasmids

questions.question: How do Salmon's bias correction and DESeq2's statistical modeling improve RNA-seq analysis, and how are these processes managed in high-throughput workflows like HTS-flow?
questions.expected_answer:
Salmon: it corrects for fragment GC content bias, and its model also covers positional biases in coverage, sequence-specific biases at the 5′ and 3′ end of fragments, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution. These bias models are used to re-estimate each transcript's effective length. The paper says this substantially improves the accuracy of abundance estimates and the reliability of downstream differential expression analysis. Uncorrected biases can lead to high false positive rates. In DE testing, Salmon's sensitivity is 53% to 250% higher at the same FDRs (main text). The Figure 1c legend gives 53%–450% over kallisto and 210%–250% over eXpress. Salmon also makes fewer false-positive DE calls.
DESeq2: it models read counts with a negative binomial (gamma-Poisson) distribution. It assumes that genes of similar average expression strength have similar dispersion, and it uses shrinkage estimation for dispersions and fold changes to improve the stability and interpretability of estimates. Dispersion shrinkage helps avoid false positives caused by underestimated dispersion. LFC estimates are shrunk toward zero, more strongly when a gene carries little information, which gives a more reliable basis for quantitative conclusions than normal MLEs. Overall, shrinkage improves stability and reproducibility compared with maximum-likelihood-based solutions.
HTS-flow: the paper does not mention Salmon or DESeq2. It offers absolute and differential expression quantification for RNA-Seq as a secondary analysis. Primary analyses (quality controls, pre-processing, alignment) run per sample as soon as the raw data are tracked in the LIMS. Users without bioinformatics skills run and track analyses through a web interface. The analyses use predefined, easily customizable modular scripts that are versioned on Github. Annotation uses standard Bioconductor metadata libraries (TxDb, BSgenome), and outputs are R data objects that follow Bioconductor standards.

Salmon corrects for sample-specific RNA-seq biases, including fragment GC bias, by re-estimating each transcript's effective length [0, 2, 3]. This improves the accuracy of abundance estimates and downstream differential expression: higher DE sensitivity at the same FDRs and fewer false-positive DE calls, where uncorrected biases can cause high false positive rates [0, 1, 4, 5, 6]. DESeq2 models counts with a negative binomial distribution and shrinks dispersions and fold changes, sharing information across genes of similar expression. This avoids false positives from underestimated dispersion, gives more reliable fold changes, and improves stability and reproducibility over maximum-likelihood solutions [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. HTS-flow names neither tool. It offers absolute and differential expression quantification for RNA-Seq as a secondary analysis that follows per-sample primary analyses started once data are tracked in the LIMS [14, 15]. These analyses are run and tracked from a web interface through predefined modular scripts versioned on Github, use standard Bioconductor annotation libraries, and produce Bioconductor-compliant R objects [16, 17, 18, 19, 20].
expected_concepts: shrinkage estimation for dispersions and fold changes

questions.question: Based on the development of Sarek, Snakemake, nf-core, and fastp, what is the emerging meta-strategy for balancing high-performance computational efficiency with scientific reproducibility in large-scale genomics?
questions.expected_answer:
No paper names a meta-strategy. Read together, they describe one approach. Analyses run in a workflow manager (Nextflow for Sarek and nf-core/sarek, or Snakemake) that scales across HPC clusters and cloud. The workflow is kept separate from the platform: in Snakemake, scaling should only change command line parameters. Efficiency comes from parallelisation (Sarek's scatter-gather, intra-sample parallelisation, FastQ sharding, interval splitting, fastp's multi-threading and output splitting) and from merging steps. fastp does QC, adapter trimming and quality filtering in a single scan of the FASTQ data and is 2–5 times faster than other preprocessing tools. nf-core/sarek 3 adopts it and, with tailored interval splitting, cuts CPU hours by 66%. With CRAM storage it reports a 70% cost reduction in commercial clouds, though the same paper also gives costs reduced to approximately 30% and to 50%. Reproducibility comes from packaging software in Conda environments and Docker or Singularity containers, and from recording the exact release version, pipeline parameters and custom configs. Snakemake adds that reproducibility is necessary but not sufficient: reproducibility alone is not enough, and analyses must also be adaptable and transparent. fastp addresses efficiency only.

All three workflow papers run analyses in a workflow language that scales across HPC schedulers and cloud [4, 6, 7, 17, 22]. Snakemake keeps the workflow separate from the platform, so scaling should only change command line parameters [11], and it treats scalability as needed for reproducing results [8, 10]. Efficiency comes from parallelisation: Sarek's scatter-gather across CPU cores [3], nf-core/sarek 3's intra-sample parallelisation, FastQ sharding and interval splitting [15, 23], and fastp's multi-threading and output splitting for parallel processing [29, 30]. It also comes from merging steps: fastp does many operations in a single scan because reading data multiple times was slow and I/O inefficient, and is 2–5 times faster [26, 27, 28]; nf-core/sarek 3 adopts fastp to combine sharding and adapter removal into one step [19], cutting CPU hours by 66% [23] (approximately 70% for a single sample [21]), and with CRAM storage reports a 70% cloud cost reduction [16], also stated as costs reduced to approximately 30% [20] and to 50% [24]. Reproducibility comes from packaging each tool's software in Conda environments and Docker or Singularity containers [2, 7, 9, 18] and from fixing the release version, parameters and configs [25]. Sarek states the goal as combining software in an efficient and reproducible manner [0, 1] through narrow, independent workflows [5]. Snakemake qualifies the goal: reproducibility is necessary but not sufficient, and analyses must also be adaptable and transparent [12, 13, 14].
expected_concepts: reduces the needed CPU hours by 66%
single scan of the FASTQ data

questions.question: How do the collective methodologies across Sarek, Snakemake, nf-core, and MultiQC redefine the concept of 'quality control' from a single-sample metric to a system-wide diagnostic process?
questions.expected_answer:
The papers do not say they redefine QC or call it a system-wide diagnostic process. Together they describe QC moving from per-sample tool output to one aggregated report. MultiQC: QC logs and reports are produced on a per-sample basis, with no common approach to integrate them across tools and large sample sets. MultiQC builds a single summary report across all samples and tools. Its shared plots allow comparison between samples, aid batch effect detection, show global trends and biases, and help spot failing, abnormal or irregular groups of samples. It acts as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines. Sarek (2020): generates QC metrics with FastQC, QualiMap, BCFtools, Samtools and VCFtools, shown as an aggregated quality control review across samples with MultiQC. Its error reporting diagnoses software or hardware errors during a run, which is separate from data QC, and qualitative assessment by the user remains important. nf-core/sarek 3: QC reporting is one of four major processing units. QC tools run throughout the pipeline (FastQC before alignment; mosdepth and SAMtools after duplicate marking and BQSR; vcftools and bcftools on called variants), and their results go into one MultiQC report together with software version numbers of all executed tools. Snakemake: QC is one step in a unified representation of the whole analysis. A QC step yields QC values for each sample, and through conditional execution (a checkpoint) only samples above a threshold (greater than 90 in the example) go downstream. Snakemake also tracks the inputs, outputs, parameters, software and code of each executed job and reports them, with runtime statistics for all jobs, in an interactive HTML report. The paper does not call these reports QC.

MultiQC names the starting point: QC logs and reports are produced per sample, with no common way to integrate them across tools and sample sets [0, 1]. Its answer is a single report across all samples and tools that supports comparison between samples, batch effect detection, global trends, and the identification of failing, abnormal or irregular samples [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. It is meant to sit at the terminus of analysis pipelines [9]. Sarek 2020 applies this to a variant-calling workflow, showing QC metrics from several tools as an aggregated review across samples with MultiQC [10]. Its run-time diagnosis concerns software or hardware errors, and the authors say the user's own assessment remains important [11, 12]. nf-core/sarek 3 makes QC reporting one of four processing units, runs QC tools at the read, alignment and variant stages, and collects them with all software versions into one MultiQC report [13, 14, 15, 16]. Snakemake places QC inside a unified representation of the analysis, where per-sample QC values can automatically decide, through conditional execution, which samples continue downstream [17, 18, 19, 20]. It also tracks provenance and runtime for every job in one report, which it does not call QC [21, 22, 23]. None of the papers describes this as redefining QC [0-23].
expected_concepts: single summary report visualizing results across all samples
aggregated quality control review across samples
software version numbers of all the executed tools
yields QC values for each sample

questions.question: How does the corpus demonstrate an evolution from localized tool optimization to systemic computational efficiency across different layers of the bioinformatics stack?
questions.expected_answer:
The papers optimise efficiency at different layers. Three improve a single tool, and nf-core/sarek works on the whole pipeline. None of them states the trend; it is an inference across the four.

1. **Alignment (STAR).** The computational component is called a throughput bottleneck. STAR uses a sequential MMP search and uncompressed SAs. It scales close to linearly with cores and aligns 550 million reads per hour on a 12-core server, surpassing all other existing RNA-seq aligners by a factor of 50. Table 1 gives 549.9 million read pairs/hour at 12 threads, against 10.1 for TopHat2, with 28.4 GB peak RAM.
2. **File manipulation (SeqKit).** File I/O is named as the bottleneck. SeqKit parallelises CPU-intensive processes with Goroutines, gains a ~20× speedup from an algorithm change, and uses an MD5 digest to reduce memory usage. It finds no significant improvement beyond two threads.
3. **Preprocessing (fastp).** Reading and loading data multiple times made preprocessing slow and I/O inefficient. fastp performs many operations with a single scan of the FASTQ data, has multi-threading support, and is 2–5 times faster than Trimmomatic or Cutadapt. It can split output into multiple files for parallel processing, which the paper calls a new trend in cloud computing.
4. **Pipeline (nf-core/sarek).** The rewrite focuses on reducing compute resources across infrastructures, through CRAM and intra-sample parallelization. It adopts fastp to combine FastQ sharding and adapter removal into one step.
   - Combined steps plus interval splitting reduce CPU hours by 66%.
   - CRAM cuts work-directory storage by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB).
   - Sharding brings median mapping runtime to 37%, with a plateau at 12 shards.
   - Separately, there is no further benefit to reducing runtime beyond 21 interval groups.
   - For a single sample, CPU hours fall by approximately 70% and runtime by 84%.
   - The cost saving is stated four ways: a 70% cost reduction, a 69% reduction in compute costs, costs reduced to approximately 30%, and costs reduced to 50%.

At the alignment layer, STAR treats the computational component as a throughput bottleneck [0]. It answers within the tool:
- a sequential MMP search and uncompressed SAs [1, 2]
- close to linear multithreaded scaling [3]
- a factor of 50 over other aligners [4]
- 549.9 against 10.1 million read pairs/hour for TopHat2 at 12 threads, using 28.4 GB of RAM [5]

At the file-manipulation layer, SeqKit names file I/O as the bottleneck [6]. It optimises inside the tool through Goroutine parallelism [7], a ~20× speedup from an algorithm change [8] and MD5 digests that reduce memory [9]. It sees no significant gain beyond two threads [10] and outperforms seqtk on FASTA parsing [11].

At the preprocessing layer, fastp targets the slowness of reading data multiple times through separate, poorly multithreaded tools [12, 13, 14]. It merges many operations into a single scan [15, 18], has multi-threading support [16] and is 2–5 times faster [17]. It also splits output for parallel processing, which it calls a new trend in cloud computing [19, 20].

At the workflow layer, nf-core/sarek aims to reduce compute resources for the whole pipeline across infrastructures, through CRAM and intra-sample parallelization [21, 23]. It builds fastp in to combine FastQ sharding and adapter removal into one step [25], which is the only link between the layers that any paper states. Combined steps and interval splitting cut CPU hours by 66% [30]. CRAM cuts storage by 65% [26]. Sharding reduces median mapping runtime to 37%, with a plateau at 12 shards [27]. Separately, there is no further benefit to reducing runtime beyond 21 interval groups [31]. Per-sample CPU hours fall by approximately 70% and runtime by 84% [28]. The cost saving is reported as 70% [22], 69% [24], costs reduced to approximately 30% [29] and costs reduced to 50% [32].

That these steps form a trend from tool-level to system-level efficiency is an inference from the four papers; none of them states it.
expected_concepts: single scan of the FASTQ data
combines FastQ sharding and adapter removal into one step
reduces the needed CPU hours by 66%

questions.question: Based on the various stages of data processing described, what meta-conclusion can be drawn regarding the relationship between technical artifact removal and statistical reliability in high-throughput sequencing analysis?
questions.expected_answer:
At each stage, the papers present removing or correcting technical problems as a condition for reliable downstream inference, mainly because it cuts false positives.

- fastp: preprocessing is critical to high-confidence variants and to eliminating false positives and false negatives. Data filtered by fastp gave 6708 false positive variants, against 7174 (Trimmomatic), 7040 (SOAPNuke) and 6942 (Cutadapt). The authors read this as improved specificity of downstream analysis.
- Cutadapt: removing adapters is an essential first task. In some cases finding adapters is a sign of contamination, and those reads must be discarded entirely. A leftover adapter colour could cause a spurious mismatch during read mapping.
- MultiQC: batch-effect biases are often subtle and require careful quality control. Detecting them minimizes the risk of confounding factors affecting the study's results and reduces the risk of downstream analysis problems.
- Salmon: uncorrected biases can lead to high false positive rates in differential expression. Correcting fragment GC content bias improves the accuracy of abundance estimates and the reliability of differential expression analysis, with fewer false-positive calls.
- DESeq2: outliers require a suitable statistical approach and can impair inference. By default, in conditions with six or fewer replicates, genes with outliers are flagged and removed from subsequent analysis, including P value adjustment for multiple testing. In conditions with seven or more replicates, the outlier counts are replaced with an imputed value. Its outlier detection avoids type-I errors.

None of the papers states this cross-stage conclusion. It is assembled from what each paper says about its own stage.

Each paper treats technical problems at its own stage as a threat to the reliability of downstream results.

- Read level: preprocessing is critical to high-confidence variants and to eliminating false positives and false negatives [0, 1]. In fastp's benchmark, fastp-filtered data gave the fewest false positive variants of the four tools, which the authors read as improved downstream specificity [2, 3]. Cutadapt treats adapter removal as an essential first task, says that in some cases finding adapters is a sign of contamination and those reads must be discarded, and says a leftover adapter colour could cause a spurious mismatch during read mapping [4, 5, 6].
- QC aggregation: subtle batch-effect biases require careful quality control. Detecting them minimizes the risk of confounding the study's results and other downstream analysis problems [7, 8, 9].
- Quantification: uncorrected biases can lead to high false positive rates in differential expression. Correcting fragment GC content bias improves the reliability of differential expression analysis and gives fewer false-positive calls [10, 11, 12].
- Statistical testing: outliers require a suitable statistical approach and can impair inference [13, 15]. By default, in conditions with six or fewer replicates, genes with outliers are removed from subsequent analysis, including multiple-testing adjustment [14]; with seven or more replicates the outlier counts are replaced with an imputed value [17]. Outlier detection avoids type-I errors [16].

Combined: handling technical problems before or during each stage is presented as a precondition for downstream statistical reliability, measured mainly as fewer false positives [1, 3, 11, 12, 16].
expected_concepts: improve the specificity of downstream analysis
correct for fragment GC content bias

questions.question: How do human-animal interface factors, ranging from professional habits to physiological events in livestock, collectively define the zoonotic risk landscape for bacterial and viral pathogens in endemic regions?
questions.expected_answer:
Bovine TB in Cameroon (bacterial): high herd size, cattle aged >10 years, seizures of tuberculous organs, shepherding as a profession and contact between cattle and wildlife due to forage were associated with bTB exposure. The risk of human infection with M. bovis comes from contact between shepherd and cattle that is constant and permanent, and the risk is high where bTB is endemic and control programs are not enforced. No correlation was found between wildlife reservoirs and bTB transmission.

Brucellosis in Ethiopian pastoralists (bacterial): herd size and herd history of retained fetal membranes (RFM) were the animal risk factors. In camels, pregnancy, history of abortion and RFM were associated with seropositivity, and RFM stayed significant in the multivariable model; RFM was also a risk factor in sheep and goats. In humans, disposing of RFM and handling and disposing of aborted fetal materials were significant, with a 26-fold higher risk for close contact with RFM while disposing. Raw milk consumption (76.4% of participants) was not significantly associated. Assisting calving is not significant in the Results (OR 3.6, p = 0.16) but is called significant in the Discussion (OR = 8; 95% CI = 0.6–127).

HPAI H5N1 in Canada (viral): all severely affected human cases had direct exposure to poultry, and infection should be considered after exposure to birds or sick wildlife in the previous 10–14 days. This clade has been identified in less than 10 humans. Spillover to mammals highlights the risk of reassortment with swine or human influenza viruses.

In all three papers, zoonotic risk comes from close contact between people and animals. For bTB in Cameroon, the occupational factor is shepherding as a profession, with constant and permanent shepherd-cattle contact creating conditions for cross-infection [0, 1, 2, 3]. Contact between cattle and wildlife at feeding points is also associated with exposure [1, 5], although no correlation was found with wildlife reservoirs [6]. Human risk is high where bTB is endemic and control programs are not enforced [4]. For brucellosis in Ethiopia, the human practice is disposing of retained fetal membranes and handling aborted fetal materials, with a 26-fold higher risk for close contact with RFM while disposing [8, 14, 15]. Raw milk consumption was common but not significant [17], and the paper reports assisting calving both as not significant and as significant [18, 19]. Physiological events in livestock appear only in the brucellosis paper. Retained fetal membranes, abortion and pregnancy were associated with animal seropositivity [7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13], and Brucella abortion often leads to a retained placenta [16]. RFM is therefore both an animal risk factor and the material whose disposal carries human risk [7, 8, 15]. Herd-level factors also count: herd size for both bacterial diseases, and cattle aged >10 years and tuberculous organ seizure for bTB [1, 7]. For the viral pathogen HPAI H5N1, the interface is direct exposure to poultry and exposure to birds or sick wildlife [21, 22]. Human cases number less than 10 [23], but avian infection creates opportunities for spillover to mammals and a risk of reassortment with swine or human influenza viruses [24, 25]. The brucellosis authors conclude that close contact between humans and animals indicates a potential public health risk [20].
expected_concepts: herd history of retained fetal membranes
exposure to birds or sick wildlife

questions.question: Analyze how the choice of diagnostic methodology and specific assay thresholds influences the reported prevalence and epidemiological understanding of transboundary diseases.
questions.expected_answer:
Bovine TB, Cameroon (the only paper that tests a threshold directly): on the same 160 cattle, CIDT gave 11 positives (6.8%) at 3 mm, against 0.6% (Results, Discussion, Table-2) or 1.8% (abstract) at 4 mm; the paper assigns 1.8% and 0.6% to SITT and CIDT differently in the abstract and the Results. The authors state that 3 mm increased the sensitivity of bTB detection, that apparent prevalence at 3 mm was significantly higher, and that it increased the actual prevalence; they recommend 3 mm for Cameroon and a threshold suited to the local epidemiological context.

Brucellosis, Ethiopia: RBPT (high sensitivity; modified in sheep and goats to improve sensitivity) was used serially with cELISA (high specificity) to rule out false-positive cross-reactions; a sample was seropositive only if positive on both. Prevalence was 5% in small ruminants, 2.9% in camels and 2.0% in humans. The authors name the sensitivity and specificity of tests used, and the type of diagnostic test, among possible reasons for differences from other studies.

PPR, Ethiopia: competition ELISA (sensitivity 94.5%, specificity 99.4%), positive at S/N% <=50%, negative >60%, doubtful 50 to 60%. Seroprevalence was 32.1% (non-vaccinated), 68.8% (vaccinated) and 45.5% (unknown); the seroconversion rates are below the FAO-WOAH 80% herd-immunity threshold. Differences from other studies are attributed to geography, animal movement, population density, management and migration.

ASF, Burkina Faso: real-time PCR confirmed ASFV DNA in 20 of 62 samples. p72 placed all isolates in genotype I, while CVR (4 TRS variants) and CD2v (five variants) typing separated variants, suggesting an epidemiological link between Saaba, Nioko II and Kossodo and spread from Kossodo to Tampouy; the authors conclude molecular characterization is important to understand the link between epidemics.

Each paper's diagnostic method and positivity rule determines what is counted, but only the bovine TB study measures the effect of a threshold directly.
- Bovine TB: on the same 160 cattle, CIDT gave 6.8% at 3 mm against 0.6% or 1.8% at 4 mm, depending on where in the paper one reads [0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. The authors state that 3 mm increased sensitivity, gave significantly higher apparent prevalence and increased the actual prevalence, yielded better results, and should be applied in Cameroon, with a threshold suited to the local epidemiological context [2, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13].
- Brucellosis: a sensitive screen (RBPT, modified to improve sensitivity in sheep and goats) was used serially with a specific confirmatory cELISA, counting only samples positive on both, to rule out false-positive cross-reactions [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. Prevalence under that definition was 5%, 2.9% and 2.0% in small ruminants, camels and humans [27]. The authors list test sensitivity and specificity and the type of diagnostic test among reasons for differences from other studies [28, 29, 30].
- PPR: seropositivity is defined by a c-ELISA cut-off of S/N% <=50% with stated sensitivity 94.5% and specificity 99.4% [14, 15]; seroprevalence was 32.1%, 68.8% and 45.5% by vaccination status and is read against the FAO-WOAH 80% herd-immunity threshold [16, 17]. Differences from other studies are attributed to non-diagnostic factors [18].
- ASF: real-time PCR confirmed 20 of 62 samples [31, 32]. The genetic marker set the epidemiological resolution: p72 gave a single genotype [33], while CVR and CD2v typing separated variants that suggested links between outbreaks and spread from Kossodo to Tampouy [34, 35, 36]; the authors conclude molecular characterization is important to understand the link between epidemics [37].
expected_concepts: increased the sensitivity of bTB detection
increased the actual prevalence of bTB

questions.question: How do anthropogenic factors, such as animal management and vaccination distribution, create patterns of disease persistence in regions attempting control of transboundary pathogens?
questions.expected_answer:
The four papers show two human-driven routes to persistence: moving and keeping animals, and uneven or insufficient vaccination.

(1) Moving and keeping animals.
- LSD in Nepal: the movement of animals from the Indian border area was a potential source of the outbreak, and the movement of animals between farms spread infection. Importing animals, sharing feed and water, and herd size were linked to outbreaks in univariable analysis only. Outbreaks have recurred over the past 3 years, and animals were not yet vaccinated against LSD.
- PPR in Borena, Ethiopia: seasonal movement of livestock across the borders with Kenya and Somalia, and uncontrolled animal movement, may contribute to spread. The probability of testing positive was four times higher for animals purchased from markets, and 8.3 times higher for gifted animals, than for animals born within the flocks. Outbreaks peak in the dry season, which cited studies attribute to animal movement in search of resources.
- LSD review: large-scale animal transfers from East Africa spread the disease to Syria, Iran and Iraq. Larger farms with intensive housing and shared feeding and watering facilities can contribute to transmission.
- Rabies in Serengeti: incursions in the district centre likely result from human-mediated transport.

(2) Uneven or insufficient vaccination.
- Rabies in Serengeti: campaigns ran less consistently away from the National Park, depending on local government resources, and only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target. Outbreaks followed multi-year periods when clusters of villages remained unvaccinated. At the same mean coverage, more heterogeneous coverage raised incidence (1.4 times for a 30%/50% split against a uniform 40%). Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell below 0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually. Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district then became a major source of residual transmission, reaching 50% of cases in 2022.
- PPR in Borena: there were 53 outbreaks from 2018 to 2022. 10,000 vaccine doses were deployed for an at-risk population of 397,189, and herd immunity was 68.8%, below the 80% FAO-WOAH threshold. The paper gives inadequate cold chain management, poor vaccine handling and distribution practices as possible causes. Outbreaks were concentrated in the hard-to-reach districts of Arero and Dhas, which risk becoming persistent focal points.
- LSD in Nepal: coverage of more than 80% is needed. The LSD review describes ring vaccination within a 5-km radius in border areas, and calls vaccination the singular means to prevent recurrence.

Moving and acquiring animals introduces and spreads these pathogens. In Nepal, LSD likely entered with animals moved from the Indian border area, then spread between farms [3, 4, 5, 7]. Importing animals, sharing feed and water, and herd size were linked to outbreaks only in univariable analysis [0, 6]. In Borena, seasonal cross-border livestock movement and uncontrolled animal movement may contribute to PPR spread, and purchased and gifted animals were more likely to test positive than animals born within the flocks [21, 22, 23]. Outbreaks there peak in the dry season, which cited studies attribute to animal movement in search of resources [29, 30]. The LSD review links spread to Syria, Iran and Iraq to large-scale animal transfers, and links transmission to larger farms with shared feeding and watering facilities [34, 35, 36, 37]. In Serengeti, rabies incursions in the district centre likely result from human-mediated transport [17].

Where vaccination is absent, insufficient or uneven, disease persists. In Nepal, LSD outbreaks recurred over 3 years while animals were not yet vaccinated, and the authors call for coverage of more than 80% [1, 2, 8]. In Serengeti, campaigns depended on local government resources, and only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target [12, 13]. Outbreaks followed multi-year periods when clusters of villages remained unvaccinated, and at the same mean coverage heterogeneity raised incidence (1.4 times in one modelled example) [9, 14, 15, 16]. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell below 0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually [10, 19]. Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district then became a major source of residual transmission (50% of cases in 2022), interacting with heterogeneous vaccination [11, 18, 19]. In Borena, 53 outbreaks in 2018 to 2022 coincided with 10,000 doses for 397,189 at-risk animals and 68.8% herd immunity, below the 80% threshold [20, 24, 25, 27, 28]. The paper attributes the shortfall to cold-chain, handling and distribution problems [26], and inaccessible districts with disproportionate outbreaks risk becoming persistent focal points [31, 32, 33]. The LSD review names movement management or limitations, quarantine and vaccination (including ring vaccination in border areas) as control measures, and vaccination as the singular means to prevent recurrence [38, 39, 40, 41].
expected_concepts: persistent focal points for the disease

questions.question: What meta-conclusion can be drawn regarding the evolving clinical presentation of livestock and wildlife viral diseases and its impact on traditional early-warning surveillance systems?
questions.expected_answer:
The papers describe clinical presentation that varies more than it evolves. HPAI signs in Dutch laying flocks showed no significant differences between 2014–2018 and 2020–2022; what changed is that adult duck and juvenile chicken farms were not diagnosed before 2020. Presentation differs between virus strains, species, age groups and immune status. In chicken flocks high mortality was the main reason for notification, but mortality remained limited in ducks, where drops in feed or water intake or egg production may be the only initial signs. FMD signs can be far more subtle in animals with pre-existing immunity or in resistant breeds, and FMD in sheep is more likely to be overlooked or misdiagnosed. FMDV transmission can occur before clinical signs are apparent, subclinical FMDV is usually overlooked where surveillance is focused on clinical cases, and FMDV may circulate among partially immune animals without being noticed. LSDV infections range from asymptomatic illness to death. Wildlife testing is biased towards severely infected or dead animals, so milder disease is likely missed and identified infections represent only a minority of spillovers. The common conclusion is that early warning that relies on passive surveillance and on clinical signs or mortality misses or delays detection. The papers call for reporting criteria that differ by poultry species and age group (Dutch notification thresholds have already been adapted), sample collection from clinically unaffected animals, and pre-clinical infectiousness in outbreak modelling.

Early-warning and control systems have relied on clinical signs and mortality: HPAI notification relies on passive surveillance [1], high mortality was the main reason for notification in chicken flocks [6], and early FMD control strategies often rely on rapid detection of clinical signs [12]. The papers show presentation varying more than evolving: HPAI clinical signs in laying flocks did not differ significantly between 2014–2018 and 2020–2022 [3, 4], and the lower share of flocks with MR > 3 may reflect earlier notification [5]. The poultry types affected did change, since adult duck and juvenile chicken farms were not diagnosed before 2020 [2], and manifestations differed between viruses isolated at different timepoints of one outbreak [9]. Presentation varies by virus strain [8], by species, with limited mortality in ducks, where feed, water or egg-production drops may be the only initial signs [6, 7], by immune status and breed, with subtle FMD signs [17], and by host, with FMD in sheep often overlooked [16]; LSDV ranges from asymptomatic illness to death [22]. Surveillance based on clinical signs therefore misses infections: FMDV transmits before clinical signs are apparent [13], subclinical FMDV is overlooked where surveillance focuses on clinical cases [14], FMDV can circulate unnoticed in partially immune animals [18], and wildlife HPAI testing is biased towards severely infected or dead animals, so milder disease is missed and identified infections are a minority of spillovers [20, 21]. The papers draw the implication that early-warning criteria need improving or adjusting [0, 11], with reporting criteria specific to species and age group [7] and notification thresholds already adapted in the Netherlands [10], sampling of clinically unaffected animals [15], and pre-clinical infectiousness included in outbreak models [19].
expected_concepts: without significant differences in clinical signs
the only initial signs of infection
criteria for reporting should be different
sample collection from clinically unaffected animals
biased towards severely infected or dead animals
ranging from asymptomatic illness to death

questions.question: Identify the gaps in translating standardized, large-scale genomic workflows into the context of rapid, localized veterinary outbreak characterization based on current literature.
questions.expected_answer:
No paper names the gap directly. It has to be read off by setting the papers side by side.

1. Design target and setting. Sarek is built for germline and somatic (cancer) variant detection, at core facilities and in research groups. nf-core/sarek 3 targets large multi-site cohorts on high-performance clusters and cloud setups. Sarek's default reference is human GRCh38.

2. References. nf-core/sarek 3 can process non-model organisms, but references are provided mainly for human and mouse. For non-supported species they must be generated, the pipeline applies only where a reference genome exists, and easier custom-reference handling is left to future releases.

3. Resources and turnaround. A full 90x/90x WGS run needs at least 16 cores, 128 GB RAM and 4 TB of storage. It took 48 hours and 21 minutes (about 48 hours). In version 3.1.1, one normal sample took 12h4m and cost $20.82. Storage can be a bottleneck on the available compute system.

4. Testing and expertise. Sarek has had no systematic testing on WES or gene-panel data. Careful parameter tuning, variant filtering and qualitative assessment by the user remain important. The authors say there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

5. ASF outbreak study. The outbreak was characterized by real-time PCR and the partial P72, complete p54, partial CD2v and partial B602L genes. ASFV DNA was confirmed in twenty of sixty-two samples. Sequencing was done by LGC Genomics (Berlin) and assembly used Vector NTI 11.5. Nineteen p72 and p54, fourteen CD2v and twenty B602L sequences were obtained. The disease had started two weeks (Results: several days to two weeks) before the investigation. Breeders knew little about swine diseases, and technical support was insufficient. The authors call for continued rapid diagnostics and analysis. Whether their approach suits other serogroups and genotypes, and how the variants emerged, remain open.

6. HPAI in Canada. The animal health sector is heavily engaged in outbreak management. Wildlife surveillance has limited scope and is biased towards severely infected or dead animals. The authors call for quick identification of strains with enhanced mammalian fitness, stronger laboratory capacity and coordination between the human and animal health sectors. They also name major gaps in understanding how climate disruption affects HPAI.

The standardized workflows were built for germline and somatic variant detection at core facilities and research groups, for large multi-site cohorts run on high-performance clusters and cloud setups [0, 1, 9, 10]. Sarek's default reference is human GRCh38 [5]. nf-core/sarek 3 can process non-model organisms, but references are provided mainly for human and mouse and have to be generated for non-supported species. It applies only where a reference genome exists, and simpler custom-reference handling is left to future releases [11, 12, 13, 14]. A full 90x/90x WGS run needs at least 16 cores, 128 GB RAM and 4 TB of storage and took 48 hours and 21 minutes (about 48 hours) [2, 3, 4]. In version 3.1.1 one normal sample took 12h4m and cost 20.82 dollars [16], and storage can be a bottleneck on the available compute system [15]. Sarek has not been systematically tested on WES or gene-panel data [6]. It still needs careful parameter tuning, variant filtering and assessment by the user, and its authors say there is no one-size-fits-all solution [7, 8]. The localized ASF outbreak study used none of this. It characterized the virus by real-time PCR and four gene targets in twenty of sixty-two samples, had the sequencing done by LGC Genomics in Berlin and assembled with Vector NTI, and obtained sequences for nineteen p72 and p54, fourteen CD2v and twenty B602L targets [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. The investigation began two weeks, or several days to two weeks, after onset [22, 23]. That study reports little breeder knowledge and insufficient technical support, and it calls for continued rapid diagnostics and analysis [24, 25, 26]. It leaves open whether its approach suits other ASFV serogroups and genotypes, and how the variants emerged [27, 28]. The HPAI commentary describes an animal health sector heavily engaged in outbreak management, while wildlife surveillance has limited scope and is biased towards severely infected or dead animals [29, 30, 31]. It calls for quick identification of strains with enhanced mammalian fitness, stronger laboratory capacity and coordination between the human and animal health sectors [32, 33], and it names major gaps in understanding the effect of climate disruption on HPAI [34].
expected_concepts: most comprehensively provided for human and mouse

questions.question: How do modern workflow management systems and graphical interfaces collectively address the 'reproducibility crisis' in high-throughput sequencing analysis across different computational environments?
questions.expected_answer:
Workflow systems: they automate the analysis and deploy the software stack each step needs, using the Conda package manager or Docker/Singularity containers. Snakemake says full in silico reproducibility needs an analysis that is automated, scalable to various computational platforms and portable, meaning it deploys automatically with all required software in exactly the needed versions.
- Sarek: dependencies are encapsulated in Docker or Singularity containers or a Conda environment built with Bioconda, so users install no software by hand. Singularity is used at high-performance computing centers that do not allow Docker. Sarek installs reproducibly on all POSIX compatible systems, including secure environments for sensitive personal data. Nextflow supports Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF, Kubernetes, Google Cloud and AWS.
- Snakemake: each rule can get its own Conda environment. Containers control the execution environment down to the system libraries and make it portable across operating systems. Snakemake tracks the input files, output files, parameters, software and code of each job.
- nf-core/sarek 3: Nextflow gives portability to cloud vendors and common HPC schedulers. Each module has a (bio)conda package and a Docker and Singularity container from Biocontainers, and the single-tool-per-process approach mitigates dependency conflicts. Full-size tests on each release check portability to cloud infrastructures. Reproducibility is ensured by giving the exact release version, the pipeline parameters and the custom configs.

Graphical interfaces: they lower the skill barrier. Galaxy, KNIME and Watchdog offer graphical user interfaces with a shallow learning curve and no need for programming skills, and Galaxy is among the systems that support full in silico reproducibility. HTS-flow manages analyses through a simple web GUI for users without bioinformatics skills. It supports reproducibility through LIMS integration, standard output locations, complete traceability of datasets, metadata and analysis scripts, versioning on GitHub, standard Bioconductor annotation packages (TxDb, BSgenome) and identical workflows for data from various sources.

The papers tie reproducibility to automation by workflow management systems [7, 25]. Full in silico reproducibility needs an analysis that is automated, scalable to various computational platforms and deployed automatically with all required software in exactly the needed versions [11]. GUI-based and DSL-based systems (Galaxy, Nextflow, Snakemake, WDL, CWL) support this by deploying the software stack for each step with Conda, Docker or Singularity [10]. Sarek encapsulates its dependencies in Docker or Singularity containers or a Conda/Bioconda environment, so users install no software by hand [3, 4]. Singularity is used at HPC centres that do not allow Docker [5]. Sarek installs reproducibly on all POSIX compatible systems, including secure environments for sensitive data [2, 6]. Its Nextflow base supports Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF, Kubernetes, Google Cloud and AWS [1]. Snakemake deploys a Conda environment for each rule [12], uses containers that make the execution environment portable across operating systems [13], and tracks the files, parameters, software and code of each job [14]. nf-core/sarek 3 relies on Nextflow for portability across cloud vendors and HPC schedulers [15], and gives each single-tool module a bioconda package and Biocontainers containers, which mitigates dependency conflicts [16, 17]. It tests cloud portability on each release [18] and reproduces a run from its exact release version, parameters and configs [19]. Graphical interfaces address a different barrier, the skills of the user. Galaxy, KNIME and Watchdog offer GUIs that need no programming skills [8, 9]. HTS-flow provides a simple web GUI for users without computer-science or bioinformatics training [20, 22, 27]. HTS-flow ties reproducibility to the LIMS structure, which is otherwise commonly neglected, and to standard output locations and complete traceability [20, 21]. It also relies on GitHub versioning [29], tracked standard Bioconductor annotation packages [23, 24, 28] and identical workflows for data from various sources [26].
expected_concepts: cloud vendors and common HPC schedulers
without the need for programming skills
manages data analyses through a simple GUI

questions.question: Compare the strategies used by high-performance bioinformatics toolkits to overcome I/O and CPU bottlenecks when processing massive genomic and epigenomic datasets.
questions.expected_answer:
fastp: chained tools read and load data multiple times, so fastp does quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering, per-read quality pruning and other operations in a single scan of the FASTQ data. For CPU it is written in C/C++ (the text layer prints "C/Cþþ") for multi-threading parallel processing. Reads are packed in groups of 1000 (N = 1000) and each pack is consumed by one thread in a pool. Duplication keys are stored in a duplication array and a counting array, not a hash table. It is 2–5 times faster than Trimmomatic or Cutadapt.

SeqKit: names file I/O and sequence record parsing as the bottleneck. It parses with the authors' own high-performance package and a custom buffered file reader in place of Go's "bufio". CPU-intensive processes are parallelised with Goroutines. Two threads beat one, and three or more gave no further significant improvement. A slice lookup for complementary sequences gives a ~20× speedup over a map. For memory, most subcommands do not load all records, MD5 digests represent sequence content, and two-pass mode uses the FASTA index.

Cutadapt: mainly Python, with the alignment algorithm implemented in C as a Python extension module for speed. In practice reading and parsing the input files take more than half of the time. It trims about 1 million reads per minute on a single core.

methylPipe (WGBS): keeps data on disk as Tabix-indexed compressed files (269 MB and 380 MB compressed, 372 MB and 554 MB uncompressed) that are accessed directly from disk, saving memory. BiSeq and M3D load the entire dataset into memory and failed even with 80 GB. The code is parallelised for the most demanding tasks, such as identifying differentially methylated regions, and adjusts automatically to the available cores and RAM (45 min with 10 cores genome-wide).

All four papers name data reading or handling as a bottleneck. fastp names reading and loading data multiple times [1, 2], SeqKit names file I/O and record parsing [11, 12], Cutadapt reports that reading and parsing input take more than half its time [25], and methylPipe names the speed and memory cost of multiple WGBS datasets [27]. Against I/O, fastp runs every operation in a single scan [3]. SeqKit uses its own high-performance parser and a custom buffered reader [13, 15]. methylPipe keeps Tabix-indexed compressed files on disk and reads them directly [27, 29, 31]. Against CPU cost, fastp uses C/C++ with multi-threading, where a thread pool consumes packs of 1000 reads [0, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. SeqKit parallelises with Goroutines, and the gain levels off beyond two threads [14, 22]. methylPipe parallelises DMR identification and adjusts to the available cores and RAM [28, 33, 34]. Cutadapt moves only its alignment algorithm into C as a Python extension and reports single-core throughput [23, 26]. fastp and SeqKit both replace general-purpose structures with specialised ones: arrays instead of a hash table [9], and a slice lookup with a ~20× speedup over a map [16, 17]. SeqKit and methylPipe both limit memory. SeqKit uses streaming, MD5 digests and FASTA-indexed two-pass reading [18, 19, 20, 21]. methylPipe uses disk-based access [31], unlike BiSeq and M3D, which load the whole dataset into memory and failed at 80 GB [32].
