implemented in C as a Python extension module
reading and parsing the input files
available number of cores and RAM

questions.question: Analyze the shift from Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) to Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) across diverse ecological studies and explain why this shift is critical for cross-study meta-analyses.
questions.expected_answer:
The shift: OTUs as the standard 16S reporting unit have been challenged, and ASVs have been proposed as an alternative and as a replacement (29). DADA2, an ASV pipeline, is increasingly used, and aquaculture studies using ASVs are on the rise against a large OTU-based literature (30). In swine gut work, the paper cites other studies that reported 1,261 and 1,281 OTUs. The authors' previous study reported an average of 1,178 ASVs, and this study assigned 1,850 ASVs at single-nucleotide resolution with Deblur (23). Why it matters across studies: OTUs are internally generated and analysis-specific, with no innate biological meaning. They are artifacts of a subjective dissimilarity threshold or of the reference database. So de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies, and comparisons go indirectly through databases such as Greengenes or SILVA, typically at genus level at best (28, 29). ASVs are actual sequences that represent true sample sequence variants, accurate to a single base, and directly comparable across studies. They give valid comparison of independently generated data, cross-study tractability and database-independent biological veracity, with savings in computation time and memory. They give direct comparability between studies without the need to reanalyze original data (28, 29, 30). Switching to ASVs has the potential to allow the direct comparisons across studies that are needed (28), and ASV studies could provide relevant data for meta-analysis studies (30). Caveats: OTU and ASV pipelines gave community compositions differing by 6.75% to 10.81%, more than the treatments differed, which brings doubt to comparisons across studies that used different pipelines (28). ASVs may inflate diversity (29). ASVs are less widely accepted, partly because their names are hard to use in text (28).

The papers describe a move from OTUs to ASVs. The use of OTUs as the standard unit of 16S reporting has been challenged, and ASVs have been proposed as an alternative to OTUs and as their replacement [11, 15, 17]. The ASV pipeline DADA2 is increasingly used [21], and aquaculture studies using ASVs are on the rise against a large body of OTU-based literature [23, 24]. In swine gut work, cited studies reported 1,261 and 1,281 OTUs [25, 26], while the authors' previous study reported an average of 1,178 ASVs and this study 1,850 Deblur ASVs at single-nucleotide resolution [27, 28]. The shift matters for comparisons across studies because OTUs are internally generated and analysis-specific [0], have no innate biological meaning [13], and are artifacts of a subjective dissimilarity threshold or of the reference database [12], with biases from the algorithm or the fixed identity threshold [22]. De novo OTUs therefore cannot be compared between studies, and comparisons go indirectly through databases such as Greengenes or SILVA, typically at genus level at best [1, 2, 14]. ASVs are actual sequences that represent true sample sequence variants and are directly comparable across studies [3, 22]. They enable valid comparison of independently generated ASVs [16], cross-study tractability and database-independent biological veracity [19], and direct comparability between studies without reanalysing original data [7]. Improving comparability between studies is the stated goal, and switching to ASVs has the potential to allow the direct comparisons across studies that this requires [5, 6]. ASV studies could provide relevant data for meta-analysis studies [24], where non-standardised protocols otherwise make inter-study comparisons problematic [20]. The papers also give limits. OTU and ASV pipelines yielded compositions differing by 6.75% to 10.81% [8], greater than the differences between treatments [9], which brings doubt to comparisons across studies that used different pipelines [10]. ASVs may inflate diversity [18], and ASVs are less widely accepted, partly because their names are hard to use in text [4].
expected_concepts: de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies
without the need to reanalyze original data

questions.question: What meta-conclusions can be drawn regarding the structural and informational requirements for moving One Health surveillance from theoretical frameworks to functional digital implementations?
questions.expected_answer:
Integration has two dimensions: information integration and structural integration (36). Information integration requires well-established structural integration, meaning mechanisms that ensure inter-sectoral governance of the surveillance (36).

Structural requirements: collaboration at the policy, institutional and operational levels (34); dedicated domestic resources (financial, infrastructure and personnel) and political will (34); an interdisciplinary team and its network (35); and a multisectoral coordinating body, Kenya's NASIC (45). The level of resources and the regulatory framework played a major role in setting up integrated surveillance (36).

Informational requirements: common, standardized data elements (34), or a standard minimum set of data elements (45). Data must be shared through interoperable platforms or information sharing mechanisms (34). Each component must produce quality data (36). Lack of harmonization is the main barrier to technical performance (36).

The digital implementation: an electronic information system that integrates AMR data across sectors is critical (45). Kenya's OHAMRS combines interoperability middleware with a DHIS2 web portal and can scale to other sectors (45). Its sustained use hinged on usability and the availability of skilled personnel, which is why users were trained (45).

Barriers: absent or non-interoperable electronic information systems (45), and technical (information technology systems), budgetary and institutional constraints in LMICs (36). Operationalization is still not well established, especially in low and middle-income countries (36).

The path is tiered or stepwise and tailored to each country's resources (36). Integration has a financial and social cost and does not systematically bring greater performance (36). Open gaps remain: no agreed-upon guidelines and metrics for evaluating integration (35), evidence of added value still needed (35), laboratory infrastructure funding (45), and antimicrobial consumption and use data (45).

The papers converge on two dimensions of integration, information integration and structural integration [15, 16], and integration of information requires well-established structural integration through inter-sectoral governance [17]. Structurally, successful coordinated systems share collaboration at the policy, institutional and operational levels [3], dedicated domestic resources and political will [5], organized, interconnected components including resources and infrastructures [9], interdisciplinary teams and networks [10], and a multisectoral coordinating body such as Kenya's NASIC [27]; resources and the regulatory framework played a major role in establishing integrated surveillance [13]. Informationally, One Health surveillance needs systematic collection, coordination and communication of data across sectors [0], common standardized data elements [2] or a standard minimum set of data elements [30], quality data from each component [22, 18], and harmonization, whose lack is the main barrier to technical performance [14]. Digitally, data sharing runs through interoperable platforms or information sharing mechanisms [1] and technological tools such as software and web platforms [4]; an electronic information system integrating AMR data across sectors is critical [24, 28], which Kenya's OHAMRS provides with interoperability middleware and a DHIS2 web portal [25] that can scale to other sectors [26], and its sustained use hinged on usability and skilled personnel [31]. Absent or non-interoperable electronic systems [29] and technical, budgetary and institutional constraints [19] hamper implementation, and operationalization is still not well established, especially in LMICs [12]. Integration should therefore be tiered and stepwise, tailored to each country [21, 23], since it carries costs and may not improve performance in an unsuitable context [20]. Evaluation should trace integration through information, actionable knowledge, decisions and outcomes, across data collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination [6, 8], but agreed guidelines and metrics are lacking [7] and evidence of added value is still needed [11]; data gaps, laboratory infrastructure and antimicrobial consumption and use data remain open [32, 33].

questions.question: How do spatial and host-species heterogeneities influence the persistence of viral pathogens, and what are the implications for designing sentinel surveillance systems?
questions.expected_answer:
Spatial heterogeneity: in Serengeti district, increased heterogeneity in dog vaccination coverage among villages led to increased focal rabies incidence at the same average coverage. For example, a split of 30% and 50% coverage gave 1.4 (95% CrI: 1.3-1.6) times the incidence of homogeneous 40% coverage. Outbreaks followed years when campaigns missed many villages. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell to <0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually, and short vaccination lapses did not lead to resurgence. Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district, reaching 50% of cases in 2022, show regional connectivity driving residual transmission. For HPAI, infected farms clustered near the coast and the larger rivers, epidemics can escalate by farm-to-farm transmission in poultry-dense areas, and H5N1 spread through the four major migratory bird flyways.

Host-species heterogeneity: HPAI persisted in residential wild birds and was seen in an increasing number of wild bird species. H5N1 infected mammals including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, porpoises, sea lions and dolphins. Waterfowl-adapted clade 2.3.4.4b viruses had high infectivity and transmissibility in Anseriformes compared to Galliformes. Signs differ by host: exponential increasing mortality in layers and breeder chickens, but ducks reached MR > 3 less often, and drops in feed or water intake or egg production may be their only initial signs.

Surveillance implications: monitor fine-scale coverage, because models aggregating coverage to district level failed to show impacts on incidence. Make reporting criteria different for different poultry species and age groups (the Netherlands added thresholds such as MR > 3 in chickens and 0.15% per day for two days in ducks), with early notification. Monitor viral polymorphisms after transmission from Anseriformes to Galliformes. Focus strategic surveillance on the regions and populations at highest risk. Wildlife testing is biased towards severely infected or dead animals, so identified infections are only a minority of spillovers. Sentinel surveillance in mosquitoes, birds and horses, and animal die-offs (great apes with Ebola virus), can warn of risk to humans. Surveillance design should be standardised to strengthen its sensitivity for detecting new or unusual events.

Spatial heterogeneity sustains circulation. In Serengeti district, uneven dog vaccination coverage raised focal rabies incidence at the same mean coverage (1.4 times for a 30%/50% split against homogeneous 40%), and outbreaks followed years when campaigns missed many villages [12, 13, 16, 19]. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell below 0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually, and if persistent spatial gaps are minimal, sub-optimal coverage still has major benefits [13, 18]. Incursions linked to regional connectivity reached 50% of cases in 2022 and are now a major source of residual transmission [14, 19]. For HPAI, infected farms clustered near the coast and the larger rivers, introductions can escalate through farm-to-farm transmission in poultry-dense areas, and H5N1 dispersed through migratory flyways to all provinces and territories of Canada [5, 6, 20, 21].

Host heterogeneity also matters. HPAI persisted in residential wild birds and spread to an increasing number of wild bird species and to many mammals [0, 1, 21, 22]. Wild birds will continue to be a source of novel influenza viruses [25]. Waterfowl-adapted clade 2.3.4.4b viruses had high infectivity and transmissibility in Anseriformes compared to Galliformes [7]. Clinical signs and mortality differ by host and age: ducks reached MR > 3 less often than chickens and may show only drops in feed or water intake or egg production [2, 3, 9, 10].

For surveillance design, the papers point to the following. Monitor coverage at fine scale, since district-level aggregation hid the effects [15, 17, 19]. Set reporting criteria by species and age group, as the Netherlands did with new thresholds, together with early notification under passive surveillance [4, 6, 10, 11]. Monitor viral polymorphisms after transmission from Anseriformes to Galliformes [8]. Focus strategic surveillance on the highest-risk regions and populations [26]. Allow for the bias of wildlife testing towards severe or fatal cases, which means detected infections are a minority of spillovers [23, 24]. Use sentinel surveillance in mosquitoes, birds and horses, and animal die-offs, as early warning [27, 28]. Standardise surveillance design to strengthen its sensitivity for new or unusual events [29].
expected_concepts: criteria for reporting should be different
Sentinel surveillance in mosquitoes, birds, and horses

questions.question: Evaluate how the integration of metagenomics, culturomics, and metabolomics is advancing our understanding of the 'functional' gut microbiome beyond simple taxonomic profiling.
questions.expected_answer:
No single paper combines all three methods. Each paper contributes one layer, and the papers themselves say how the layers connect.

Metagenomics (22_pig_mags): MAGs connect taxonomy with potential metabolic functions such as carbohydrate degradation and short-chain fatty acid production.
- Genes for acetate, butyrate and propionate production were found in 68.5%, 18.8% and 8.3% of MAGs.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes for arabinose oligosaccharides and mixed-linkage glucans were predicted to be the most prevalent.
- 327 MAGs carry antimicrobial resistance genes.
- 82% of MAGs belong to species that lack cultured representatives. The authors say metabolic reconstruction of these MAGs may inform strategies for cultivation, and that more known species are needed.

Culturomics (23_swine_cultivation): culture-dependent (CD) and culture-independent (CI) samples were read by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.
- CD methods detected more ASVs than CI (415, 675, 808 and 823 against 378, 482, 565 and 555 across the lactation, nursery, growing and finishing stages).
- CD methods found 244, 411, 507 and 510 ASVs that CI missed.
- 1,299 colonies were Sanger sequenced, giving 148 taxa in 28 genera. About 50% of ASVs and 75% of genera and families were culturable.
- Sequencing targeting only the V4 region underestimates diversity.
- The authors argue that CI associations and multi-omics give insights, but isolation and validation in animal models are the most convincing way to prove function. Sequencing pure cultures can expand the reference genome bank for metagenomics.

Metabolomics (24_chicken_microbiome): quantitative microbiome profiling (QMP) was paired with time-course untargeted serum metabolomics.
- The metabolomics revealed six metabolite clusters.
- mmvec predicted microbe-metabolite interactions. Foregut microbiota had more connections with serum metabolites, and gut microbes were closely related to lipid and amino acid metabolism.
- 11 metabolites came specifically from the gut microbiota, and 16 came from both host and microbiota (including L-lysin and L-tyrosine).
- The authors stress that these links rest only on association analysis and need experimental validation.

Review (26_gut_meat_quality): understanding the functions of key bacteria and the host-microbiota interaction is crucial. SCFAs from gut microbiota have positive effects on muscle and fat tissue. Butyrate-producing bacteria are linked to less fat deposition, and methanogenesis functions to more efficient fat deposition.

Metagenome-assembled genomes go beyond taxonomy by connecting species with potential metabolic functions [4, 5]: SCFA production genes in 68.5%, 18.8% and 8.3% of MAGs [0], carbohydrate degradation [1] and antimicrobial resistance [2]. 82% of these MAGs come from species that lack cultured representatives [3]. Their metabolic reconstruction may inform cultivation, and expanding the number of known species is called for [6, 7]. Culturomics read out by sequencing detects more ASVs than culture-independent profiling, and recovers ASVs that profiling misses [8, 9, 10]. It yields isolates [11, 12], shows that about 50% of ASVs are culturable [17], and together with culture-independent sequencing it expanded known richness [18]. It also shows that V4-only profiling underestimates diversity [16]. Sequencing isolates can expand the reference genome bank for metagenomics [14]. Functions suggested by culture-independent or multi-omics data are proven most convincingly by isolation and validation in animal models, which culturing makes possible [13, 15, 19, 20]. Metabolomics adds a host-facing layer. Combined with quantitative profiling, which gives a better correlation with host changes [24], it linked absolute microbiota changes to serum metabolites [21]. It revealed six metabolite clusters [22] and, through mmvec, tied microbes to lipid and amino acid metabolism [23, 25]. It also attributed 11 metabolites to the microbiota and 16 to both host and microbiota [26]. These microbe-metabolite links are associations that need experimental validation [27]. The review likewise holds that the functions of key bacteria and the host-microbiota interaction are crucial [28]. It cites SCFAs, butyrate production and methanogenesis as functional links to fat deposition and meat quality [29, 30, 31]. No single paper integrates all three approaches.
expected_concepts: connected taxonomy with potential metabolic functions
validation through pure cultures is imperative

questions.question: Assess the role of Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) in replacing or augmenting phenotypic testing for international antimicrobial resistance (AMR) monitoring.
questions.expected_answer:
Both contributing papers present WGS as augmenting phenotypic AMR testing, not replacing it. Paper 41 (Salmonella) says WGS detects AMR determinants with a high level of concordance with phenotypic tests while also assigning species, serovar and genotype. It reports a high correlation with phenotypic testing in this study and highly accurate prediction in earlier work on non-typhoidal Salmonella. It states that sequencing data complement phenotypic methods and that WGS is "not without limitations and cannot totally replace phenotypic methods". Applied to global surveillance, it can show the early emergence and spread of AMR and inform policy, and routine genomic sequencing will enable real-time monitoring of AMR genes entering the food chain. Paper 42 (Campylobacter, Thailand) calls WGS an essential tool for genotypic AMR surveillance from national to global scales (GLASS). It notes that several countries with established systems, for example the US NARMS, have started to integrate WGS. In its data, genotype matched phenotype for some drugs and not others. The gyrA T86I mutation was found in 96% of quinolone-resistant isolates and tet(O) matched tetracycline resistance at 100%. Macrolides showed a lower association: erm(B) was present in only 2 of 9 erythromycin-resistant isolates, possibly because of unexamined determinants such as L4 and L22 mutations. Paper 42 also warns that different computational pipelines may give considerably different results and that accuracy depends on how comprehensive the reference databases are. It recommends WGS-based AMR surveillance under One Health in Thailand and other low- and middle-income countries. Paper 43 does not address WGS.

Both papers present WGS as a tool for AMR surveillance beyond the national level. Paper 41 says its application to global surveillance can provide information on the early emergence and spread of AMR and inform policy [1]. Paper 42 calls it essential for genotypic AMR surveillance from national to global scales and notes that several countries, including the US through NARMS, have integrated it [7, 8, 9, 10]. Paper 41 reports high concordance and correlation between WGS-based AMR prediction and phenotypic tests [0, 4, 5]. Paper 42 finds that agreement depends on the drug class: 96% for the gyrA T86I mutation with quinolone resistance and 100% for tet(O) with tetracycline, but a lower association for macrolides, where erm(B) was present in only 2 of 9 erythromycin-resistant isolates [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. Paper 42 attributes the macrolide discordance possibly to unexamined determinants such as L4 and L22 mutations [17], and notes that predictions vary between computational pipelines and depend on the comprehensiveness of reference databases [18, 19]. Paper 41 accordingly describes WGS as complementing phenotypic methods and states that it cannot totally replace them [2, 3]. Both papers point to routine or new WGS-based monitoring: real-time monitoring of AMR genes entering the food chain [6], and WGS-based One Health surveillance in Thailand and other low- and middle-income countries [20].

questions.question: How do anthropogenic factors and agricultural industrialization facilitate the environmental spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and what does this imply for future mitigation strategies?
questions.expected_answer:
How spread is facilitated: improper management of antimicrobials, inadequate infection control, agricultural debris, pollutants in the environment and migration of people and animals infected with resistant bacteria facilitate the spread of resistance (31). Use in animals is estimated to be greater than in humans, and an estimated 50∼80% of all antibiotics are applied to animals in Africa, the European Union and United States, primarily to promote growth and prevent infection (31, 33). Growth promoters are the main reason for the large volumes used (31). Animal agriculture has shifted to widespread industrialization with intensive farming systems (40). Group antimicrobial treatment causes overuse and inconsistent dosing, and delivery through feed and water causes suboptimal dosing and downstream environmental contamination with antimicrobial residues (40).

Routes into the environment: most of the antimicrobials given are excreted, 75%–90% (31), approximately 75% on one page and 70% on another (33), and more than 70% (40). Excreted residues persist and exert selective pressure on environmental bacteria; residues alone can select resistant variants in soil and water (40, 31). Manure used as fertilizer increases resistant bacteria and resistance genes in the environment and can transfer ARGs to soil, crops and then the human microbiome; ARGs in manured soil are approximately 28,000 times higher than in un-manured soil (33, 40). Farm wastewater, runoff, contaminated water sources and farm waste, debris and pollutants spread resistance and create new resistance reservoirs (33, 40). ARGs were dispersed from farms through the air to a distance of 10 km (33). Simple waste treatments such as anaerobic digesters or lagoons did not effectively remove antibiotics (33).

Implications for mitigation: reduce unnecessary use of antimicrobials in agriculture and their dissemination to the environment, and use them only as a treatment, rarely for prophylaxis and never as growth promoters (31). Restricting antibiotic application is closely related to a decrease in ARB and ARGs (33), and growth-promoter bans gave significant decreases in consumption but have yet to reach many LMICs (40). Give more attention to residues in animal waste; develop novel technologies (nanotechnology, anaerobic digestion, biochar composting), alternatives to antibiotics (herbal plant extracts, probiotics, vaccines) and antibiotic administration (33). Control and monitor resistant bacteria spreading to the environment and integrate surveillance of humans, food products, farm animals, wildlife and ecosystems (31, 40). Better prevent and manage zoonoses, develop novel therapies, take “multi-pronged” measures across human, animal and environmental sectors, and systematically reconsider animal agricultural practices (40).

All three reviews tie the environmental spread of AMR to how humans use antimicrobials in agriculture. Paper 31 names mismanagement, inadequate infection control, agricultural debris, environmental pollutants and migration of infected people and animals as facilitating factors [0, 1], and paper 33 names anthropogenic activities as a contamination source in one river study [19]. Animal use exceeds human use, mainly for growth promotion and prevention [2, 6, 12]. Paper 40 places this within the industrialization of animal agriculture, which raised production efficiency but drastically impacted the environment [24, 25, 29]. Its intensive systems rely on group treatment and feed or water delivery, causing overuse, inconsistent or suboptimal dosing and downstream contamination with residues [26, 30]. Most antimicrobials given are excreted: 75%–90% in paper 31, approximately 75% or 70% in paper 33 and more than 70% in paper 40 [9, 13, 17, 37]. Excreted residues persist and select for resistance in environmental bacteria, soil and water [5, 27, 38], and residues, resistant bacteria and resistance genes circulate in the ecosystem and reach humans and animals [28]. Manure fertilization increases resistant bacteria and ARGs in soil, approximately 28,000-fold in manured soil, and can pass them to crops and the human microbiome [3, 16, 34, 35]. Wastewater, runoff, contaminated water sources and farm waste create new resistance reservoirs [20, 33, 36, 43], ARGs dispersed through the air to 10 km [14], aquaculture residues remain in aquatic environments [4], and simple waste treatments did not effectively remove antibiotics [15]. For mitigation, the papers call for reducing unnecessary agricultural use and the load reaching the environment [7, 18, 21], using antimicrobials only as treatment and never as growth promoters [8, 10], supported by the link between restricting use and fewer ARB and ARGs and by the fall in consumption after growth-promoter bans, which have yet to reach many LMICs [22, 31, 32]. They also propose waste-treatment technologies, alternatives to antibiotics and antibiotic administration [23], control and monitoring of environmental spread with integrated surveillance [11, 40], zoonosis prevention and novel therapies to cut use [39, 42], and multi-sector measures with a systematic reconsideration of animal agricultural practices [41, 44].

questions.question: What collective evidence exists regarding the importance of 'viewpoint' and 'location' in the design of next-generation sequencing experiments, from chromosome conformation to rumen sampling?
questions.expected_answer:
4C-seq (50_4cseq_protocol): the viewpoint fragment should overlap the site to be analyzed or lie within <1 kb of it. A non-blind viewpoint with a fragment end >200 bp is preferred. Distance from the viewpoint decides reproducibility. Far-cis (>5 MB) and inter-chromosomal contacts are generally not reproducible between replicates, while near-cis contacts (<1 Mb) should be quantitatively reproducible. Independent of the viewpoint's genomic location, a successful experiment shows strong enrichment of contacts flanking the viewpoint, and preferably >60% of reads map to the cis chromosome, most within 1 Mb of the viewpoint.
Gut microbiome sampling (29_16s_best_practices): choosing the sample location is an essential, and commonly complicated, design step. It must rest on the hypothesis and/or objective(s) and on the physiology of the host species and/or target tissue. The rumen microbiome is distinct from the lower GIT, so fecal sampling should not typically be considered a proxy for the ruminal microbiome. In poultry, feces from 163 birds had similar bacteria to the ceca but not in the same relative abundances. Location within poultry houses also matters, and a small pilot study answers many questions on sampling location.
21_livestock_gut_microbiome_review reports marked heterogeneity across GIT locations (sheep, cattle, goats), GIT location as a source of variation in pig microbial diversity, location-specific microbial hosts, and significant differences in predicted metagenomic profiles among GIT locations in dairy cows, sheep, goats and pigs.
25_dairy_cow_feed only describes its own sampling: rumen fluid taken with an orogastric tube on a single day, cows between 66 and 105 DIM.

In 4C-seq, the viewpoint must overlap the site to be analyzed or lie within <1 kb of it, and a non-blind fragment with a fragment end >200 bp is preferred [0, 1, 2, 3]. Distance from the viewpoint governs reproducibility: far-cis (>5 MB) contacts are generally not reproducible between replicates, while near-cis (<1 Mb) contacts should be quantitatively reproducible [4, 5]. Independent of the viewpoint's genomic location, success is judged by strong enrichment of flanking contacts, preferably >60% of reads on the cis chromosome [6, 7]. In gut microbiome 16S studies, choosing the sample location is an essential and commonly complicated design step that must follow the hypothesis and the host's physiology [8, 14, 15], and a small pilot study answers many questions on sampling location [17]. Easily accessible samples may not represent the location of interest [13]: the rumen microbiome is distinct from the lower GIT and intestine, so feces should not typically be a proxy for the rumen [9, 10], fecal and cecal microbiota in poultry shared bacteria but not relative abundances [11, 12], and location within poultry houses also matters [16]. Livestock studies found heterogeneity, location-specific microbial hosts and different predicted metagenomic profiles across GIT locations in cattle, sheep, goats and pigs [18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23]. One dairy study sampled rumen fluid directly, with an orogastric tube [24, 25].
expected_concepts: near-cis contacts (<1 Mb from the viewpoint)
fecal sampling should not typically be considered as a proxy
based upon the hypothesis and/or objective(s)
marked heterogeneity across different GIT locations

questions.question: The fastp paper states that fastp requires separate tools for adapter trimming and quality filtering, processing data in multiple sequential passes. Is this accurate?
questions.expected_answer: No. The fastp paper says the opposite. fastp is an all-in-one FASTQ preprocessor. It can perform quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering, per-read quality pruning and many other operations with a single scan of the FASTQ data. The paper describes the separate-tool approach as past practice: a different tool for each operation (for example FASTQC, Cutadapt and Trimmomatic), with the data read and loaded multiple times. It says this made preprocessing slow and I/O inefficient. fastp includes most features of FASTQC, Cutadapt, Trimmomatic and AfterQC, and runs 2–5 times faster than any of them alone.
expected_concepts: single scan of the FASTQ data
a different tool is used for each operation
In the past, multiple tools were employed

questions.question: According to the DESeq2 paper, the method uses raw read counts without any normalization or variance stabilization. Is this true?
questions.expected_answer: No. In DESeq2 the mean of each gene's counts is scaled by a normalization factor (μij = sijqij). The size factors account for differences in sequencing depth between samples and are estimated by default with the median-of-ratios method; gene-specific normalization factors can be supplied instead. The package also provides the regularized logarithm transformation (rlog) and the VST. After the rlog, gene variances are stabilized (approximately the same, or homoskedastic). The only true part of the claim is that the differential expression inference employs the raw counts, not transformed data. Normalization still enters that inference through the size factors in the model.
expected_concepts: differences in sequencing depth between samples
Both the rlog transformation and the VST
employs the raw counts, not transformed data

questions.question: The Snakemake paper describes a system that uses a simple first-come-first-served job queue without any optimization of task scheduling. Is this correct?
questions.expected_answer: No. The paper says Snakemake solves the scheduling problem with a mixed integer linear program (MILP). It solves this problem at the beginning of the workflow execution and whenever a job has finished and new jobs become pending. The aim is to select the subset of pending jobs that leads to an efficient execution of the workflow without exceeding the given resources, such as hard drive space, I/O capacity and CPU cores. The maximization optimizes four criteria in lexicographical order: prefer jobs with high priority, maximize the number of used cores (parallelization), delete existing temporary files as soon as possible, and reduce the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass. Only the first releases of Snakemake used a greedy scheduler. The current implementation solves a MILP to get more efficient schedules.
expected_concepts: maximize the number of used cores
first releases of Snakemake used a greedy scheduler

questions.question: The nf-core framework paper reports that switching from BAM to CRAM format increased storage requirements by 65%. Is this finding correct?
questions.expected_answer: No. The paper reports the opposite: switching from BAM to CRAM reduced storage. Work-directory storage for pre-processing dropped by 65%, from 170.4 TB (BAM) to 59.7 TB (CRAM). The paper also describes this as reducing storage requirements by two-thirds. What increased was memory: a 34% increase in memory usage (higher memory requirements).

questions.question: According to the Salmon paper, transcript quantification is performed using traditional full alignment of reads to the reference genome. Is this accurate?
questions.expected_answer: No. The Salmon paper says Salmon quantifies abundance via a built-in, ultra-fast read-mapping procedure (quasi-mapping), a lightweight mapping procedure. In quasi-mapping mode it takes as input an index of the transcriptome and raw, unaligned reads and performs quantification directly without generating any intermediate alignment files; quasi-mapping is faster than traditional alignment. The paper describes traditional quantification algorithms that use alignments of reads to the genome or transcriptome as requiring significant computational resources. Salmon can alternatively use pre-computed alignments provided in SAM or BAM format (tested as "Salmon(a)" with Bowtie2 alignments as input).
expected_concepts: without generating any intermediate alignment files
pre-computed alignments provided in SAM or BAM format

questions.question: The LSD Nepal paper reports that pregnant cows had a significantly lower risk of LSD infection compared to non-pregnant cattle. Is this correct?
questions.expected_answer: No. The paper reports the opposite. Pregnant cows were counted in the dry cattle group, and that group was the most affected, with the highest morbidity: 47.62% (90 of 189), against 28.02% overall. The authors say this matches earlier reports of higher disease incidence in pregnant and young cows. The paper does not analyse pregnant cows separately, and pregnancy is not one of the risk-factor variables it tests, so it reports no significant result for pregnancy in either direction.

questions.question: The HPAI Netherlands paper found that clinical signs of avian influenza are identical across all poultry species, with no species-dependent differences. Is this true?
questions.expected_answer: No. The paper found species-dependent differences in clinical signs. Neurological, locomotor and reproductive tract signs were often observed in ducks, whereas laying- and meat-type poultry more often showed mucosal membrane and skin signs, including cyanosis and hemorrhagic conjunctiva. Nervous and locomotor signs were seen on 67.7% of duck farms (66.7% in Table 5), against 48.4% of meat-type and 15.0% of layer-type poultry (p < 0.001). Mucosal membrane and skin signs were seen in 55.0% of layer-type and 67.8% of meat-type poultry, against only 4.7% of duck farms (p < 0.001). Respiratory signs were seen in 61.3% of meat-type poultry, 37.5% of layers and 23.8% of ducks (p = 0.02). Reproductive tract signs were seen in 100% of ducks, against 19.4% of layer-type and 28.6% of meat-type poultry (p < 0.001). Fisher's exact tests found these four differences significant. Only signs of general disease and gastrointestinal signs showed no difference between poultry types. The authors conclude that reporting criteria should be different for different poultry species and age groups.

questions.question: According to the MultiQC paper, the tool can only process output from a single bioinformatics tool at a time and does not support aggregation across tools. Is this correct?
questions.expected_answer: No. The MultiQC paper says the opposite. MultiQC creates a single report visualising output from multiple tools across many samples. At the time of writing it supported 22 common bioinformatics tools, including aligners, processing tools and QC programs. Its general statistics table gathers metrics from a number of different tools for each sample, and MultiQC can function as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines.
expected_concepts: metrics from a number of different tools

questions.question: The rabies Tanzania paper concludes that vaccination campaigns in the Serengeti achieved uniform coverage across all areas, completely eliminating spatial heterogeneity. Is this accurate?
questions.expected_answer: No. The paper does not report uniform coverage or the elimination of spatial heterogeneity. Village campaign coverage varied from 0.3-98% (mean 31%), and only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target. Coverage heterogeneity was higher in 2007 and 2011-2013. Those peaks followed multi-year periods when groups of villages in the northwest were not vaccinated. Once district-wide vaccination was made routine, heterogeneity was reduced, and it was relatively low from 2019-2022. Groups of villages were still not vaccinated in 2018 and 2021, and later campaigns were late and incomplete. The paper concludes that heterogeneity in coverage was reduced, not eliminated, and that incidence then declined to low levels (<0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually).
expected_concepts: relatively low levels of coverage heterogeneity
